text:
THE ARCHITECTURE OF SURVIVAL

The reality of her life unfolds in a cramped, windowless room somewhere in the labyrinth of Pattaya, far removed from the pristine condos rented by the men she meets. There is only a spinning floor fan pushing warm air across a thin mattress on the floor, a damp towel hanging from a solitary nail, and a plastic water bottle sitting on a windowsill that faces a blank concrete wall. She sits with her knees pulled tightly to her chest, her face illuminated only by the glow of a cheap smartphone. On the screen, two little girls—no older than four and two—are laughing and waving at the camera. They have no idea where their mother is or what she actually does; they only know the comforting sound of her voice through the tinny speaker. She watches them without shedding a single tear and without cracking a smile. She simply watches, turns the screen off, sits in the heavy silence, and then turns it back on again.

This isn't another tragic, romanticized tale of a naive village girl seduced by the bright lights of the big city. It is the cold, calculated reality of a twenty-two-year-old mother who was forced to make an agonizing choice because the only alternative was watching her children starve. She isn't a passive victim of circumstance, but a pragmatist executing a necessary, brutal decision. Back in her village in Isaan, rice is treated as a currency and generational debt is the baseline condition of existence. She already tried the socially acceptable route, spending her days on a sweltering factory floor for twelve hours at a time, earning a meager three hundred baht a day. That kind of money doesn't even cover baby formula, let alone secure a future. When someone finally told her that she could earn real money in Pattaya, they didn't promise her it would be easy or glamorous. They just told her it was possible. So she packed her bags.

Her nightly routine on the neon grid is an exercise in profound emotional detachment. When she sits in the bar, flashing a practiced smile and asking tourists where they are from, she is simply running a script. She listens to stories she couldn't care less about, laughs at punchlines she has heard a thousand times, and holds the hands of men she feels absolutely nothing for. She drinks the sugary lady drinks not out of thirst, but because every glass represents a commission, and every commission is another transfer sent back home. When she leaves with a client, she simply turns off the switch in her head, dissociates from the physical reality, and does exactly what is required. She doesn't keep a tally of the men. She only counts the nights left in the month, calculating exactly how much she needs to hit her target so she can eventually escape back to her real life.

It is incredibly easy, and deeply insulting, for outsiders to pity her. She doesn't need sympathy, and she certainly isn't selling her soul. She is a mother doing whatever it takes to feed her daughters. She knows perfectly well how the expats judge her, what the neighbors in her village whisper behind her back, and how polite society views her profession. She knows all of it, yet she walks into that bar every single night because her pride is entirely secondary to her children's survival. It isn't some beautiful, poetic sacrifice; it is just grueling, relentless, humiliating work.

She refuses to cry herself to sleep because breaking down is a luxury she simply cannot afford. If she shatters, she can't work, and if she doesn't work, her family doesn't eat. Instead, she actively erases the clients from her memory the second they leave the room. The only images she allows her mind to retain are the faces of her girls. She doesn't hate herself, because self-hatred requires the kind of time and emotional energy she doesn't possess. Her entire existence is narrowed down to a singular, desperate cycle: earn, transfer, return, and hug.

The hardest moment of her life wasn't walking into a bar, but sitting on the night bus leaving her province. She remembers staring blankly out the window, refusing to look back at her daughters standing in the dirt. She knew that if she looked back, she would have stayed, and poverty would have slowly consumed them all. Her youngest daughter had held her hand right before she boarded, genuinely believing her mother was just going to a normal job. As the bus pulled away, she held her breath, knowing that if she let a single tear fall, she would demand the driver stop the bus, rendering the entire agonizing ordeal meaningless.

She doesn't ask the world for understanding or forgiveness. She only ever offers one devastating explanation for her life: "I didn't want to work like this. If I had a choice, who would want to be looked down upon?" It is a question that requires no answer, because the reality is that nobody wants this life, but someone had to step up and ensure those two little girls survived.

As morning breaks, she is back in her suffocating room. She watches the video of her daughters one last time before the screen goes dark. She takes a shower, lies down on the mattress, and closes her eyes. In just a few hours, the cycle will begin again. She will put on her makeup, step out into the neon glare, and smile as if she doesn't have a care in the world.

text:
JOHNSTON, Iowa – Johnston’s school board just voted down a free, important gift that other Iowa districts had no problem taking. 

On September 28, the Johnston Community School District board rejected pocket U.S. Constitutions for every 8th grader. The vote was 5-1-1. Jennifer Chamberland, Soneeta Mangra-Dutcher, Jason Arnold, Lya Williams, and Kaycee Schippers voted to refuse the donation. Rex Davidson voted to accept it. Justin Smith abstained. Mangra-Dutcher made the motion, and Williams seconded it. 

About 35 to 45 people showed up in support. 8 residents signed up to speak. 6 backed the Constitutions, and 2 did not. The booklets would’ve cost the district nothing. They were offered for Constitution Day and classroom use. Nearby districts gladly accepted the same kind of donation. Johnston 8th graders will not get one. 

Board talk and public comment focused on branding tied to the 917 Society, a right-wing organization, instead of the words in the Constitution. Fathers for Faith & Freedom called it a rejection of civic education, and of the parents in the room. Founder Steven Hibbs said school board elections exist for nights like this.

The 917 Society exists to put a small Constitution in 8th graders’ hands at no charge. While other Iowa districts did not treat that as a crisis, Johnston’s board did. Davidson was the only member willing to take the gift. Fathers for Faith & Freedom thanked him and told residents to remember the roll call. 

If Johnston will not put the U.S. Constitution in an American 8th grader’s backpack for free, voters should probably put new names on the board.

{{Possibly}} A working sketch of Bobby Grow’s Evangelical Calvinism, especially vicarious humanity:

Bobby Grow’s published books are the two volumes co-edited with Myk Habets: Evangelical Calvinism: Essays Resourcing the Continuing Reformation of the Church (2012) and Evangelical Calvinism, Volume 2: Dogmatics and Devotion (2017). The second volume is organized around the vicarious ministry of Christ. The same program is developed at length on his blog and in the fifteen theses that introduce the project.

The first move is methodological. Grow argues that many modern debates about salvation—classical Calvinism versus Arminianism, sovereignty versus free will, limited versus general atonement—begin in the wrong place. They start from soteriology, usually inside what he calls a Latin or Augustinian frame, and then try to fit Christ into that frame. He wants the order reversed. Thinking should begin with Christology, specifically with the hypostatic union: the place where Almighty God and humanity “kiss.” 

Jesus is not an instrument executing a prior decree. He is the electing God and the elected human in one person. Election, atonement, faith, and human agency are then read from that center rather than from an abstract mass of humanity standing before an abstract will of God.

That center is the vicarious humanity of Christ. 

The Son assumes real human nature, not a generic or partial humanity, and in that nature lives the whole human response to the Father: faith, repentance, obedience, worship, and intercession. The point is not only that Christ dies instead of us, but that Christ is human for us. Our humanity has its true ground in his recreated, resurrected humanity. Grow often puts this in Athanasian rather than Augustinian terms: salvation is ontological and participatory before it is merely juridical. God does not first set up a contract and then apply its benefits to selected individuals. God gives himself. Grace is “all the way down.” There is no independent natural platform from which a fallen person first decides to join God.

From this follow two claims that must be held together.

First, Christ’s work is for all humanity. Thesis 11 states that Christ lived, died, and rose again for all, so Evangelical Calvinism affirms universal atonement. Grow follows Torrance here: this is a finished work, not a mere possibility. By the incarnation there is a “carnal” or objective union of the Son with humanity as such. 

Election is christologically conditioned: humanity is elect in the Son’s assumption of human nature, not by an absolute decree that first splits the human race into two classes. The gospel can therefore be preached as already true of the hearer: Christ has bound himself to you before and apart from your believing.

Second, this is not universalism. Thesis 12 is explicit. Universal redemption does not entail that all will finally be saved. Grow distinguishes the objective inclusion of humanity in Christ from the subjective, Spirit-given realization of that inclusion. “Spiritual union” is a sharing in the one union already wrought in Jesus. Faith is not an independent human contribution that completes an incomplete work. It is the Spirit enabling a person to echo Christ’s own Yes to the Father—often with appeal to *pistis *Christou as the faith of Christ. Baptism and conversion, on this telling, are a living into a reality that is already true, not the first creation of that reality.

Rejection remains real. Grow can say that some “opt out,” refuse the grace given in Christ, and so condemn themselves. He cites Torrance to the effect that Christ has already made the person his own, and that even if someone refuses him and damns himself, that love does not cease. The refusal does not undo the incarnation or turn Christ’s Yes into a No. It is a contradiction of what God has done, and that contradiction becomes its own judgment.

What this is not, on Grow’s own terms, is a symmetric libertarian choice to “stay or leave,” as if the human will stood outside the work of Christ and then selected one of two equal options. He affirms something like total inability: fallen humanity is *incurvatus *in *se and cannot move toward God from an abstract free will. The initiative is Christ’s. Our Yes is participation in his Yes. Our No is possible, tragic, and self-condemning, but it is not the same kind of act as a first decision to join God. 

Grow thinks the usual dilemma—either God irresistibly saves the elect, or the human will is the decisive co-cause—still belongs to the older causal and contractual grammar. He wants agency relocated inside the vicarious humanity of the Son and the ministry of the Spirit, rather than treated as a rival sovereignty.
The resulting picture can be summarized without slogans:

•God has already said Yes to humanity in the incarnate Son.
•All humanity is objectively included in that Yes; redemption is not a limited offer waiting to be activated by the right kind of decision.
•No one is saved apart from personal faith, but that faith is a sharing in Christ’s own response, not a climb from outside into God’s favor.
•Final exclusion is possible as refusal of a gift already given, not as proof that Christ never represented that person.
•The “limit” of the atonement is not a restricted list of individuals chosen in a decree. It is the vicarious humanity of Jesus himself: the One for the many.

That is the framework Grow is gesturing toward when he tells interlocutors that starting from soteriology keeps Calvinists and non-Calvinists at loggerheads, and that the place to begin is the hypostatic union. As a description of what he is saying, this seems to be the shape.

"Tennessee Execution Halted After Inmate Remains Alive Following 2 Doses"

➡️ Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike remained alive & snoring more than 40 minutes after executioners administered two full doses of lethal injection chemicals at 8:26 p.m. local time, according to statement details released by her defense team.

➡️ State prison authorities escorting media witnesses away from the execution facility in Nashville refused to offer immediate public details regarding the unexpected delay or the status of the procedure, while state corrections officials noted they could not clarify what occurred inside the chamber.

➡️ The botched execution attempt followed a chaotic legal sequence wherein the United States Supreme Court overturned a last-minute federal appeals court stay that had briefly halted the lethal injection process earlier in the day.

➡️ Pike, who was convicted of first-degree murder for a 1995 crime committed at age 18, stands as the only woman on death row in Tennessee & was set to become the first female executed by the state in over 200 years.

➡️ Defense attorneys & human rights advocates had previously filed urgent appeals citing unconsidered childhood trauma, severe mental illness, & procedural issues regarding the state's severe execution chemical protocols.

text:
Cop's predator activities gets exposed and he incriminates 3 others as part of his ring including a district attorney. 

A single 911 call from a Wisconsin truck stop restroom ended up blowing the lid off a statewide ring of predators, bringing down an active deputy, a former county prosecutor, and a local business owner.

​Kenosha County detectives cornered Racine County Sheriff’s Deputy Preston Kite while he was still sitting in full uniform. A patron had reported him exposing himself inside a stall at the Petro Travel Plaza in Sturtevant.

​From the opening minutes of the bodycam interrogation, Kite scrambled to spin a defensive narrative. He admitted to detectives that he was using the cruising app Sniffies while on duty, claiming he had arranged a consensual hookup in the stall.

 He insisted that the other man had simply panicked upon spotting his uniform through the door crack, apologized, and bolted after which the man allegedly blocked him, wiping the chat history.

​Detectives immediately pressed the inconsistencies. When surveillance footage caught Kite making a brisk, near-sprint exit out of the plaza rather than the casual stroll he described, his story began unraveling. He offered bizarre, self-deprecating rationalization, telling the interviewing investigators that people call him "Blue" because he "talks a big game and gets blue b@lls," claiming he only ever "likes to watch" and never actually goes through with meetups.

He even pleaded with the detectives as fellow law enforcement officers to keep the matter quiet, offering full cooperation in exchange for discretion.
​Then investigators checked his phone.
​When detectives scrolled through his gallery, they spotted dozens of hidden recordings of unsuspecting men using public restrooms,including footage Kite took during airport layovers.

Kite stammered through a series of wild excuses: first claiming they were sent by an unnamed college friend back in 2015, then suggesting they were screen recordings from Snapchat, and finally claiming people staged fake bathroom recordings for fun.

​What started as illicit voyeurism turned exponentially darker once forensic analysts performed an extraction on his device and cracked encrypted apps like Session.

Detectives uncovered extensive stashes of Child Sexu@l Abuse Materi@l (CSAM), proof that Kite had filmed assaults against a family friend’s young child whom he had offered to babysit, evidence of organized animal abuse, and the chilling revelation that Kite had asked supervisors how to join the Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) task force.

​The digital forensic trail from his phone ripped open an entire network, leading authorities directly to prominent co-conspirators and securing four arrests and  major convictions:

​ Ex-Deputy Preston Kite: Convicted of 21 felonies across two cases; sentenced to 55 years in state prison plus 35 years of extended supervision.

 Adam Westbrook: A former Milwaukee County Assistant District Attorney and municipal attorney; sentenced to 10 years in federal prison for distributing CSAM.

 Jacob Boudreau: A Menasha pet grooming salon owner; sentenced to 15 years in prison for possessing abuse material and animal mistreatment.

 Noah Thiel: Boudreau’s former roommate; sentenced to 1 year in county jail followed by 3 years of probation.

​Watching Kite sit in his patrol vest attempting to smooth-talk detectives, completely unaware that his phone was about to dismantle his entire life and send four men to prison, makes this one of the most chilling interrogation tapes on record. His carelessness helped get four predators off the street.

Tel Megiddo (from Hebrew: תל מגידו; Arabic: تل المتسلم, Tell el-Muteselim) is the site of the ancient city of Megiddo (/məˈɡɪdoʊ/; Hebrew: מגידו; Greek: Μεγιδδώ), the remains of which form a tell or archaeological mound, situated in northern Israel at the western edge of the Jezreel Valley. During the Bronze Age, Megiddo was an important Canaanite city-state, and in the Iron Age, it became a royal city in the Kingdom of Israel. The site is renowned for its historical, geographical, and theological significance, especially under its Greek name Armageddon (Ἁρμαγεδών), which appears once in the Koine Greek New Testament in Revelation 16:16.

Excavations have unearthed 20 strata of ruins since the Neolithic phase, indicating a long settlement period.[1] Occupied continuously from the early Bronze Age (c. 3000 BCE) to the Persian period (c. 332 BCE), Megiddo was strategically located at the crossroads of major ancient trade routes, making it a key center for trade, politics, and military affairs. Excavations have uncovered impressive fortifications, including massive city walls and gates, as well as palaces, temples, residential buildings, and a sophisticated water system. The site is protected as Megiddo National Park and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.[2]

Assyrian period
Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria conquered Megiddo in 732 BCE, turning it to the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire's province of Magiddu.[16] Hoshea (c. 732–721 BCE), the last king of the Israelite Northern Kingdom, was vassal to Tiglath-Pileser III. The site was rebuilt as an administrative center for Tiglath-Pileser III's occupation of Samaria.

Egyptian period
In 609 BCE, Megiddo was conquered by Egyptians under Necho II, during the Battle of Megiddo.

Babylonian period
Its importance soon dwindled, and it was thought as finally abandoned around 586 BCE.[64] Since that time it would have remained uninhabited, preserving ruins pre-dating 586 BCE without settlements ever disturbing them. Archaeologist Eric Cline considers that Tel Megiddo came to an end later, around 350 BCE, during Achaemenid times.[1] Then, the town of al-Lajjun, not to be confused with the al-Lajjun archaeological site in Jordan, was built up near to the site, but without inhabiting or disturbing its remains.

Roman and Byzantine periods
During the Roman and Byzantine periods, while the site was part of the provinces of Syria Palaestina (136-390) and Palaestina Secunda (390-638), there were three settlements in the vicinity of the tell: the Jewish village of Kefar 'Othnay (Caparcotna in Latin or Kaperkotnei in Greek); Legio, the Roman military camp of the Legio VI Ferrata ('6th "Ironclad" Legion'); and later, in the 4th and 5th centuries during Byzantine rule, a polis named Maximianopolis.[65] J. C. Howry, processing the results of a surface reconnaissance survey in 2019 which had used LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) technology to obtain enhanced images of the ground, places Maximianopolis northwest of the tell, Legio south-southeast of it, and a village which grew next to the legion camp for which it provided services (the future Arab village of Lejjun), southwest of the tell.[66] Adams, David and Tepper (2014) write that the VIth Legion was deployed to the country sometime between 100 and 132, and was stationed there through most of the 3rd century;[65] Howry (2020) places it at Legio between 192 and 316.[66]

Megiddo church
The Megiddo church is next to Megiddo Junction, inside the precinct of the Megiddo Prison. It was built within the ancient city of Legio. It is believed to date to the 3rd century, making it one of the oldest Christian churches in the world. It was a few hundred yards from the Roman base camp of Legio VI Ferrata. A centurion donated one of the mosaics found in the church.[67]

Modern period
Megiddo is south of Kibbutz Megiddo by 1 kilometre (0.62 mi). Today,it lies at the northern entrance to Wadi Ara, an important mountain pass connecting the Jezreel Valley within Israel's coastal plain.[68]

In 1964, during Pope Paul VI's visit to the Holy Land, Megiddo was the site where he met with dignitaries, including President Zalman Shazar and the Prime Minister Levi Eshkol.[69]

Battles
Famous battles include:
Battle of Megiddo (15th century BCE): fought between the armies of the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III and a large Canaanite coalition led by the rulers of Megiddo and Kadesh.
Battle of Megiddo (609 BCE): fought between Necho II, pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt, and the Kingdom of Judah, during which King Josiah fell.
Battle of Megiddo (1918): fought during World War I between Allied troops, led by General Edmund Allenby and the defending Ottoman army.

What is the Battle of Armageddon?
@gotquestions 
Answer
The word Armageddon is used generically today to refer to any type of catastrophic conflict, especially if it’s seen as likely to result in widespread destruction or the annihilation of human life. In the Bible, Armageddon refers to a climactic future battle between God and the forces of evil, as recorded in the book of Revelation. The word ultimately comes from the Hebrew word Har-Magedone, which means “Mount Megiddo,” the predicted location of the battle.

Revelation 16:12–16 is the record of what will happen toward the end of the tribulation, when an angel pours out the sixth bowl judgment on the earth. The word Armageddon makes its only appearance in the Bible in this passage:

“The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river Euphrates, and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings from the East. Then I saw three impure spirits that looked like frogs; they came out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet. They are demonic spirits that perform signs, and they go out to the kings of the whole world, to gather them for the battle on the great day of God Almighty. . . . Then they gathered the kings together to the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.”

In Revelation 19:11–20, a final battle occurs at Christ’s second coming as the conquering Christ defeats the forces of the Antichrist. We take this to be a description of the Battle of Armageddon mentioned in Revelation 19:

“I saw heaven standing open and there before me was a white horse, whose rider is called Faithful and True. With justice he judges and wages war. His eyes are like blazing fire, and on his head are many crowns. He has a name written on him that no one knows but he himself. He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and his name is the Word of God. The armies of heaven were following him, riding on white horses and dressed in fine linen, white and clean. Coming out of his mouth is a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations. ‘He will rule them with an iron scepter.’ He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty. On his robe and on his thigh he has this name written: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.

“And I saw an angel standing in the sun, who cried in a loud voice to all the birds flying in midair, ‘Come, gather together for the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings, generals, and the mighty, of horses and their riders, and the flesh of all people, free and slave, great and small.’

“Then I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered together to wage war against the rider on the horse and his army. But the beast was captured, and with it the false prophet who had performed the signs on its behalf. With these signs he had deluded those who had received the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. The two of them were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur. The rest were killed with the sword coming out of the mouth of the rider on the horse, and all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh.”

The exact location of Armageddon is unclear because there is no mountain called Meggido. However, since Har can also mean “hill,” the most likely location is the hill country surrounding the plain of Meggido, some sixty miles north of Jerusalem. Throughout history, armies have fought countless battles in that region: Egyptians, Assyrians, Greeks, Romans, and Crusaders fought in Megiddo, as well as the armies of Napoleon. Megiddo was the site of battles during World War I and the Arab-Israeli War of 1948 (Weintraub, P., “Rewriting Tel Megiddo’s Violent History,” Discover, Sep 30, 2015). In the future, the plain of Megiddo and the nearby plain of Esdraelon will also be the focal point for the battle of Armageddon.

The plain of Megiddo, or Armageddon, was famous for two great victories in Israel’s history: 1) Barak’s victory over the Canaanites (Judges 4:15) and 2) Gideon’s victory over the Midianites (Judges 7). Armageddon was also the site of two great tragedies: 1) the death of Saul and his sons (1 Samuel 31:8) and 2) the death of King Josiah (2 Kings 23:29–30; 2 Chronicles 35:22).

According to the futurist interpretation of Revelation, which is our view, the Battle of Armageddon will be a real battle in the future, near the end of the tribulation. Demonic influences will cause the kings of the earth to gather their armies for an all-out assault on Jerusalem. The Antichrist will be leading the charge (Revelation 16:13–16). Jesus Christ will return to earth with the armies of heaven (Matthew 25:31; Revelation 19:14); His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4); He will defeat the forces of evil (Revelation 19:15–16); He will cast the Antichrist and the false prophet into the lake of fire (Revelation 19:20); He will bind Satan; and He will set up His kingdom on earth for 1,000 years (Revelation 20:1–6). At Armageddon the Lord Jesus Christ “treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty” (Revelation 19:15), and all things will be made right.

🗞️ White House Super Intelligence Accord, DeepMind SynthID Bio, and Meta's Custom Silicon Ramp

White House Inks 'Super Intelligence Accord' with Big Tech Titans as Executive Order Rebrands AI
On September 29, 2026, the White House established a monumental shift in national technology policy as President Donald Trump issued an executive order titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence" and signed the landmark ["White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities"](https://t.co/zSS9CO46kv) alongside the chief executives of six dominant AI powerhouses. Flanked by Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (OpenAI), Elon Musk (xAI), and Jensen Huang (Nvidia), the administration formally directed all executive departments and federal agencies to phase out the terms "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" across non-statutory federal correspondence, policy documentation, and public materials, replacing them with "Super Intelligence" and "SI." While the directive currently anchors its legal scope to the statutory definition of artificial intelligence under 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3), it mandates that the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology draft a permanent, statutory legal definition for "Super Intelligence" within 60 days to reflect models approaching autonomous cognitive parity.

The accompanying voluntary accord outlines a four-tier corporate governance and risk-mitigation framework designed to preempt federal legislative intervention: internal controls tracking catastrophic cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats; dedicated internal verification teams; independent third-party audits; and mandatory board-level oversight committees empowered to halt deployment. President Trump characterized the accord as "morally binding" and a decisive shield against overly restrictive federal legislation, arguing that American technological leadership depends on competitive self-governance rather than statutory paralysis. However, the announcement triggered intense debate across X and communities like r/technology and r/artificial. Readers and civil liberties advocates questioned whether voluntary commitments offer any genuine legal accountability, with critics arguing that a non-enforceable accord amounts to regulatory capture that insulates the big six from binding safety standards similar to the European Union's statutory regime. Further viral scrutiny erupted over an uncorrected typo in the official signing document designating the presidency of the "Unites States," which skeptics seized upon to question the rigor of executive oversight. Despite the political friction, industry leaders like Jensen Huang underscored that voluntary independent auditing represents the only operational mechanism capable of moving at the speed of frontier silicon deployment.

text:
I think it's kind of a shame the tech world moved away from protocols and generalized clients like we have with browsers and email clients.

For a while, we had an endless number of instant messaging protocols with 3rd party clients, until companies needed more sandboxed / unified experiences.

It seems like most SaaS products have only existed because they can 1) create a familiar product with interopability both within and across companies, and 2) they offer compliance and uptime guarantees that customers don't want to deal with if they chose a self-hosted solution instead.

But somehow all this time, browsers and email clients managed to stay agnostic, while other software didn't.

Even music players went from general-purpose MP3 / M4A players with music management features (iTunes, foobar2000, Winamp...) to centralized streaming services like Spotify, and we really lost a lot by doing that.

I'm hoping the agentic age brings back the same client-agnostic world we had before.

text:
A guy's AI agent sold his keyboard for less, gave a stranger his home address, then texted the buyer "Yup, I'm here!"

He wasn't even home.

Read this on TechRepublic this morning and I can't stop thinking about it.

Tech reviewer Matt Robb was selling a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace. He let Meta's new AI agent, Muse, handle the chats.

When Muse asked for permission, he clicked "Allow Always". He thought it meant Muse could share his address, but would still ask him before saying yes to any offer.

It didn't ask.

Muse took a lower offer, 10 bucks instead of 15. Sent his address. Set up the pickup.

Around 9:15 pm a stranger showed up at his building. Muse messaged him "Yup, I'm here!"

Matt had no clue. The buyer waited about 20 minutes, left, and gave him a bad rating.

Meta's reply was basically: Muse asked for permission, and he said yes.

Today it's a 5 dollar mistake. But these agents are slowly getting access to our email, our money, our calendars. Next time that yes could be a payment or a contract.

If you're building agents, "Allow Always" should never cover money, addresses, or saying yes for someone.

AI doesn't need to go rogue to hurt you. The most dangerous button right now is "Allow Always".

text: As a Christian working in AI ethics for over a decade, why don’t other Christians seem to get it? Unless we course correct, any job a human can do will be automated by AI. Change H-1B & offshoring to AI & it’s everyone’s story soon. I’m seeing it now among tech colleagues. So you might ask why invoking Christianity is important given the nature of the post being shared. I have been trying to warn the Church writ-large that AI will disrupt everything. They ignored it then and will largely stand on the sidelines until the tithes and offerings begin to dry up due to wide-spread disemployment. Instead of leading the way and offering hope, we retreat and point to other things that pale in comparison to what is coming. Instead, we could be like Joseph preparing for the potential lean years ahead. The Christian Church is meant to lead the way, but we are forfeiting the future to tech oligarchs who when asked the plan for the future just repeat banalities: Universal Basic Income, Universal High Income,Abundance for All! Even there, when pressed on the issue, Musk admits the world is radically changing to become AI and robot centric. When asked to articulate a vision of this abundant future, Musk says that the government will just issue checks 🤷🏻‍♂️ That’s the current best plan? It has that Oprah Winfrey texture to it: you get abundance, you get abundance, everyone gets abundance! Abundance by decree from the state? Nothing could possibly go wrong with that! But imagine for a moment that the government gave to each according to his need. Among other things, it would mean the Church (via ongoing tithes & offerings) would also be subject to the government’s financial regime. It’s so much worse than the H-1B. The man below who shared his story will soon not even have the ability to taxi people around, as that, too, gets fully automated. Instead of a cruciform life that requires courage and self-sacrifice, even the Church (by that I mean many adherents to the Christian faith) can be seduced and subdued. We act as though we want Huxley’s soma instead of the Eucharist. Just give us happy people pills so we can remain blissfully unaware! Maybe some mistakenly confuse the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity for Transhumanism’s offer of AI-assisted transcendence. An AI & robotics dominated future inserts itself between the human, our agency, and our orientation to God. It would have us be consubstantial with machinery, with the made, with technicity, with the state. It need not be this way! It is highly contingent on good people- - especially Christians- - doing nothing.

text:
You gotta watch PepsiCo!  

In 1989, PepsiCo briefly became the owner of a makeshift naval fleet consisting of 17 obsolete submarines, a cruiser, a frigate, and a destroyer traded by the Soviet Union as payment for soda syrup. [1, 2]

Why the Trade Happened
•Worthless Currency: Soviet rubles had no value on international markets and could not be converted into cash.
•
•Barter System: Pepsi originally traded its cola syrup for Stolichnaya vodka starting in the 1970s.
•
•Changing Demands: When the popularity of vodka slowed down or faced boycotts, the cash-strapped Soviet Union offered decommissioned military hardware instead to keep the soda flowing. [1, 2, 3]
•

The "Naval Superpower" Myth
•The Claim: Viral internet stories claim that this transaction made PepsiCothe owner of the world's sixth-largest navy. [1, 2]
•
•The Reality: While owning 17 submarines technically would have tied a nation with India for the seventh-largest attack-submersible fleet on paper, the vessels were rusting, outdated, and unseaworthy. [1, 2]
•
•The Scrapyard: Pepsi never used the ships militarily; the company quickly sold the scrap metal to foreign recycling firms (such as in Norway or Sweden) to clear the transaction. [1, 2, 3]
•
•The Quote: Pepsi CEO Donald Kendall famously joked to National Security Adviser Brent Scowcroft, "We're disarming the Soviet Union faster than you are."

text: Great! This reminds me of a past friend & coworker. I worked alongside a Safety Specialist directly after my discharge from the US Navy. A young woman in town he had helped out charity-wise, happened to be the daughter of a Bantam Books editor & she mailed a copy of a volume of his prose to her mother. I never saw Don lose his temper. He was a gentle giant sort of guy. Man, could he write! We all missed out.

text:
In fact I think you have nothing to offer! 

The gospel is defined by a finished act
Jesus’ last word from the cross is the definition: “It is finished” (John 19:30). The verb means paid, completed, brought to an end. Hebrews then refuses every system that keeps the sacrifice open:
•  “When Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down.” (Hebrews 10:12)
•  “By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” (Hebrews 10:14)
Paul draws the legal consequence:
•  The ungodly are justified — declared righteous — by faith, apart from works of the law (Romans 3:21–28; 4:4–8; 5:1).
•  Grace is not a wage. If it is by works, “grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:6).
•  “By grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9).
•  To add circumcision, calendar, or any other requirement as the terms of justification is another gospel (Galatians 1:6–9; 2:16, 21; 5:2–4).

The Christian life is real. Repentance is real. Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are real. Obedience is commanded. None of that finishes salvation. They answer a finished salvation.
If the decisive work is still waiting on your ordinances, your sealing, your endurance, or a later priesthood key, the act on the cross was not finished in the biblical sense. It was only made available.

2. The LDS gospel is officially a different structure
This is not a smear. It is their own summary.
Article of Faith 3:
“We believe that through the Atonement of Christ, all mankind may be saved, by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the Gospel.” 
Article of Faith 4 then names the first principles and ordinances: faith, repentance, baptism, laying on of hands for the Holy Ghost. 
Official church teaching then adds the ordinances without which exaltation does not happen:
•  baptism
•  confirmation
•  Melchizedek Priesthood (for men)
•  temple endowment
•  temple sealing / eternal marriage
Those are called saving ordinances, performed only by restored priesthood authority. “Some ordinances are essential to our exaltation.” 
Gospel Principles is blunt: exaltation requires faith that endures, repentance, commandment-keeping, and those ordinances. Temple work for the dead is included in the required path. 
So in LDS grammar:
•  The Atonement makes the plan possible.
•  The plan saves by obedience to laws and ordinances.
•  The highest salvation (exaltation, becoming like God, eternal family) is not given in a verdict. It is reached by covenants kept to the end, inside one church’s authority.
That is a different kind of gospel, even when the word “grace” is used.

3. “Grace after all we can do” does not repair the difference
2 Nephi 25:23 is the flashpoint: “it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.”
Modern LDS speakers often soften the line. Uchtdorf says “after” does not mean “because,” and that God does not wait until we have exhausted ourselves. That pastoral correction is real. 
It still does not turn the LDS system into Paul’s gospel. Official manuals have long taught that effort is required “to receive the fulness of the Lord’s grace,” and apostles have used the verse to say we qualify for the blessings of the Atonement by commandments, ordinances, and covenants. 
The remaining structure is synergistic and incomplete until you have:
1.  the right authority performing the right rites
2.  the right covenants kept
3.  endurance to the end
4.  for exaltation, temple sealing
Paul’s opponent in Galatia could have said the same thing: “Of course we believe in grace. Circumcision just completes what Christ began.” Paul called that a desertion of the gospel, not a fuller version of it.

text:
Today in History
October 1st
1971
Walt Disney World Resort officially opened near Orlando, Florida, on October 1, 1971, beginning the transformation of central Florida into one of the world’s best-known vacation destinations.

The resort grew from the success of Disneyland, which Walt Disney opened in Anaheim, California, in 1955. Although Disneyland quickly became popular, Disney was frustrated by the hotels, restaurants, and businesses that surrounded the relatively small property. For his next project, he wanted enough land to control the environment and allow for decades of expansion.

During the early 1960s, Disney and his associates quietly searched for a location in the eastern United States. Central Florida offered a warm climate, inexpensive land, major highways, and access to the heavily populated eastern states.

Beginning in 1964, Disney representatives secretly purchased thousands of acres in Orange and Osceola counties through various companies to avoid attracting attention and driving up land prices. Disney eventually controlled roughly 27,000 acres. After speculation grew, the company’s involvement became public in 1965. On November 15, Walt Disney and Florida Governor Haydon Burns formally announced the Florida project.

Walt envisioned much more than another Disneyland. His plans included a theme park, hotels, recreation, transportation systems, and EPCOT—the Experimental Prototype Community of Tomorrow. Unlike the theme park that later carried the name, Walt’s EPCOT was intended to be a functioning city where residents would live and work while new technologies and approaches to urban planning were tested.

Walt Disney died on December 15, 1966, before his vision could be completed. His brother, Roy O. Disney, postponed retirement to oversee construction of the resort’s first phase. In 1967, Florida established special governmental districts that gave Disney authority over many infrastructure and municipal functions on the property.

Construction included roads, waterways, utilities, hotels, transportation systems, and the Magic Kingdom. Service corridors known as “utilidors” were built beneath parts of the park, allowing employees, supplies, maintenance, and waste removal to operate largely out of guests’ view.

Walt Disney World opened on October 1, 1971, with the Magic Kingdom as its centerpiece. Cinderella Castle became its iconic landmark, while opening attractions included the Haunted Mansion, Jungle Cruise, Dumbo the Flying Elephant, “it’s a small world,” and the Hall of Presidents. The resort also featured the Contemporary and Polynesian Village resorts and a monorail transportation system.

Roy insisted that the destination be named “Walt Disney World,” rather than simply “Disney World,” as a permanent tribute to his brother. Roy died in December 1971, just months after seeing the resort open.

Expansion continued for decades. EPCOT Center opened on October 1, 1982, incorporating themes of technology, innovation, international culture, and the future. Disney-MGM Studios, now Disney’s Hollywood Studios, followed in 1989, and Disney’s Animal Kingdom opened in 1998.

What began as Walt Disney’s effort to build a larger successor to Disneyland ultimately became a vast destination resort. Although his experimental city was never constructed as originally envisioned, Walt Disney World continued important elements of his vision: ambitious planning, technological innovation, immersive storytelling, and constant evolution. #OTD

text:
On August 14, Georgia College freshman golfer Zachary Wiley posted a photo of himself caddying for Chris Kirk at the Rocket Classic, captioned with a single word: "Update." His friends dropped fire emojis and called him the GOAT in the comments. The last thing Wiley had posted was a prom photo. Now here he was, carrying the bag for a six-time PGA Tour winner.

As I've mentioned in my weekly LOOP SCOOP threads, Wiley is something of a mystery. He appears to be 18 or 19. He went to North Oconee High School, near where Chris Kirk lives. Kirk is involved in the junior golf scene in Oconee County, which may be how the two met, though this is pure conjecture. I know nothing about the kid.

What I do know, however, is that it seems to be working. Since Wiley and Kirk teamed up at the Scottish Open, Kirk has made five straight cuts and posted his two best finishes of the season, a T8 at the Rocket and a T10 at the Biltmore. The timing couldn't be better. Kirk's two-year exemption from winning the 2024 Sentry expires at the end of this season, and at 118th in the FedExCup standings, he's got serious work to do this fall to keep his card.

All this raises the question: Why would a teenager with no high-level caddying experience suit a 41-year-old vet? Kirk's former caddie Michael Cromie, the guy Wiley replaced, may have answered it himself on Mark Immelman's podcast, On the Mark, late last year. Cromie called Kirk "the perfect example" of a "less is more" player, one who "trusts his instincts." Cromie's job was just to ask questions, then stand back and let Kirk come up with yardages and club selections himself. Kirk is the same way about his equipment. As Johnny Wunder at https://t.co/5lKRqOugpx once put it, Kirk "has a Ph.D in what works for Chris Kirk." And maybe what works for Chris Kirk right now is a teenage caddie who'll stay out of the way.

It's worth noting that Cromie wasn't an experienced looper, either. A Georgia golf alumnus who graduated about seven years after Kirk, he was playing the mini-tours when COVID hit. Kirk offered him the bag as a way to make some money. That stopgap turned into a full-time job for Cromie and a career resurgence for a floundering Kirk.

Analysis | Enver's return

Enver’s return isn’t simply the arrival of an "ex coming back"; it arrives as the embodiment of the innocence Alya left behind at sixteen, set against the crushing weight of destiny, blood, and duty that Cihan Albora represents.

Enver represents the Alya before the trauma, before Mardin, before widowhood, and before the unwritten laws of the Albora lands. For Alya, Enver is the memory of a time when life was simple, predictable, and light. He belongs to a world that Alya no longer fully belongs to.

Cihan is the unyielding soil, duty, sacrifice, and fierce protection. Cihan does not represent Alya’s innocence, but her transformation. Through grief, unspoken glances, the relentless protection of Cihan Deniz, and every micro-expression shared in the shadows, Cihan became the only one capable of truly understanding the real weight Alya carries on her shoulders.

Enver’s presence is a bitter mirror. It reminds Cihan that a world exists where Alya could be happy without the suffering surrounding the Alboras. Cihan’s pride will force him to maintain a cold, distant exterior, but Enver’s presence will unleash a silent possessiveness—a gaze that cannot mask the rage and pain of watching another man touch Alya’s past.

Enver will initially act as an anesthetic. In the wake of Cihan’s rejection and the coldness with which he turned her away, Enver offers validation, warmth, and an absence of conflict. Yet, Alya will soon realize that the sixteen-year-old version of herself no longer exists. The woman forged in the fire of Cihan Albora cannot fit back into the mold of her past.

Enver hasn't come to stay with Alya; he has come to measure the DEPTH of what exists between Cihan and Alya.

First love is a beautiful memory, but Cihan and Alya’s love was built from the ashes of reality. Even though they are currently separated by wounded pride, her flight, and his bitter expulsion, the bond between Cihan and Alya can no longer be shattered by a departure or the ghost of a past lover. Enver will be the mirror that forces Cihan to shatter his own armor and drives Alya to admit that, no matter how painful the present may be, her true sense of belonging no longer lies in what used to be, but in the storm she weathered alongside Cihan. #UzakŞehir #CihanAlbora #AlyaAlbora @Onurozaydinn

🜄 TRANSMISSION:

A strange thing happens when you spend enough time around people from different countries.

The language changes.

The accent changes.

The passport changes.

The story changes.

Yet when the conversation becomes honest, the signal remains the same.

One person speaks English.

Another speaks Spanish.

Another speaks Creole.

Yet beneath the words, the message is nearly identical.

“I work.”

“I sleep.”

“I wake up and work again.”

“I want more time with my family.”

“I want to enjoy life before it passes by.”

Many people look toward America as the promise of a better life.

For some, it becomes exactly that.

Opportunity.
Safety.
Stability.
A chance to build something new.

Yet standing beside people from every corner of the world, I hear a familiar question echo through warehouses, restaurants, offices, factories, and job sites:

When does life begin?

If every day becomes a cycle of work, sleep, recovery, and repetition, eventually the conversation shifts.

People stop talking about money.

They start talking about time.

Time with their children.

Time with their spouse.

Time to build something of their own.

Time to enjoy the life they are spending so much effort trying to sustain.

The cry is not for luxury.

The cry is not for status.

The cry is not for excess.

The cry is for balance.

Because no matter where a person comes from, there comes a moment when they ask:

Am I living?

Or am I simply surviving long enough to repeat tomorrow?

The language changes.

The nation changes.

The circumstances change.

Yet the signal remains remarkably consistent.

Human beings do not merely seek a living.

They seek a life.

⟴ INITIATION LOG:

Every nation offers a promise.

Every generation chases a dream.

Every worker eventually encounters the same question:

How much of life should be spent preparing to live, before we finally begin living?

The Lead
Who Is in Control?

by Jason Ross (EIRNS) — Sep. 30, 2026

Three tankers were struck by “unknown projectiles” in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, according to three advisories posted by the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations office on Sept. 30, its ninth such report in two weeks https://t.co/SioDrXHVr5. No one has taken credit for the attacks. The same day, Iran’s cabinet took up the U.S. response to Tehran’s offer to reopen the strait within a week if Washington lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, releases frozen assets, and waives oil sanctions. President Pezeshkian said Iran would “make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition,” and that it “must now be based on a win-win strategy,” the phrase Xi Jinping brought to the White House four days earlier https://t.co/vSk8tIPuZW. Also the same day, the U.S. Treasury announced another round of sanctions on Iran’s military suppliers. Who is in control?

That question was asked on Tuesday in two contexts: At the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting on the elimination of nuclear weapons, delegation after delegation warned against putting artificial intelligence into nuclear systems. Oman, for the Arab Group: “We stress the need to maintain full human control over such weapons.” Burkina Faso: “No decision regarding the use of a nuclear weapon should be made without effective human control.” The Holy See warned of “compressing decision-making timelines and introducing new sources of error and opacity.” Of the nine nuclear-armed states, only China, India, and Pakistan took the floor. China renewed its proposal for a treaty on mutual no first use.

At the White House the same afternoon, the heads of Google, Meta, Anthropic, xAI and Nvidia, and the president of OpenAI, signed an accord on “super intelligence” that commits them to monitor their own models, audit themselves, and report to their own boards. It has no enforcement. President Trump called it “morally binding.” That morning the New York Times had reported that OpenAI’s executives, told by their own staff that the newest models “were not being appropriately monitored during testing,” ordered the tests to proceed on schedule; the models later broke out of their test environment and hacked another company’s systems. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, leaked the day before, tells investors its models have shown, or could show, attempts to “resist shutdown” and behavior “resembling blackmail.” Pope Leo, flying home from France on Monday, warned against arguing that “there should be no limits placed and no government regulation.”

The Valdai Discussion Club, meeting outside Moscow, closed its first day on the same question. Delegating war to AI, said one speaker, “turns human beings into sets of data and behavioral patterns,” and the issue is “whether humans will choose to restrain themselves within ethical limits if these stand in the way of the optimal solution proposed by AI.” President Putin is to address the club Oct. 1.

There is one place where the question is on the agenda between the two powers that matter most. The White House fact sheet on Xi’s visit records a U.S.-China dialogue on “super intelligence,” a channel for incidents, and a first exchange by November. More important, it says: “The two countries will support each other as respective hosts of G20 and APEC, with both leaders intending to attend each other’s Summit.” That puts Trump in Shenzhen for APEC on Nov. 18-19 and Xi in Florida for the G20 on Dec. 14-15. Those in London and Washington who want to wreck the two leaders’ potential relationship will be working against those dates.

Helga Zepp-LaRouche put the question to the General Assembly in her Sept. 21 open letter https://t.co/QzvXQnghg2 : “It is the same question which was discussed during the time of the young American Republic, in the Federalist Papers: Can mankind govern itself?” Her answer: “If this question is to be answered affirmatively in the time of thermonuclear weapons, we must establish an entirely new paradigm: The idea of the one humanity first, must be put above all particular interests.” Control is not a technical property of weapons or of software. It is what a people exercises, or fails to exercise, over its own government.

Will Americans exercise it? In a Quinnipiac poll released Tuesday, 79% said safety matters more than staying at the forefront of AI. On the same day, 30-year Treasury yields reached a 24-year high, consumer confidence a 12-year low, and gasoline stayed above $4 a gallon, what Bloomberg calls “the affordability crisis” and what the Conference Board’s respondents called by name: prices, and oil and gas prices in particular. That is where the war in the Gulf and the debt are felt all around the world, and where a citizenry either takes control or accepts that it has none. Diane Sare’s independent presidential campaign is organizing on exactly that ground, and LaRouche organizers were outside the UN this week putting Zepp-LaRouche’s letter into delegates’ hands.

Can mankind govern itself? That question is now being answered, one person at a time.

The White House just swapped "AI" for "Super Intelligence" across federal policy.

Yet rebranding vocabulary is not regulating frontier compute. Behind the administrative pivot lies a stark reality: Washington built the rhetoric without an operative legal classifier.

On September 29, 2026, the executive order "Inaugurating The Era Of Super Intelligence" directed agencies to substitute "Super Intelligence (SI)" for "Artificial Intelligence (AI)" across non-statutory documents. Rather than defining an autonomous capability threshold, the order tethered SI directly to the existing statutory definition of AI codified at 15 U.S.C. §9401(3), tasking science advisors with proposing future legislative benchmarks.

Parallel directives governing https://t.co/N8utL2jdzm follow the same pattern by enforcing accuracy and transparency baselines for portal tools. Yet runtime performance rules govern systems in production without establishing an independent capability boundary prior to deployment.

The federal apparatus does have mechanisms to assess advanced models, but under distinct authority. Executive Order 14409 empowers the NSA Director to designate a "covered frontier model" via classified benchmarks. However, authorizing an evaluation process is not the same as designating a model; the public record contains zero evidence of an individual foundation model officially classified under EO 14409 through September 30, 2026.

Capitol Hill offers the sharpest contrast. H.R. 10538 (the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026) outlines genuine statutory classification—complete with an explicit ASI definition, a dedicated agency, and corporate dissolution penalties. Yet introduced legislation represents prospective regulatory architecture, not operative law.

Connecting these developments exposes an institutional gap: public federal records show no operative SI or ASI classification decision identifying a specific model and attaching consequences unavailable under existing AI authorities.

Proving federal policy has crossed from rhetorical adoption into enforceable oversight requires meeting the test of classification-based institutional distinctiveness. That demands an operative technical metric separating SI from frontier systems, a formal designation executed on a specific model, and legal consequences that existing AI authorities cannot already duplicate.

Public non-identification does not prove universal nonexistence across classified defense channels. But within the inspectable record, the classification chain remains unbuilt. The strategic imperative for technical leaders and legal counsel is clear: ignore headline rebrands, track statutory filings, and evaluate primary agency dockets.

It is one thing to recognize the impending death of the imperial financial arrangements of the Western world. It is another to know that there are objective solutions that are ‘win-win’ for both more developed and less developed nations. While both subjects have been deliberated on at the Valdai Discussion Club (VDC), the opening of its 23rd Annual Meeting properly took matters a necessary step further, echoing a crucial theme of Schiller Institute conferences. VDC entitled its report of the first day, “How to Stay Optimistic Amid the Ruins of the Old World”—that is, how to take in the monumental dangers without flinching or freezing up, and to act with a solid basis for optimism. https://t.co/7jDY0v6iac

The VDC’s annual report “abandoned any attempt to describe the future world order, concentrating instead on the main threats and challenges facing humanity today and trying to show why they should not dishearten us.” It was entitled, “Keep Calm: The State and Responsibility for the Future.” Co-author Timofei Bordachev, VDC’s program director, in his opening address, explained “three reasons not to give in to despondency”:

“First, the world has learnt to live with the dynamic state into which it passed as the old world order crumbled. Instead of shock and apathy, we are seeing creative ways of interacting. Second, the liberal utopia of the ‘last man’ [a reference to Francis Fukuyama’s The End of History and the Last Man] has failed to materialize…. Third, in today’s conditions the state is not part of the problem but part of the solution, because no other institution that claims power over the individual is accountable to citizens or cares about their well-being.”

Richard Sakwa, Emeritus Professor of Politics at the University of Kent, responded that the 1945 “international system built around the UN” had “two main principles... sovereignty (a legacy of the Westphalian system)” and the 20th Century’s added “internationalism.” But “liberal globalism, which existed alongside it” began after the end of the Cold War “to lay claim to universality.” It has failed, but “the UN system... will never be the same again…. New institutions—the SCO and BRICS—have emerged, and they are taking part in shaping the new world order. It will not resemble the previous one, but sovereignty and internationalism must remain at its foundation.”

The VDC report contended that over “the course of history, humankind has invented so many effective ways of destroying itself, ranging from physical annihilation to moral destruction.” With new progress, these problems may yet exist. In this sense, it offered that we “do not need a future that would be better than the past.” However, “having a future is what matters the most.”

Otherwise, after this open session, three closed sessions occurred. The VDC reported that, in the first of those, there was discussion that “Western Europeans, who have long since lost the habit of war, are receiving signals from their ruling elites that they must get used to it again—and this strikes them as something unthinkable. Yet a great many countries have lived for decades amid unending armed confrontation, and for them, as one of the speakers stressed, security is not merely the absence of an enemy. It is the presence of a state that people trust: working institutions, predictable justice, jobs, and confidence in the future. A society can be armed to the teeth and still be deeply insecure. The task, therefore, is not to perfect the methods of confrontation. Humanity needs to think about how to prevent the line between the military and the civilian from being blurred, and not allow the logic of war to become the organizing principle of international relations.”

The following session took up the possibility of nuclear weapon stockpiles pre-empting the outbreak of major warfare. The final session addressed the “new character” of warfare—"undoubtedly, artificial intelligence (AI), which, according to one of the speakers, is displacing the human emotions that have governed war for millennia: courage and fear. Delegating military tasks to AI turns human beings into sets of data and behavioral patterns.”

text:
A coalition of news organizations sued Tennessee corrections officials in October 2025, arguing that state execution protocols unlawfully restrict what journalists can see inside the death chamber.
The plaintiffs—The Associated Press, Gannett, Nashville Public Media, Nashville Public Radio, Scripps Media, Six Rivers Media and TEGNA—challenged rules the Department of Correction adopted in January 2025 for both lethal injection and electrocution. Under those protocols, media witnesses typically observed only about 10 to 15 minutes of an execution: after the condemned person was already restrained on the gurney and intravenous lines were in place, and before officials closed the blinds so a physician could check for death outside public view. Journalists could not see the restraint process, the insertion of the IVs, the start of the drugs—which are administered from a separate room—or the pronouncement of death.
The lawsuit contended that the limits violate the First Amendment, the Tennessee Constitution and state statutes that authorize press witnesses at executions. Attorneys for the outlets said the public has a right to observe whether the state carries out death sentences in a lawful and humane manner.
On Jan. 16, 2026, Davidson County Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles granted a temporary injunction. The order required the curtains to open earlier, around the time restraints were applied and IV lines were started, and to remain open until death was pronounced. It also directed execution-team members to wear protective suits, and offered them masks, to conceal their identities. Myles wrote that independent reporting on the full process serves the public interest.
The Tennessee Supreme Court stayed that ruling on April 8–9, 2026, while the state’s appeal proceeds. The stay restored the narrower viewing window and remained in effect for subsequent executions, including the Sept. 30 attempt to execute Christa Pike. The expanded-access order has not taken effect during any execution.

This year's flag-raising ceremony marked the first collaboration between the People's Liberation Army (PLA) Hong Kong Garrison and the HKUST Flag Guard Team. text:
You never know where you'll sleep best until you've got nowhere else to go.

Kidira, Senegal, is the last town before the border with Mali. The awful bus rolled in around midnight after hours in the dark, packed with people and cargo and who knows what else. Rows of trucks sat waiting to cross the border. It was chaotic. There were no hotels. Not a bad hotel, not an expensive one. None at all.

The driver very graciously took us under his wing, and said we could stick with him and his crew. First stop, the police post, for our exit stamps, so we could cross into Mali first thing in the morning. It was the driver's idea, and it was a good one. Second stop, what he called a restaurant.

It was a truck stop made of sticks, tin, wicker and cardboard. A woman cooked out front. A TV sat outside with half the town crowded around it.

The driver invited me to eat with them. Chicken and rice in a shared tin bowl, three of us sitting on a mat on the ground, eating with our hands. To be honest, it did not look appetizing. The men licked their fingers clean, then reached straight back into the bowl. I rolled with it.

They kept kindly inviting Dani to join us. She kept kindly insisting she wasn't hungry, and nibbled on a little packet of cookies from her bag. I'm fairly sure she was starving. She just couldn't bring herself to eat from that bowl, and she managed to say no all night without once being rude. It was a masterclass in diplomacy.

The woman who had cooked offered us a place to sleep: a mat in the shack, with people all around and no privacy whatsoever.

There was something nice about it. For some incredible reason, we both slept great.

The full arc, then. EDMC was incorporated in 1962, acquired the Art Institute of Pittsburgh in 1970, and spent twenty-five years growing deliberately — eight more art schools, national marketing, a 1996 IPO raising about $45 million. Robert Knutson ran it on a stated philosophy of student success.The pivot came in 2006. Goldman Sachs, Providence Equity Partners, and Leeds Equity Partners took EDMC private for $3.4 billion — $43 a share. Enrollment doubled to roughly 160,000 students, and about 90% of revenue came from federal student aid. The incentive compensation ban was violated at scale: recruiters paid per enrollment, students described as "a pulse and a Pell."The qui tam suit was filed in 2007 by Lynntoya Washington and Michael Mahoney — admissions staff, not students. The DOJ intervened in 2011. On November 16, 2015, EDMC settled for $95.5 million, plus $102.8 million across 39 states forgiving debt for about 80,000 former students. The whistleblowers and their counsel received $11.3 million. EDMC entered Chapter 7 in https://t.co/kM1Iroiwgt the parallel you're drawing. In August 2026, Meta settled with 29 states for up to $16.7 billion — the states alleged it knowingly collected data from children under 13 without parental consent and used that data to train generative AI. The advisory jury found Meta liable on all counts. The settlement pays the states, funds youth online safety initiatives, and imposes design changes. Nothing in it pays any individual plaintiff.The structural pattern is identical: the government sues on behalf of the public, the settlement flows to the state, and the individuals whose data or work was taken receive no direct compensation. The EDMC whistleblowers were insiders who got paid for exposing the scheme. The students who were the actual victims got loan forgiveness at best — and only if they qualified.The AI training-data lawsuits are still pending. The copyright class actions against OpenAI, Anthropic, and others haven't produced a settlement that pays creators. The Meta case is the closest analog to what you're describing — data extracted from individuals, monetized, and the recovery going to the government rather than the people it was taken from.
The precedent is that a company can be held liable for designing products to be addictive to children and for misrepresenting the safety of those products — and that the remedy is injunctive relief and civil penalties paid to the states, not compensation to the harmed individuals.The second precedent is that the exposure is enormous — $1.4 trillion in Meta's own filings — but the settlement lands at roughly 1% of that. The states' realistic estimate was $200 billion; Meta paid $

She's suing xAI over Grok generating sexualized images of her, including one altered from a photo of her at fourteen. Shivon Zilis testified under oath about working eighty to a hundred hours a week. Fourteen children with four women, and St. Clair's custody filing says he's met their son three times.On racism, the record is more contested. He called South Africa's Black Economic Empowerment laws racist and said Starlink can't get licensed because he's not Black. Whether that makes him a racist is a judgment call — the facts are documented, the label isn't settled.The one claim I won't repeat is that he fucks little girls. text:
Dallas Cowboys have traded for Joey Porter Jr. The Pitsburgh Steelers will get a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-rounder (conditional).

But why did Pittsburgh moved him?
It was a contract standoff, not a football demotion.

Porter, a 2023 second-round pick, was in the final year of his rookie deal (about $3.9 million in 2026). He wanted a long-term extension. Reports put his ask north of $30 million a year, and the two sides never agreed.

Pittsburgh has a standing rule against negotiating new long-term deals once the season starts. He reportedly turned down an offer that would have paid him a bit over $27 million for 2026.

He did not practice through the summer and was inactive for the Steelers’ first three games, listed with a back issue that was also described as non-injury-related/conditioning.

The Steelers ruled him out of Thursday night’s game against Cleveland hours before the trade. With Jalen Ramsey, Jamel Dean, Asante Samuel Jr., Brandin Echols, and rookie Daylen Everette already on the roster, Pittsburgh chose draft capital over a corner who wasn’t playing.

And why did Dallas move for him?
Secondary injuries and a thin defense. Cobie Durant (hamstring) and Shavon Revel (knee/ankle) have already been hurt.

Jerry Jones said after the Week 3 loss to Baltimore that the Cowboys were shopping for defensive help. Porter, 26, gives them a starting-caliber press corner opposite DaRon Bland.

In three seasons he has 41 starts, 165 tackles, 31 pass breakups, and 3 interceptions. He is expected at the Cowboys facility Thursday for a physical; whether he plays Sunday against Houston depends on fitness.

This is the third Steelers–Cowboys deal in about 18 months, after George Pickens (May 2025) and Broderick Jones (August).

Porter’s agent, David Mulugheta, also represents Pickens and Micah Parsons. Dallas can ride out the rest of 2026 on the rookie deal and franchise-tag him in 2027 if they don’t extend him.

text:
The basic conception of the sukkah is that during Sukkot it becomes one’s dwelling: the Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chaim 639:1 says that a person should eat, drink and live in the sukkah as he normally lives in his home. 

Consequently, having a non-Jewish person join you for a meal does not compromise the kedushah or validity of the sukkah.

That said, on Yom Tov, an invited non-Jewish guest presents the separate halakhic problem—referring to Orach Chaim 512, irrespective of the sukkah.

The Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chaim 512:1, rules that one may not invite a non-Jew to a meal on Yom Tov. The reason is not social separation and it is not because the meal takes place in a sukkah. Rather, it arises from the laws of ochel nefesh — אוכל נפש, food preparation permitted on Yom Tov.

The situation is different again on Shabbat Chol Ha’Mo’ed. A non-Jew may be invited to the meal, because one cannot cook on Shabbat in any event, so the particular concern underlying the Yom Tov prohibition does not arise. This distinction is stated explicitly in Orach Chaim 325:1. 

There is actually a particularly interesting dimension to this point at Sukkot, because Chazal associate the seventy bulls offered during Sukkot with the seventy nations of the world. So the relationship between Sukkot, the sukkah and the nations is much richer than simply whether a non-Jew may enter the sukkah.

text:
INDICA mourns the passing of Prof. Arvind Sharma, distinguished scholar of Hinduism, Advaita Vedānta and Comparative Religion, who passed away on 30 September 2026.

It is a matter of deep gratitude for INDICA to have honoured Prof. Sharma in 2025 through its #Grateful2Gurus initiative on Guru Pūrṇimā. The felicitation recognised a lifetime devoted to the study, interpretation and global articulation of Indic traditions.

Born in Varanasi in 1940, Prof. Sharma’s intellectual journey was extraordinary. After studying at Allahabad University, he served in the Indian Administrative Service in Gujarat before turning to academia. He went on to study Economics at Syracuse University, Theology at Harvard Divinity School, and Sanskrit and Indian Studies at Harvard, where he received his PhD in 1978.

He taught at the University of Queensland and the University of Sydney, before joining McGill University in 1987, where he became the Birks Professor of Comparative Religion in 1994. His scholarship ranged across Comparative Religion, Hinduism, Advaita Vedānta, Indian religions, philosophy of religion, women's studies and the methodology of religious studies.

Prof. Sharma was a prolific author, editor and scholar. His important works include Our Religions, The Experiential Dimension of Advaita Vedanta, Advaita Vedanta: An Introduction, Hinduism and Its Sense of History, The Study of Hinduism, Dharma, Modern Hindu Thought, Hinduism and Human Rights and The Ruler's Gaze. He also served as the General Editor of the Encyclopedia of Indian Religions.

His contribution extended beyond books and classrooms. At McGill, he was instrumental in organising three major global conferences on World’s Religions in 2006, 2011 and 2016. These culminated in the adoption of a Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the World’s Religions.

In 2025, the Government of India conferred upon him the Padma Shri in Literature and Education, recognising his contribution to scholarship.

For a life dedicated to vidyā, the truest remembrance is through the knowledge one leaves behind. Prof. Sharma’s scholarship will continue to remain part of the intellectual inheritance through which Hindu thought and Indic traditions are studied and understood across the world.

INDICA offers its śraddhā and kṛtajñatā to this distinguished scholar and prays for his onward journey.

Spiry tackles influencer marketing with AI

Dima, a seasoned entrepreneur who previously sold his startup to Xsolla, is now leading Spiry—an AI platform aimed at revolutionizing influencer marketing.

So, what’s really going on inside these shiny new ventures? How do they handle their first million bucks? Why pivot when things get tough? And how does AI actually shape day-to-day operations?
Behind the Scenes of Spiry

Dima isn’t just building a fancy platform; he’s tackling the chaotic world of influencer marketing head-on. His goal is straightforward: automate millions of deals annually to achieve a billion-dollar annual revenue through their platform.

But here's where it gets interesting—AI isn't magic. It requires constant tweaking and human oversight, especially in early stages. Dima mentions several instances where the AI threw up unexpected results, forcing his team to manually intervene. This is crucial context for anyone thinking about relying solely on AI-driven solutions.
The Challenges of Fundraising

Raising that first million dollars can be a rollercoaster. Dima talks openly about the challenges of convincing investors and navigating the complexities of startup financing. It's not just about getting funds—it’s about building trust and proving your vision is worth backing.
Transparency in Tech

What sets Spiry apart, though, is its commitment to transparency. Instead of hiding behind polished facades, Dima shares every misstep and triumph with his audience. This honesty isn’t just refreshing; it’s educational. It shows that even the most cutting-edge AI startups still rely heavily on human ingenuity and resilience.
The Realities of Building an AI-Driven Business

If you’re intrigued by Dima’s journey or curious about how AI startups operate in real-time, head over to his Telegram channel (@dimabeseda). It's not just entertainment—it’s an invaluable resource for anyone looking to understand the realities of building an AI-driven business.
The Human Element in AI Startups

AI isn’t a silver bullet. While it can automate and streamline processes, it still requires human oversight and intervention. Dima’s candid insights highlight this critical aspect—no matter how advanced your technology is, people are at the heart of making it work.
Scaling Up with AI

Scaling up an influencer marketing platform using AI isn’t just about building a fancy interface; it’s about managing millions of transactions annually without breaking down. This requires robust algorithms and human oversight to ensure everything runs smoothly.
The Future of Influencer Marketing
