BREAKING: Christa Pike still alive and snoring after two lethal injection doses tonight￼

After the Supreme Court vacated a Sixth Circuit stay, Tennessee began Christa Pike's lethal injection at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution around 8 p.m. CT. Defense counsel told courts she received both syringes of pentobarbital yet remained conscious with a heartbeat and was audibly snoring.￼

Witnesses reported she said her arm felt like it was about to burst. Lawyers filed emergency motions seeking an immediate halt and lifesaving measures as the death warrant neared its midnight cutoff. Pike, convicted for the 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer when she was 18, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.￼

Pike believed Slemmer was attempting to “steal her boyfriend.” Pike lured Slemmer to a gathering framed as reconciliatory & offered her marijuana then taunted, beat and slashed Slemmer.

According to court testimony, for the next 30 minutes, Slemmer was taunted, beaten, and slashed. Shipp used a box cutter to carve a pentagram into her chest while she was still alive. Finally, Pike smashed Slemmer's skull with a large chunk of asphalt, killing her. Pike kept a piece of Slemmer's skull.

Pike began to show off the piece of skull around the school, and the three were arrested within 36 hours. The log book showed that Pike, Shipp, Peterson, and Slemmer left together, and only three returned. Detectives found the piece of skull in Pike's jacket pocket. Soon after her arrest, Pike waived her Miranda rights and confessed to the police how she had participated in Slemmer's killing.

Tennessee’s new lethal injection protocol, calling for a single drug (pentobarbital), is plagued with the same issues that have marked botched executions for decades: secrecy, intentional omission, inattention to detail, and untrained and unlicensed prison personnel attempting to fill a medical role.

Tadaryl Shipp is alive & imprisoned in Tennessee, reportedly at Northwest Correctional Complex. He received life with parole eligibility, plus a consecutive 25-year conspiracy sentence. He was not eligible for the death penalty because he was 17 at the time of Colleen Slemmer’s 1995 murder. His parole was denied in October 2025; the next review is set for October 2031. 

Shadolla Petersonis alive & as far as public reporting establishes, though has stayed out of public view for years. She cooperated with prosecutors, pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact, and received probation. She completed that sentence long ago. She is not in prison.

Following the guilty verdict, Pike "launched, cancelled and then re-launched" an appeal of her conviction in the Tennessee state courts. In June 2001, then again in June 2002, against the advice of her lawyers, Pike asked the courts to drop her appeal and sought to be executed via electrocution. Criminal Court Judge Mary Beth Leibowitz granted the request, and an execution date of August 19, 2002, was set. Pike soon thereafter changed her mind and on July 8, 2002, defense lawyers filed a motion to allow the appeal process to continue. This motion was denied. 

Pike has sought relief from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. On November 16, 2020, she submitted a petition to the IACHR, alleging that the United States had violated the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man.

The Commission called on the United States to review her case and to consider mental and intellectual disability when conducting judicial proceedings.

Her scheduled execution was brought to the public's attention by the publicized trial of Lindsay Clancy Pike saying she felt kinship with her: "We are both females who got into trouble because of uniquely female issues. One thing is different, however, is that times have changed a lot on awareness of women's issues since I was put on trial."

Shipp never pointed to instances of childhood abuse as evidence against a guilty verdict.

text:
Tell me you don’t think the death penalty is warranted after reading this and imagining the victim was your daughter:

On January 12, 1995, 18-year-old Christa Pike, her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp (17), and friend Shadolla Peterson (18) lured 19-year-old Job Corps classmate Colleen Slemmer from their Knoxville dorm to a secluded wooded area behind an abandoned steam plant on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus near Tyson Park.
Pike had become jealous, believing Slemmer was trying to steal Shipp. The day before, she told a friend she intended to kill Slemmer because she “just felt mean that day.” They signed out together around 8 p.m. Slemmer was told they wanted to make peace and offered marijuana. Pike brought a box cutter and a small meat cleaver.
At the site, Pike and Shipp attacked Slemmer while Peterson acted as lookout. Slemmer was thrown down, kicked, and slammed against concrete. When she tried to run, they dragged her back. Over 30 minutes to an hour she was taunted, beaten, slashed across the back, chest, abdomen, arms, and neck (multiple times, including a large gaping wound to the throat), and had a pentagram carved into her chest while she was still alive (Shipp later said he did the carving). Pike used a rag or hairband to try to silence her and later said she kept cutting because Slemmer would not stop talking.
Pike then repeatedly struck Slemmer’s head with a large chunk of asphalt, causing multiple skull fractures. That was the cause of death. Pike took a piece of skull as a souvenir, later showing it to other students and bragging about the killing. Slemmer’s body was found the next morning, semi-nude from the waist up, badly beaten and slashed. Autopsy showed hundreds of wounds; the medical examiner catalogued only the major ones because there were so many.
Pike confessed in a lengthy recorded statement, describing the events in detail. Blood matching Slemmer was found on Pike’s and Shipp’s clothing. All three were arrested within about 36 hours. Pike was convicted of premeditated first-degree murder and conspiracy; she received the death penalty. Shipp received life with parole eligibility. Peterson testified for the state and received probation.
Pike has said they only meant to scare Slemmer and it escalated. Prosecutors and the jury treated it as a planned, prolonged torture killing motivated by jealousy.

text:
New Jack City does not sit politely among the gangster pictures of its hour and ask to be compared. It arrives like a verdict. In the long procession of crime films that promise rise, glitter, and ruin, this one is the sermon that refuses to let the congregation leave with the villain’s wardrobe still looking like a dream. It is Harlem at the moment crack stopped being a rumor and became weather. It is a fortress of apartments turned into a factory. It is a man who climbs so high the building itself becomes his argument, and then the argument collapses on him. What you are meant to carry out of it is not a tour of shootouts. It is a set of laws the film treats as older than the city: there is no such thing as my brother’s keeper once the money is criminal, the heroes worth trusting are the ones nobody would cast as heroes, crime never pays in any currency that survives the morning, and the higher the throne the longer and uglier the fall. That is why it stands outside its field instead of inside the pack. Other films in the line let you rent the king’s confidence for two hours and settle the bill in a last reel you can half ignore. This one makes the bill the point.

Call the field what it was in that season. American screens already knew the immigrant don, the Cuban meteor, the syndicate boardroom, the cowboy with a ledger. Scarface had already taught a generation to quote excess as if excess were philosophy. The mob picture had already taught loyalty as a sacrament that breaks only when the plot needs a funeral. New Jack City walks into that inheritance and changes the substance under the ritual. The drug is not an exotic import handled by men in linen. It is a cheap, vicious alchemy cooked for the block, sold to the block, and used to seize the block. The empire is not a mansion on a hill. It is the Carter, a whole residential complex occupied, wired, guarded, and converted into a vertical plant where neighbors become inventory. The king does not inherit a family name. Nino Brown builds the Cash Money Brothers out of childhood proximity and calls it blood, then spends the movie proving the name was advertising. The picture is special because it refuses the glamour alibi. It shows the efficiency, the suits, the gold, the weekly fortune, and it also shows the apartments that stop being homes, the bodies that stop being people, and the oath that cannot survive a threat. You are not supposed to leave impressed by the architecture of the hustle. You are supposed to leave convinced that the architecture was a scaffold.

The climb is the first lesson, and it has to be understood before the fall can mean anything. Gee Money puts the future in his friend’s hand and names it. Crack is cheaper to make, crueler in the vein, and endless in demand. Nino does not merely sell it. He industrializes it. Rivals are removed. A building is taken. Floors become departments. Lookouts, cookers, counters, enforcers, a woman with a gun, a cousin who understands numbers, a childhood friend installed as partner: the Cash Money Brothers dress a street crew in the language of a firm. Nino will later say you have to rob to get rich in the era, and the line is the film’s most dangerous piece of rhetoric because it is half diagnosis and half permission slip. The era did abandon blocks. Work did vanish. The drug did arrive like a policy no one voted for and everyone paid for. The film lets that truth stand so that Nino cannot hide inside it. He uses the abandonment as origin story and as business plan. He hands out turkeys and runs a fortress. He speaks like a man who has read the country correctly and then answers it by becoming the thing that finishes the neighborhood. That is the takeaway buried in the ascent. Seeing the wound does not license you to infect it. The higher he gets, the more the Carter stops being a metaphor and becomes a measurement. Every floor is altitude. Every million a week is another story between him and the pavement. You watch the height so you can feel, later, that the drop was priced in from the first handshake.

There is no such thing as my brother’s keeper in crime, and the film does not whisper that law. It stages it until it cannot be mistaken for a twist. The Cash Money Brothers are named like a covenant. Nino and Gee Money come up together. Gee is the one who sees the drug first and brings it to the man who will wear the crown. For a while the picture lets you believe the old street gospel, that the crew is family, that the man beside you from childhood is the exception to greed. Then the empire needs a sacrifice more than it needs a memory. Pressure arrives from the street and from the police. Trust becomes a liability with a pulse. When the question is finally put in the oldest words, Am I my brother’s keeper, Nino answers it the way Cain answered it, by refusing the duty and performing the refusal. Gee Money, the friend who helped invent the throne, dies by the logic of the throne. That is not a shock for shock’s sake. It is the curriculum. In legitimate life, brotherhood can be costly and still be real, because the bond is not a revenue stream. In this life the bond is a tool, and tools are discarded when they jam. The film wants you to stop romanticizing the code. The code is what they say before the money is threatened. After the money is threatened there is only the man who intends to remain standing. You are supposed to learn that loyalty in a criminal house is a costume that fits until it doesn’t, and that the person who calls you brother is rehearsing the eulogy he will not give. Watch Nino’s face when the covenant breaks and take the chill as instruction. If the pact can be murdered by its author, it was never a pact. It was a merger.

The unlikely heroes are the other half of the same scripture, and they matter because the film will not let the villain be the only magnetic body in the room. Scotty Appleton does not arrive as a pristine knight. He is a cop who knows the pavement the way the prey knows it, a man with a private grave in the story, sent undercover into the very weather that made him. Ice cold on the surface, he is the picture’s argument that the person closest to the fire may be the one willing to walk back into it. He is not elevated because he is clean. He is elevated because he chooses the case over the comfort of looking away. Beside him the task force is a scrap assembly of people the department does not quite believe in, led by a commander who has to build a unit out of whoever will take the assignment. The heroism is institutional only in the thinnest sense. It is personal, grudging, and outnumbered. Then there is Pookie, and Pookie is the heart the empire cannot counterfeit. A stickup kid eaten by the pipe, played with a desperation that made audiences forget they were watching a comedian, he claws his way to a clean hour and offers that hour to the investigation. He goes back into the Carter wearing a wire and a hope so thin it looks like an insult. He fails the hope. The drug takes him again. The house kills him for the attempt. If you learn nothing else, learn him. The unlikely hero is not the man who never falls. It is the man who falls, stands up long enough to tell the truth into a microphone, and is destroyed for the telling. His death is the film refusing to let recovery be a montage. Recovery, in that building, is a combat posting. You are supposed to leave with the knowledge that the smallest, least credible person in the story may be the one who paid the real price for everyone else’s plot.

And when the system finishes its part and still cannot close the account, the last unlikely hand belongs to an old man the Carter taught to be invisible. Nino reaches a courtroom and performs the final trick of the high climber. He speaks as a product, a symptom, a man manufactured by a decade of abandonment, and the speech is not empty. The film has already shown the decade. What the speech cannot do is refund the dead. A sentence that looks like survival is not survival. Outside, the elder who lived under the occupation ends the reign in a second that no boardroom philosophy can appeal. Crime never pays, and the film defines payment with a cruelty that is also clarity. It does not mean the criminal never holds cash. Nino holds fortunes. It means the cash is a loan sharked by violence, and the due date is not negotiable. Gee Money is paid in betrayal. Pookie is paid in a body on a floor. The soldiers are paid in raids and graves. The women closest to the crown are paid in disposability. Nino is paid first in a verdict that mocks his invincibility and then in a bullet that mocks the verdict. You are supposed to watch the gold and hear the invoice. Every suit is rented from the future. Every week of a million dollars is a week of interest compounding in blood. The takeaway is not a slogan for a poster. It is an accounting rule. If the profit requires a building full of hostages and a friend in a bag, the profit is a number that has already been spent.

That is also why the height is the trap and not the prize. The Carter is a sermon in concrete. From the street Nino looks like a man who beat the country at its own game, a Black entrepreneur of the forbidden market, quoting the era back to itself. From inside the building he is a warden who cannot leave his own prison without an army. The higher the operation rises, the more it depends on terror, on secrecy, on the silence of people who hate him, on partners who will eventually want his chair or his mercy. Altitude multiplies the witnesses and the enemies at the same rate. A corner dealer can vanish. A man who owns a complex cannot. He has too many floors to defend and too many mouths that remember the turkeys and the corpses. When the fall comes it is not one tumble. It is a sequence of demotions: the wire inside the house, the friend who becomes a problem, the raid that turns the fortress back into evidence, the courtroom where the king has to beg the language of victimhood, the sidewalk where a citizen with nothing left to lose finishes what the badge could not. The higher you get, the more stories you have to fall past, and each story has a face. That is the lesson to keep. Ambition in this world is not a ladder. It is a measurement of how far the ground is prepared to travel up to meet you.

Set against the field, the mastery is in that moral engineering. Plenty of crime films can stage a rise and a shootout. Few can make the brotherhood, the junkie, the undercover man, and the forgotten tenant into one continuous proof. New Jack City is unique because its pleasures are bait. The clothes, the walk, the soundtrack hammering under the images, the snap of Nino’s certainty: all of it is real charisma, and all of it is placed in service of a warning that will not blink. Wesley Snipes does not play a monster who announces himself. He plays a man who could persuade a room that the monster is a mayor. That performance is why the picture became a legend instead of a headline. You believe the height, so you believe the fall. Chris Rock makes the cost human enough that the legend cannot drift into pure style. Ice T, already a voice the street trusted, stands on the other side of the wire and makes the law feel like a man rather than a lecture. The film stands out because it was made from inside the music, the slang, and the emergency, not from a tourist’s notes, and because it still refused to hand the audience a king it was allowed to keep.

Its afterlife is the proof that a warning can be misunderstood and still be immortal. The Cash Money Brothers gave a name and a posture to a record label that would later own radio. The Carter gave a title to albums. Rappers spent decades quoting the walk, the cancel, the brother’s keeper line, sometimes as caution and sometimes as costume. That contradiction is part of why the movie remains a cultural icon rather than a solved case. It was accurate enough to scar, seductive enough to be sampled, and moral enough that the sampling never quite washes the ending off. A lesser film in the field becomes a reference because of a suit or a quote. This one remains a reference because people are still arguing with its ending in their own lives, still testing whether the crew will hold, still discovering that the pipe and the payroll do not care about the speech. You watch it now and the block has changed, the drug has changed costumes, the building in the frame has a different rent, and the law inside the story has not moved an inch. That endurance is the classic. Not nostalgia. Recognition.

It is a must watch because it condenses a national disaster into a fable tight enough to remember and hard enough to respect. You do not need every alley. You need the general shape, and the shape is this. In a city already bleeding from policy and neglect, a crew seizes a home and calls the seizure a business. A broken man tries to undo it and dies trying. A cop from the same world walks into the disguise. A friend discovers he was inventory. A king discovers that height is just delayed impact. If you take those turns as entertainment only, you missed the film. If you take them as instructions, you have the whole education: do not mistake a partner in crime for a keeper of your life, do not wait for a likely savior when the unlikely ones are the ones bleeding on the job, do not audit a criminal fortune before the invoice arrives, and do not envy the top floor of a building that has been turned against its tenants. The legend status is not a marketing phrase. It is what happens when a picture tells a decade’s truth in a hundred minutes and the decade keeps agreeing.

The making of it belongs at the end because the film’s authority does not depend on the trouble behind it, though the trouble explains the heat. Mario Van Peebles was directing his first feature and playing the commander at the same time, a new jack in the chair as well as on the poster, and the studio’s faith arrived in part because Clint Eastwood, who had stood with him on an earlier picture, told Warner to give the kid the shot. The role of Nino had been written for Wesley Snipes, who wanted the cop and was steered toward the king, a redirection that won him an NAACP Image Award and fixed his face to the character forever. Barry Michael Cooper and Thomas Lee Wright built the story out of the crack emergency Cooper had already reported, with the Detroit takeover by the Chambers Brothers echoing under the Harlem fiction, while the camera seized Graham Court and the Bronx and made them the Carter. The budget sat near eight million. They ran so close to the wall that a planned car chase became a bicycle chase, Chris Rock pedaling, Ice T running, poverty turning into the most remembered pursuit in the movie. Dealers, after release, pressed drugs into Rock’s pocket because they thought Pookie was a documentary. The film played Sundance in January of 1991 and opened wide that March, about seven million in the first weekend across fewer theaters than the competition, then ran to roughly forty seven million at home and stood as the highest grossing independent film of that year. The soundtrack climbed to the top of the R&B albums chart and nearly the top of the main chart, Queen Latifah and the rest of that moment welded to the images until the songs became another door into the warning. Producers Doug McHenry and George Jackson got it made. Actors improvised. Money almost killed it. None of that trivia is the reason it lasts. It lasts because the finished object still knows what it is for. A first film, a thin budget, a rapper, a comedian, a leading man redirected into evil, a city playing itself: unlikely hands, again, carrying a story about unlikely hands. The production rhymes with the lesson. What was not supposed to become a monument became one, and the monument still says the same four things. No keeper in that house. No likely saint required. No profit that clears. No height that does not invoice the fall.

Human beings have desires, aspirations, and needs that they will always seek to satisfy—even those most devoid of basic instincts: eating, pooping, and peeing. But here, we are talking about desire and satisfaction.

Their own #Only100 program will provide that sense of "being special" and having exclusivity. All of their fans—even myself, working in this business—follow them for this very reason: to belong to "something" that sets us apart from other groups of people and makes us equal among ourselves. To begin with, we love rock and metal music, beautiful girls, partying, and a certain degree of freedom—which goes hand in hand with respectful interaction on our part, but without censorship on theirs.

There is no deception in that dynamic; there is a very human connection, and the response you give is also deeply human. Not even an "official fan club"—no matter how large its following—can offer you that. The artists' "army," on the other hand, is a community that does not need to be reduced to a number and organizes itself out of pure passion. Here, I am contrasting the corporate approach with fans driven purely by passion.

As for AI-generated content versus content created by humans, as with everything, there is both quality and junk. It is like choosing between a Ferrari and a Fiat: both serve the same purpose—transportation—but exclusivity and performance set them apart. 1/+

A Major U.S. Technological Breakthrough with Global Potential!

A technology that could potentially correct vision to approximately 20/13 in about one minute.

It is reasonable to foresee that, if this technology is successfully translated into human clinical use, industries that depend heavily on selling eyeglasses—and even some laser-based vision-correction technologies—could eventually face disruption from a technology called electromechanical reshaping (EMR).

Despite the name, EMR is not electromagnetic. There is no magnetic field involved. Instead, it uses a weak direct current to electrolytically and temporarily alter the pH of the cornea, then uses a mold to reshape and stabilize its curvature.

The research is led by Michael Hill, a chemistry professor at Occidental College in California, in collaboration with Brian Wong, a professor of surgery and biomedical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

Wong began collaborating with Hill around 2014. The technology was originally developed for reshaping soft tissues, including ex vivo rabbit ears and pig-skin scar tissue. The cornea became a later application.

In 2023, they published a proof-of-concept study in ACS Biomaterials Science & Engineering. In August 2025, they presented more systematic parameter results at the American Chemical Society’s fall meeting.

How the technology works

The cornea’s refractive power comes primarily from layers of collagen fibers within the stroma. These fibers maintain their structure through negatively charged glycosaminoglycans and ionic interactions.

1. Creating the reshaping electrode

A 25-micrometer-thick platinum foil is pressed onto a 3D-printed hemispherical mold to create a “contact-lens-like” electrode with a precisely defined curvature. The electrode is approximately 8 mm in diameter and contains a silver wire as a reference electrode.

2. Applying a weak electrical current

An ex vivo rabbit eye is immersed in saline designed to simulate tears. The platinum electrode is placed against the cornea, and approximately 1.5 volts of direct current is applied in pulses rather than continuously.

3. Temporarily softening the cornea

The electrode drives electrolysis of water in the tissue, generating protons that diffuse into the corneal stroma and lower its pH.

At approximately pH 2, ionic interactions within the collagen matrix loosen, temporarily softening the cornea. Within roughly one minute, the cornea conforms to the curvature of the mold.

4. Locking in the new shape

After the electrical stimulation stops, the pH returns toward physiological levels and the ionic interactions are re-established, effectively stabilizing the newly reshaped cornea.

The entire process is performed without cutting tissue, removing tissue, or using a laser.

However, the pH window is extremely narrow. Around pH 2, the cornea can be reshaped, while dropping toward approximately pH 1.5 can cause the tissue to become cloudy. That is why pulsed stimulation is important: the goal is to bring the entire cornea into the appropriate pH range without allowing the region immediately adjacent to the electrode to become excessively acidic.

In early experiments using continuous electrical stimulation, collagen signals became weaker and less uniform. After switching to pulsed stimulation, microscopic examination showed that collagen organization and cellular viability were largely preserved.

What comes next?

The next steps include in vivo animal studies and the development of electrodes capable of monitoring corneal curvature, hydration, and transparency during treatment.

The researchers have suggested that, if eventually developed for clinical use, the technology could potentially be less expensive than LASIK and might offer some degree of reversibility.

Potential applications for conditions such as corneal opacity and keratoconus have also been discussed as possibilities, but these were not demonstrated in the reported experiments.

Psychology of Child Serial Killer  
Franklin D. McMillion  
School of Law Enforcement Supervision  
Session LIII
Introduction 
Serial murder is one type of homicide which involves the killing of three or more people 
for one month and is characterized by a period of cooling off. The cooling-off period is a time 
whereby the killers do not commit any murder (Knight, 2006, p. 1192). The people who commit 
serial murder are known as serial killers. The crime is not recognized in the United States., as 
there is no current legal code on it. In the history of serial killing, the earliest recorded case of 
serial killers was in 69 CE in the Roman Empire. The serial killer by the name Locusta was 
executed for poisoning individuals from the royal family. In the middle ages, there were serial 
killers recorded in European countries (Vronsky, 2018, p. 15). It has likely been occurring in 
other parts of the world, though it might not be recorded. Research has attempted to suggest 
explanations of the behavior of serial killers and provide an analysis of their personal 
development (Ostrosky & Alfredo, 2017, p. 70). There are two types of serial killers, such as 
child and adult serial killers, in essence (Harmening, 2014, p. 102). A great number of theories 
has been developed to address their actions. Most serial killers have psychological issues, and it 
is through killing that they feel satisfied. History has introduced many serial killers, who are 
adults, but in recent decades the cases connected with children, who are serial killers, are 
becoming frequent. They are dangerous, just like the adults, as they indicate the same 
psychological behavior (Knight, 2006, p. 1198). 
Types of Serial Killers 
Hedonistic Serial Killers 
These are serial killers, who receive pleasure from killing, and thus the experience of 
murder gives them pleasure. There is a strong link between the violence of the murder and the 
sexual gratification. They can have sex with the victim before or after killing the victim (James 
& Proulx, 2014, p. 595). They plan their crime well, and they dismember the body of the victim 
after the murder. They have an insatiable hunger when they feel that it could be satisfied only by 
killing. An example of a serial killer of this category is Jeffrey Dahmer, who was a serial killer in 
the period between 1978 and 1991 (Ostrosky & Alfredo, 2017, p. 77). 
Power and Control Serial Killers 
These serial killers need to exercise their power and control the victim. They first 
humiliate the victim, torture, and then kill their victim. They do not respect the law of the land, 
and they feel that they are above the law. They also seek sexual gratification. Their main goal is 
to gain power and domination, and thus killing makes them feel powerful and in control. Anyone 
they feel to be threating to them is killed as they assert dominance (Vronsky, 2018, p. 49). 
Visionary Serial Killers 
The serial killers in this category are considered psychotic, as their visions and other dark 
forces compel them to commit murder. Whoever these voices and visions tell them to kill; these 
killers go ahead and kill them. Some of them have undertaken psychiatric tests, which proved 
their being mentally unstable. Some of this type of serial killers are possessed by evil forces, 
which drive them to kill.  
Mission-Oriented Serial Killers 
These are considered as ordinary persons, and they kill a particular group of people. They 
may focus on killing people from a specific religion, social class, or race. Their goal is to 
eliminate the group or exterminate as many of its members as possible. An example of these 
serial killers is Joseph Paul Franklin, who killed young black males, because they had white 
girlfriends (Vronsky, 2018, p. 78). 
Characteristics of Serial Killers 
There are numerous characteristics of serial killers, and these are some of them. First, 
serial killers indicate varying levels of psychopathy, which leads to destructive tendencies. They 
are mostly categorized in the type of visionary serial killers. They see things and forces which 
compel them to kill certain people or group of people. After their action, psychotic serial killers 
are gratified and do not show any remorse. In normal circumstances, they are charming and 
brilliant. Psychiatrists have identified that these people can be dangerous because people will not 
know if they are vulnerable until they become victims of their psychopathic actions. (Ostrosky & 
Alfredo, 2017, p. 73). The second characteristic is that when they were young, most serial killers 
were abused in the family. The abuse might have been emotional, physical, and sexual. This 
abuse causes them to be bitter and sometimes seek revenge by killing people (Knight, 2006, p. 
1194). 
The other characteristic of serial killers is that they are aroused by the activity, and they 
find pleasure in the action. Another aspect is that some of them experience one or all the 
Macdonald triad predictors of future violent behavior. The Macdonald triad predictors are a 
fascination with fire-setting, involvement in sadistic actions, and bed-wetting (Seltzer, 2013, p. 
112). The serial killers were isolated during their childhood and teenage years. This isolation 
involved bullying, and the person is seeking to prove that no one can bully him or her since he or 
she has grown up. Some of the serial killers’ targets are people who bullied them or showed 
particular behavior associated with bullying (Carlisle, 2017, p. 17). Some other characteristics 
are that the serial killers might have been involved in petty crimes, and they had trouble staying 
employed (Ostrosky & Alfredo, 2017, p.81). 
Psychological of Child Serial Killer: The Drive and Motivation 
The mental changes that stimulate a child to become a killer originate in the mind. The 
fantasy to kill is the idea conceived in the mind, and the first victim creates a cyclical 
mechanism. A cyclical mechanism is an addiction, and in the brain it creates the circular mental 
process which prompts the person to execute more murders to satisfy his or her fantasy. In mind, 
the mental images created need to be repeated. The primary drive which prompts the brain is the 
creations of imagination (Malizia, 2017, p. 45). 
For example, if a person was abused and feels rejected by family or isolated by society, 
the fantasy of killing would occupy his imagination. The image of killing gives pleasure in the 
mind of a child. The child then replaces the reality in his life with what he has imagined, and this 
gives the potential killer something new to change his past (Seltzer, 2013, p. 112). The fantasy of 
having killed someone gives him or her a misguided opportunity to change his or her past and 
anticipates a better future. Both children and adults, who have created this fantasy, have the 
potential to kill. The imaginative process gives the person gratification to substitute his unhappy 
life experiences. The satisfaction originating from the activity cannot be obtained from any other 
event, but only killing (Malizia, 2017, p. 46).  
The child plans every detail in the fantasy. In the imagination, he or she is choosing the 
victim and the manner of the execution of the crime. Further, he or she establishes the 
relationship with the victim of the crime. There are some fantasies of sexual perversions, as the 
majority of serial killers have utilized paraphilia in their murder execution. Before execution, the 
criminal places himself in the imagination, and then chooses methods in which to assert control 
and dominance over the victim during execution (James & JEAN, 2014, p. 599). 
After the formation of this fantasy in mind, any negative emotion can initiate the child to 
act and commit murder and gain enjoyment in the act. Although in most cases the serial killers 
are adults, children have also proved to be serial killers. The imagination and creation of killing 
fantasy begin when children are old enough to imagine anything. According to environmental 
and family context, in which the children are growing; they have different fantasies and 
imaginations. If the child grows in a family, where violence or any other abuse is common 
practice, they will take refuge in the imagination of how they could be living in other conditions 
or how they can change it (Malizia, 2017, p. 47).  
The imagination creates a fantasy on how the child can dominate over other people. 
These fantasies reach a peak, and then it is time to act. After killing the first time, the cyclical 
mechanism occurs in the brain whereby the child repeats the killing to have the pleasurable 
experience he or she felt the first time. The murder period of another victim will depend on the 
emotional necessity originating from the new fantasies. All serial killers, regardless of their 
killing motive, have the psychological issue with creating fantasies, which they execute. Some of 
these fantasies are fueled by observing violence in videos, so the person becomes obsessed with 
replacing the realities with imaginations from the movies. The execution is triggered when the 
child feels hurt by others either physically, or emotionally, and decides to exert control by 
murdering. 
A child serial killer differs from an adult in that his or her fantasies are developed as 
mechanisms in defense of existing traumatic realities that he or she is denying and not accepting. 
In the case of an adult serial killer, he or she relives the childhood traumatic experiences, but 
since they are not a victim now, they become the aggressors. The child becomes a serial killer 
when imaginations and entertaining fantasies are staying just fantasies, not impressing or 
satisfying him or her anymore, so he or she decides to embody their fantasies into reality (Miller, 
2014, p. 7).

By his own admission Sirhan practiced self-hypnotism using literature supplied at a meeting of a group called the Rosicrucians, an organization that dabbled in the occult.

Sirhan got the “chills” following his arrest and exhibited similar symptoms at the end of hypnosis sessions with a defense psychiatrist. The prosecution psychiatrist also attempted to hypnotize Sirhan but was unable to elicit the assassin’s cooperation. The prosecution psychiatrist said Sirhan had been feigning. 

Additionally, Sirhan was known to enter trance-like states. For the conspiracy-minded this was proof indeed he had been a hypnotic subject. 

However, there is compelling evidence that Sirhan had used his knowledge of a real-life character in Truman Capote’s In Cold Blood (1965) to promote the idea that he had been in a hypnotic state when he shot RFK. Sirhan identified and felt great empathy with murderer Perry Smith, according to author Robert Blair Kaiser. Smith had bouts of “shivering,” “amnesia” and “trance-like states.” Like Smith, Sirhan engaged in “mirror-gazing” and fell into “trances.”

Sirhan, therefore had prior knowledge of hypnotism, trance-like states and amnesia. In fact, he may also have gained some of that knowledge from psychology books he acquired from the local library. Ignoring Sirhan’s numerous lies that he told his lawyers and writer Robert Blair Kaiser, conspiracists preferred instead to take Sirhan at his word. 

Yet, to those who knew Sirhan, this was not at all unusual. Sirhan frequently became fascinated by things around him which prompted him to stare at people or objects. Sirhan told his police interrogators, “Everything . . . life itself is a challenge. . . . When you watch a barber, sir, I just stand and watch that barber for hours. . . . from the time I’m watching him I want to be nothing but a barber. You know, if I’m watching a dentist, boy, he fascinates me, and I want to be him. I was talking to [LAPD officer] Frank here a while ago. The way he talked, you know . . . I was very fascinated and, you know, I was sort of superimposing myself in his position for . . . temporarily.” 

Additionally, those who promote the conspiracy line never question the ludicrous nature of this purported plot. If plotters had successfully hypnotized Sirhan then they would have been equally successful in making sure he didn’t do anything to bring attention to himself before the shooting. But that’s not what happened.

Sirhan uttered contempt for RFK to Enrique Rabago and Humphrey Cordero with whom he engaged in conversation at the hotel. Had these men reported Sirhan to the hotel’s security the alleged plot would have collapsed.

It is also preposterous for plotters to have used an illegal pistol during the commission of their crime. Had police officers and security guards on duty that night stopped and searched Sirhan he would have been arrested. Additionally, the notion of a hypnotic assassin is, by its very nature, an erratic tool. Not even true believers in the robotic assassin notion could possibly be sure Sirhan would not suddenly remember who hypnotized him then secure an immunity deal with the DA to avoid the death penalty.

Sirhan’s familiarity with Capote’s mirror-gazing killer very likely helped construct a diminished-capacity defense for himself to escape the death penalty. He wouldn’t have to confess to or at least recall for a jury his murder of Robert Kennedy if it happened during an “amnesiac episode,” perhaps induced by a “trance state” brought on by “mirror-gazing.”

However, it’s an LAPD interview on tape of a Sirhan acquaintance, Merla Stephens, who worked at a bar in Pasadena, that clinches the idea that Sirhan had full knowledge of how hypnotic subjects behave. 

In the few years before the assassination, Sirhan associated with Arab students during his short time at Pasadena College and afterwards when he flunked out. Stephens talks about how Sirhan and a friend she calls Ali frequented her establishment and acted out a scene in which Ali would pretend to hypnotize Sirhan who then began to behave as though he was a controlled automaton. It is likely Sirhan and his friends were clearly attempting to impress girls. If we are to take their efforts seriously then we must assume they were clearly exposing an alleged conspiracy which included a Manchurian Candidate-type assassin at the center of the purported plot.

Sirhan’s unsuccessful ploys in attracting young women were not unknown to those who knew him. In fact, at one point in his adult years he was so enamored with a beautiful local young woman, Peggy Osterkamp, he wrote about her in his diaries, but knew, as he confessed to author Robert Blair Kaiser, he did not have any chance in attracting her attentions. 

Sirhan’s claims that he had been suffering an amnesiac state and that he could not remember his time in the Ambassador Hotel – he said he only remembered the time he was drinking coffee to sober up to the time of his arrest – is also debunked by his own words. In 2011 Michael McCowan, who acted as a defense investigator for the Sirhan trial defense team, produced a manuscript of notes he made with Sirhan present. 

A statement Sirhan made to McCowan reveals Sirhan’s lies. In response to one of McCowan’s questions, Sirhan told how his eyes had met Kennedy’s in the moment just before he shot him, before Kennedy had fully turned to his left to shake hands with the kitchen staff.

This new evidence in the case, first publicized by author Dan Moldea, effectively destroys the amnesia defense Sirhan continually used at his parole hearings. It shows, clearly and vividly, in Sirhan’s own hand, that he did in fact remember the events of 4/5 June 1968, directly refuting his defense that he suffered from amnesia or was hypnotized and then programmed to not remember.

text:
FIVE9 $FIVN SELLS AI THAT ANSWERS THE PHONE. THE HUMAN SEATS STILL GREW:

The Momentum Len5 is watching Five9 (FIVN) at $34.01, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Wednesday. The San Ramon, California company rents cloud software that runs customer-service call centers, and much of its fee is charged per human agent seat. It is sixth of 30. The verdict: the climb was earned on two report days, and so far its AI is adding revenue without shrinking the seats it already sells. The price has stalled 15% under the $40.00 it touched on September 23, and the next proof is the September-quarter report.

April 10 closed at $13.61. Wednesday is 2.5 times that, and two report days did about half the work:

- May 1, after the March quarter: $22.24, +$5.04 / +29.3%.
- August 7, after the June quarter: $33.99, +$5.62 / +19.8%.

A two-session jump then took it from $32.47 on September 18 to a $38.65 close on September 22. Most of that is gone. Wednesday traded from $33.36 to $34.53 and closed exactly where Tuesday did.

August 6, quarter ended June 30. Revenue, money from customers, was $312.4M, up 10% from $283.3M. Subscription revenue, the recurring fees, rose 14%. AI revenue, software that answers calls on its own or coaches the person on the line, was about $39M, up 78%, about 15% of subscription revenue against 9% a year earlier, management said. The core contact-center line grew 7%.

That is the tension. On the call, management said human seats in use are growing in line with that 7% core, with no sign of customers cutting them. It also said contracts commit customers to a spending level they can shift between human seats and AI agents over three to five years. That protects revenue if seats shrink. It does not show they won't.

The AI cost something. Adjusted gross margin, what is left of each sales dollar after the cost of running the service, fell to 61.4% from 63.0%. Adjusted profit, the company's figure that leaves out stock paid to employees and one-time items, was $0.70 a share, down from $0.76. The year stayed at $3.22-$3.30 a share, while the AI outlook rose to at least 60% growth, from more than 40%.

Two profit figures give two prices. On the $3.26 midpoint, $34.01 is about 10.4 times adjusted profit, 9.6 cents per dollar of stock. The last four quarters of reported profit were $59.5M, 2.3 cents per dollar of the $2.54B market value. The 10-year Treasury yield, what the US government pays to borrow for 10 years, closed Wednesday at 5.293%. The adjusted figure clears it. The reported one does not. The biggest piece of that gap is stock pay: $65.6M in the first half, about equal to the $64.6M of free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment and software.

- MOMENTUM - PARTIAL, sixth of 30. Hunts a stock climbing on real news, with the short climb and the longer one pointing the same way. From March 31's $15.17: +$18.84 / +124%. From June 30's $21.32: +$12.69 / +59.5%. From August 31's $34.56: -$0.55 / -1.6%. The longer climbs agree and came on reported quarters. The month went nowhere. What would knock Five9 off the Momentum Len5: a close under $28.37, the August 6 close, giving back the whole report-day jump. A close above $38.65 after the September quarter would make it a full fit.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT. Hunts a hard-to-copy business at a discount. 10.4 times adjusted profit is the cheap half, and it leans on leaving stock pay out. The hard-to-copy half is unproven: the core grows 7%, and the margin slipped in the quarter AI grew 78%. The Quality Len5, a profitable, sound business at any price, is met, barely: gross profit was $166.7M in June, the last four quarters earned $59.5M on a $784.8M owners' stake, and $747.5M of convertible notes sits $37.3M under it. What would put Five9 on the Quality-Value Len5: seats still growing once AI passes a fifth of subscription revenue, with the margin back above 63.0%. What would knock it off the Quality Len5: buybacks or losses pushing that stake under the $747.5M owed.

- DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - NOT A FIT. Hunts a price below a cautious reading of worth, or an event that changes the math. Cash and investments of $654.1M are less than the notes, and the price is 2.5 times April's. What would put Five9 on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: an offer for the company, or a price back near $13.61 with the June-quarter business intact.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Hunts rising profit at a price that has not paid for the next rise. Reported profit went from a $4.5M loss in the September 2024 quarter to $59.5M over the last four. But June's adjusted $0.70 was under $0.76, September is guided to $0.77-$0.81 against $0.78, and the year leaves about $1.01 for December against $0.80. What would put Five9 on the Growth Len5: that December quarter delivered, with reported profit rising beside it.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT. Hunts very fast sales growth at a size that is already real. $312.4M a quarter is real size; 10% is not the speed. The AI line has the speed, at an eighth of revenue. What would put Five9 on the Hypergrowth Len5: company-wide sales growing several times that 10%.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT. Hunts cash handed to owners that the business can keep paying. No dividend. First-half buybacks were $100.0M against $64.6M of free cash flow, while stock pay kept adding shares. What would put Five9 on the Income Len5: buybacks inside free cash flow, and a share count that actually falls.

Five9 has not set the day for the September quarter. Outside calendars list November 5, after the close. The seat count decides it. Seats keeping pace with the core while AI grows at least 60% makes September's drift a pause. Seats slipping would mean the 78% is coming out of the business Five9 already sells.

Not investment advice.

🔌 The Truth Behind the Data Center Electricity Bill (S. 5028)

The U.S. Senate just blocked the Ratepayer Protection Act (led by Ohio’s own Sen. Jon Husted). It passed the House 417–3 but hit a wall in the Senate.

There is a lot of noise about what this bill actually did—here are the quick, un-spun facts:
T
he Goal: Protect everyday utility ratepayers from footing the bill for massive AI and tech data centers (sites using 100+ megawatts of power).

The Plan: It directed state utility regulators to consider making tech companies pay 100% of the upfront costs for the massive grid and power upgrades they require.

The Catch: It did not mandate anything. Tech companies wouldn't have been legally forced to pay a dime under this federal bill. It simply gave states a 2-year window to look into the idea, leaving the final decision up to local regulators.

⚖️ Why the Senate Split

Critics say: It was a "toothless messaging bill" and an election-eve political stunt. Because the standards were completely optional, they argue it offered no real protection for consumers and lacked actual enforcement power.

Supporters say: It was a crucial first step. They argue it created a much-needed federal blueprint to force states to confront grid equity and shield families from skyrocketing utility bills.
Bottom Line: The bill was essentially a formal, strong suggestion to states to look into making Big Tech pay their fair share—not a mandatory federal law.

text:
OpenAI Launches Marketplace for Enterprise Users

OpenAI has rolled out its new Marketplace, a platform designed specifically for companies already invested in their services. This isn’t your typical app store; it's more like a loyalty program with a twist.

So, what exactly is this Marketplace all about? Well, if you’re an enterprise user who’s already made a financial commitment to OpenAI, you can now use part of that money to purchase products from other partners in the ecosystem. Think Adobe, Figma, Salesforce, ServiceNow, HubSpot, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks, and more. The idea is to leverage your existing investment with OpenAI to get discounts or credits on complementary tools.

But why would companies care? Isn’t this just another way for tech giants to lock in their customers? Not quite. The real value here lies in integration and efficiency. By tying together different enterprise solutions through a single platform, businesses can streamline their workflows and potentially save money by consolidating payments. It’s like having all your utilities under one roof instead of paying for them separately.
What Changed?

The key change is the introduction of this Marketplace as an extension of OpenAI's existing services. Instead of just offering its own products, it now acts as a hub connecting enterprise users to a variety of complementary tools and platforms. This shift means that companies can optimize their tech stack by leveraging discounts or credits from their current investment in OpenAI.
How It Works

The Marketplace operates on the principle of cross-subsidization. If you’re an enterprise user who has already committed significant funds to OpenAI, you can use a portion of those funds to purchase products from other partners within the ecosystem. For example, if your company is heavily invested in OpenAI’s AI services and tools, you might be able to get discounts on Adobe Creative Cloud or Figma for design collaboration.
Concrete Use Cases

Imagine an enterprise that uses OpenAI's language models extensively for customer service chatbots and content generation. This company could now use its existing investment with OpenAI to purchase Salesforce CRM solutions at a discounted rate. By integrating these tools, the business can create a seamless workflow where customer interactions are managed from initial contact through post-sale support.

Another example might be a marketing firm that relies on OpenAI’s AI-driven analytics and content generation services. They could use their existing investment with OpenAI to purchase HubSpot for CRM and marketing automation at a discounted rate, thereby creating an integrated suite of tools tailored specifically to their needs.
What Is Stored?

The Marketplace stores information about your current financial commitments to OpenAI and tracks how you allocate those funds towards partner products. It also keeps records of any discounts or credits earned based on your existing investment. This data helps ensure that the ecosystem remains fair and transparent for all participants.
What Is Excluded?

This platform is not open to individual users or small businesses without a pre-existing commitment to OpenAI. The Marketplace focuses solely on enterprise-level customers who have already made significant investments in AI technologies through OpenAI’s services.
User Controls

As an enterprise user, you control how much of your existing investment with OpenAI you want to allocate towards partner products. You can also choose which partners and products to purchase based on the discounts or credits available. This level of customization allows you to tailor the Marketplace experience to fit your specific business needs.

For instance, if a company has already spent $100,000 on OpenAI’s services, they might decide to allocate 25% of that investment towards purchasing Adobe Creative Cloud licenses at a discounted rate. The flexibility here is key, as it allows companies to strategically invest their existing funds in the tools and platforms that best suit their needs.
Availability

The Marketplace is currently available exclusively for enterprise users who have already made a financial commitment to OpenAI. There are no plans to extend this service to individual developers or small businesses at this time.

This exclusivity means that smaller players might miss out on some of the benefits offered by the Marketplace, such as discounts and credits. However, it also ensures that the ecosystem remains stable and reliable for enterprise-level customers who have already made significant investments in OpenAI’s services.
What This Does Not Prove

While the Marketplace offers potential benefits in terms of integration and cost savings, it does not prove that such an ecosystem will be successful beyond enterprise users. The real test lies in whether smaller players can find value in a tightly-knit partnership model like this one.

For example, while large enterprises might benefit from streamlined workflows and discounts on complementary tools, small businesses or individual developers may not have the same level of investment with OpenAI to take advantage of these benefits. This raises questions about the long-term viability of such an ecosystem for users outside the enterprise space.
Practical Takeaway

If you’re part of an enterprise that’s already invested heavily in OpenAI's services, the Marketplace could offer significant benefits by streamlining your tech stack and potentially saving money through discounts or credits. However, if you're not yet committed to OpenAI, there might be little immediate value for you.

So, what's your take on this? Do you think this kind of ecosystem will catch on beyond just big businesses? Will smaller players find any value in such tightly-knit partnerships?

Let us know in the comments below!

text:
Grok Bot joins OpenAI as 24/7 AI teammate

As we sip our coffee and catch up on the latest in AI, one announcement stands out from OpenAI’s recent Dev Days event. Dots, a persistent AI agent that operates 24/7, is here to change how we interact with technology. But what exactly are these Dots, and why should you care?
What Are These Dots?

Imagine having an AI assistant that doesn’t just wait for your commands but actively monitors your work patterns and steps in when needed. Unlike traditional agents that require explicit instructions, Dots run autonomously, handling tasks like debugging code or managing projects without any input from you. This shift represents a significant change in how we think about AI assistance.
How Do They Work?

Dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra technology and operate on their own cloud-based computer. This setup allows them to access thousands of services through plugins, making them incredibly versatile tools for various tasks. For instance, if a bug report comes up, Dots will notice it, analyze the issue, write a fix, test it, and prepare a pull request—all without you needing to lift a finger.
Early Feedback

Initial reviews suggest that while Dots are promising, they sometimes overstep their boundaries or fail to engage when necessary. It’s like having an overly eager assistant who doesn’t know when to take a break. However, as the technology matures, these issues will likely be addressed and ironed out.
Pricing and Availability

Dots are available on Pro and Business Premium plans in supported countries. Enterprise and educational institutions can get beta access through administrators. The pricing is steep but offers unparalleled convenience for power users who rely heavily on AI assistance. So, if you’re a heavy user of AI tools, Dots might be worth the investment.
Cached Input: A Game-Changer?

OpenAI also introduced Ultrafast, which promises up to 300 tokens per second and significant speed boosts in Codex tasks. However, this feature is exclusive to the Pro plan at $500 per month and Enterprise users. The cached input feature for long-running agents is particularly interesting as it drastically reduces costs by reusing context.
GPT-6.1 Sol: A Cheaper Alternative

GPT-6.1 Sol offers performance close to GPT-6 Astra but at a fraction of the cost. Input tokens are priced at $2 per million, cached input at $0.10 per million, and output at $10 per million. This makes it an attractive option for developers looking to save on AI costs without sacrificing too much performance.
Code Review in Desktop ChatGPT

Code review has become a standalone product within desktop ChatGPT, allowing users to view summaries and diffs before sending reviews to GitHub or GitLab. Codex can even conduct automatic reviews in the cloud, streamlining the process for developers.
Decisions API: Streamlining Choices

The new Decisions API allows you to present specific questions with predefined answers, such as "Is this spam?" or "Which department should I send this request to?" This feature is particularly useful for automating decision-making processes within applications. For example, it can help route customer service inquiries more efficiently.
Plugins and ChatGPT Integration

OpenAI has opened up its platform to developers, allowing them to create plugins that integrate seamlessly into the ChatGPT interface. These plugins can have their own interactive interfaces, workspaces, and viewers for supported file types—essentially becoming full-fledged applications within ChatGPT itself.
Grok Bot: The New Kid on the Block

Interestingly, https://t.co/pGDqzasups now redirects to Grok Bot—a new AI teammate that OpenAI acquired in July. This raises questions about how Elon Musk knew about Dots so early and what role Grok Bot will play in future developments. Will it become a key player alongside Dots?
Sign In with ChatGPT

One of the most intriguing features is “Sign in with ChatGPT,” which allows users to authorize third-party applications using their ChatGPT account, effectively turning it into a universal AI wallet. This feature could revolutionize how we manage and allocate our AI resources across different platforms.
Pro Plan: More for Your Money

The new Pro plan costs $500 per month but offers 25 times more usage than Plus plans, including access to GPT-6 Astra Ultrafast. It’s a significant upgrade for power users who need extensive AI capabilities.
OpenAI Marketplace: The Next Big Thing?

With each iteration, OpenAI continues to refine its marketplace strategy, aiming to create a robust ecosystem of applications and services built around ChatGPT. While past attempts have been met with skepticism, the latest updates show potential for real growth.
What’s Stored and Excluded

Dots store information about your work patterns, tasks they handle autonomously, and any context needed to perform their duties efficiently. However, sensitive data like personal identification numbers or financial details are excluded from storage unless explicitly required by task requirements.
User Controls

Users have control over the extent of Dots’ autonomy through settings that allow them to define boundaries for when and how tasks should be handled. Additionally, users can review and approve actions taken by Dots before they are finalized.
Availability Details

Dots are currently available on Pro and Business Premium plans in supported countries. Enterprise and educational institutions can access beta versions through administrators. Pricing varies based on plan type, with the Pro plan costing $500 per month for extensive AI capabilities.
What This Does Not Prove

While Dots demonstrate significant advancements in autonomous AI assistance, they do not prove that fully self-sufficient AI agents will replace human oversight entirely. There are still limitations and potential risks associated with complete autonomy.
Practical Takeaway

Dots represent a step forward in how we integrate AI into our daily workflows, offering both convenience and efficiency for power users who rely heavily on AI assistance. However, it’s important to approach these advancements with an understanding of their current capabilities and limitations.

What do you think about these new features from OpenAI? Are you excited to try out Dots or Grok Bot? Share your thoughts and experiences in the comments below. Let’s discuss how these advancements might change our tech landscape!

text:
Elon Musk offered $97.4 billion for OpenAI. Sam Altman answered in one line:

"no thank you but we will buy twitter for $9.74 billion if you want"

Exactly one tenth of the offer. Musk replied with one word. "Swindler."

The two started OpenAI together in 2015 as a nonprofit. Musk left the board in 2018 and has been fighting Altman ever since, including in court.

The bid landed in February 2025, right when OpenAI was trying to turn itself into a for-profit company. A few days later OpenAI's board rejected it unanimously. Altman's own guess was that Musk was "probably just trying to slow us down."

I don't think either of them expected a sale. Musk's offer made OpenAI's restructuring harder and more expensive. Altman's reply turned a serious legal move into a meme the whole internet shared.

Still, it's wild to watch two of the richest men in tech fight like this over a company they started together.

Who won this round, Musk or Altman?

The mechanism behind the Bitget affiliate program is quite distinctive. During the campaign, Bitget allocates 30% of its eligible trading fee revenue to a USDT prize pool, a figure updated daily. On the surface, this is merely an update to the prize pool; in reality, however, it offers a glimpse into Bitget’s operational status, allowing the market to track the platform's trading activity and recovery in real time. Of course, fee revenue cannot be directly converted into precise trading volume figures. Fee rates differ between spot and futures markets, and factors such as VIP discounts and zero-fee trading pairs also influence the final data. Nevertheless, with daily public updates to the prize pool, fluctuations in business activity are difficult to conceal. Maintaining this practice for nearly a month, especially in the wake of a security incident effectively places the platform under continuous market scrutiny. 
This is a rather bold move. No sign-up is required, and rewards are settled every seven days: 60% of the prize pool is allocated based on eligible trading volume, while 40% is allocated based on the value of eligible assets. The eligibility threshold for each prize pool is 100 USDT, and rewards will be distributed in USDT within two business days of settlement. Eligible V1–V7 users will automatically receive 30 days of VIP status protection; users who upgrade their tier during the event can still enjoy the benefits of their new VIP level. Publicly displaying select operational data demonstrates the team's confidence in the platform's activity. There is no need to rush to conclusions about business recovery or the return of trust, the daily updated prize pools will speak for themselves. #BitgetAllianceProgram @bitget https://t.co/WFz4C9Lxfh

The old clown caravan is narrow, stale, and overcrowded with the remains of another life: hanging costumes, cracked makeup cases, faded wigs, broken props, and painted faces staring from shelves where no faces should be watching. The ceiling seems lower with every breath. The walls lean inward. Even the little windows offer no escape, only fragments of a dead fairground outside.

There is one door.

And someone is standing in it.

A large clown fills the entrance almost completely, its body framed by the weak carnival lights beyond. It does not step inside. It does not reach for her. It simply stands there, blocking the only obvious way out, its painted smile fixed beneath eyes that do not share the expression.

She recoils instinctively.

The movement lasts only a moment.

One ankle is chained to the floor of the caravan, allowing her just enough freedom to believe she might still escape before the chain pulls tight and proves otherwise. Her wrists are locked behind her back. A soft leather scarf is wrapped firmly across her mouth, swallowing the scream she desperately hopes might wake her.

Her fear has nowhere to go.

The caravan is too narrow to pass the clown. Too cramped to hide. Too sealed to offer another route. She stares toward the doorway with tearful, frantic eyes, caught between the urge to flee and the certainty that there is nowhere left to flee to.

And the clown still does nothing.

It only waits.

In this dream, that is enough.

Coulrophobia — Dreams Behind the Painted Smile

This collection continues our exploration of the unsettling inner world of nightmares.

This time, however, the entire project revolves around a single fear: coulrophobia — the commonly used term for an intense fear or deep unease associated with clowns.

For some people, the painted smile, exaggerated features, artificial expressions, unfamiliar proportions, and strange contrast between comedy and concealment can create something very different from amusement. What is intended to make others laugh may instead provoke anxiety, discomfort, or genuine fear.

And fears carried through waking life do not always remain there.

Our dreaming heroines fall asleep in the safety of their own rooms. The real world is quiet. Nothing threatens them. But somewhere between sleep and subconscious memory, their fear finds another stage.

The clowns return.

Not as performers in an ordinary circus, but as distorted manifestations of the phobia itself.

Across twelve nightmare fragments, abandoned circuses, ruined variety theaters, decaying fairgrounds, forgotten caravans, mirror mazes, silent backstage rooms, old amusement attractions, and other impossible spaces are transformed by dream logic. Familiar entertainment becomes threatening. Cheerful colors decay into something oppressive. Painted smiles become impossible to trust.

Reality bends around the dreamers.

Clowns appear where they should not exist. Sometimes they approach. Sometimes they simply watch. Sometimes their presence is reflected, repeated, magnified, or multiplied until the dreamer no longer knows where the threat truly is.

And sometimes the most frightening clown is the one that does absolutely nothing.

The emotional core of these images is not physical violence.

It is anticipation.

The knowledge that something deeply feared is nearby.

The certainty that escape should be possible — combined with the terrible experience, so familiar from nightmares, that the body suddenly refuses to cooperate.

Running becomes difficult.

Movement becomes slow.

The exit remains visible but unreachable.

And the dream continues.

Symbolic restraints intensify this helplessness throughout the collection. Handcuffs, chains, shackles, ropes, straps, and other forms of confinement transform the familiar paralysis of a bad dream into something visible. They do not define the nightmare. They make its psychology tangible.

The dreamers know what they want to do.

Run.

Hide.

Turn away.

Wake up.

But the dream has already made those simple actions almost impossible.

Even screaming may fail.

Leather gags, tightly wrapped scarves, and different forms of the Mask of Dream Silence repeatedly appear as surreal manifestations of another classic nightmare experience: the desperate attempt to cry out and force oneself awake, only to discover that no voice will come.

The fear therefore remains trapped inside.

Every image captures one of those unbearable moments before awakening — when the nightmare still feels completely real, the clown is still there, escape still seems impossible, and the mind has not yet found the door back to consciousness.

Eventually, morning will come.

The bedroom will return.

The restraints will disappear.

The painted faces will be gone.

But these photographs remain inside the moment before that mercy arrives.

Welcome to twelve fragments of coulrophobic dreaming.

Welcome to the place behind the painted smile.

text:
engine that could never travel the road.
“and be not entangled again”
The command now turns negative: “be not entangled again.” The word pictures something becoming wrapped, caught, or ensnared. The danger is not merely holding an incorrect theological opinion somewhere in the corner of the mind. Legalism wraps itself around Christian experience until liberty becomes difficult to enjoy. A believer begins with one added requirement, then another, then another, until his spiritual life resembles a man trying to run while tangled in fishing net.
The word “again” is especially striking. Many Galatian believers had come from Gentile paganism rather than Mosaic Judaism. Paul had already written in Galatians 4:8 that when they “knew not God,” they “did service unto them which by nature are no gods.” Yet in verse 9 he asked why they turned “again to the weak and beggarly elements” and desired “again to be in bondage.” Pagan religion and Mosaic law were not morally or historically identical, but when sinners use outward religious systems as means of acceptance, both can place men into servant-like bondage. They had escaped one prison and were being offered another cell with more respectable furniture.
This explains why legalism can be attractive even to saved people. Bondage provides visible measurements. It offers lists, comparisons, badges, calendars, and external markers. Grace tells the flesh it has nothing to boast about. Legalism hands Adam a clipboard and tells him to inspect everybody else. The flesh would rather carry a heavy chain it can polish than enjoy a liberty for which Christ receives all the credit.
The warning also shows that doctrinal regression is possible. A believer may be secure in Christ and still become confused in practice. Paul does not say the Galatians need to be saved again; he says they need to stop becoming entangled again. Their standing and their state must be distinguished. Security does not make bad doctrine harmless any more than owning a ship makes sailing onto rocks harmless.
“with the yoke of bondage.”
Paul calls the legal system being imposed upon them “the yoke of bondage.” A yoke was placed upon an animal so another could direct its labor. The image emphasizes restraint, burden, and subjection. Acts 15:10 uses similar language when Peter asks concerning imposing Mosaic requirements upon Gentile believers, “why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples?” Paul’s warning therefore fits the larger New Testament rejection of forcing Gentile believers beneath Mosaic obligation as the basis of spiritual acceptance.
Again, the problem is not that God’s law was evil. The problem is using law for a purpose God never assigned to it. Romans 7:12 calls the law holy. Galatians 3:21 says it could not give life. Those statements fit perfectly together. A yoke designed for one administration does not become the Church’s means of justification merely because God originally made it. No farmer proves reverence for a yoke by fastening it around the neck of somebody God has already set free.
The yoke also stands opposite Christ’s invitation in Matthew 11:29–30: “Take my yoke upon you... For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”Christian liberty is not a life without a Master. Christ remains Lord, believers remain servants in practical service, and obedience remains real. But service to Christ proceeds from life, grace, love, and sonship rather than an attempt to earn righteousness.
Paul therefore closes the verse with a prohibition that reaches beyond Galatia. Do not let anybody make religious bondage sound like spiritual maturity. Do not let a man measure your justification by ceremonies Christ never made conditions of justification. Do not confuse strictness with sound doctrine. A chain can be made of very respectable metal and still be a chain.
