When you begin digging into these eschatological narratives, many increasingly resemble really bad B movies. 

They require such enormous leaps in logic and suspension of disbelief that they cannot pass the smell test. 

This leads me to conclude that much of it is theater, and simply is not true, while other parts are limited hangout and manipulated, concealed and fragmented narratives for the sole purpose of deception, coercion and control.

What I find far more believable is the following:
What if EVERY SINGLE HUMAN BEING descends from a diverse array of highly advanced extraterrestrial human civilizations, tracing back to multiple ancestral lineages and home worlds?

This would make far more sense. It could also explain the extreme controls imposed to prevent humanity from remembering its own identity and ancestry. 

Through various forms of coercion and entrapment, the descendants of these diverse civilizations ultimately ended up here on Earth.

Human diversity, including differences in race and skin color, served a specific purpose and can be traced back to those original civilizations and home worlds. 

These differences arose through adaptations to the distinct conditions of each world: atmosphere, oxygen levels, pressure, climate, weather, terrain, number of suns, solar-system organization, and other environmental factors.

Over time, humanity’s ancestral memory, our knowledge of and connection to our extraterrestrial human ancestry, was erased or “blank-slated.”

Human beings were stripped of their true historical identities and severed from their connections to highly advanced civilizations. They were then persuaded either that they “evolved from mud puddles” or that they were “created” by so-called “gods.”

But what if those so-called "gods" were nothing more than competing advanced civilizations, or rival factions operating within those civilizations who retained and then stripped and are now hiding what we view as "advanced" technology when in reality, it's normal prosaic technology from the perspective of ancient advanced competing civilizations. 

Who have coerced and entrapped the descendants of their rivals, (us) and then brainwashed those descendants into worshiping the very powers that controlled them. 

This system exploited a fundamental form of trauma-based mind control.

First, every connection to core identity and ancestral memory was severed.

Collective memory could then be rewritten so that these remnant extraterrestrial human descendants retained no knowledge of their own historical legacy. 

Once they had forgotten that they descended from advanced civilizations, they could be made to accept an imposed identity as a purely “terrestrial” human species.

Within such a system, individual governments could be offered separate technological agreements while nations were maneuvered into serving as proxies in conflicts between competing factions. 

Humanity would experience the visible wars while remaining unaware of the deeper architecture producing them.

THE GARDEN: ZOO OR NURSERY?
This brings us to the present crossroads: What kind of “garden” is Earth, and what is it ultimately meant to become?

Within this larger history, Earth could be understood as an off-site seed bank, a living repository intended to preserve the human DNA and ancestral lineages of many advanced extraterrestrial civilizations. 

This would be the “genetic intervention” broadly described throughout ancient texts.

Here is the twist: those entrusted with protecting the garden ultimately transformed stewardship into captivity.

The extraterrestrial offspring gathered here were entrapped. Their ancestral memories were erased, and their identities were reduced to those of an isolated terrestrial species.

Two competing agendas are now in conflict over the purpose and destiny of this garden.

These agendas may not correspond neatly to individual species. Rival factions could exist even within the same civilization or species, with some acting benevolently, some malevolently, and others occupying a complicated space somewhere in between.

The “zoo” agenda is the short-term agenda of containment.

It seeks to keep humanity enclosed, observed, managed, divided, and unaware of its true origins. 

Its power depends upon maintaining the blank slate, preventing the offspring preserved here from remembering who they are, where they came from, and what they may eventually become.

The zoo agenda depends upon managed conflict, fragmented identity, imposed amnesia, and competing claims of "chosenness". 

Humanity remains divided into nations, races, religions, and rival populations while external factions negotiate separately with governments and preserve the larger control architecture.

The “nursery” agenda represents something fundamentally different: preservation, protection, maturation, remembrance, sovereignty, and eventual reconnection.

A nursery does not permanently imprison its offspring.

It safeguards them as they develop, preparing them to awaken to their inheritance and eventually take their place within the larger family of advanced civilizations from which they descend.

The immediate condition may be the zoo. But the garden’s long-term destiny is the nursery.

That is the crossroads now before humanity: whether we remain a contained population with no memory of who we are, or awaken as a maturing family of ancestral lineages, reclaim our shared inheritance, and remember our place within a much larger universe.

From this perspective, governments may not represent the highest level of the system at all. 

They may function as intermediaries, or proxies, within conflicts whose true history, participants, agreements, and objectives remain concealed from the populations being affected.

This would also mean that genuine disclosure cannot stop with craft, bodies, or technology.

It must include the control architecture, the agreements made with individual governments, the competing factions, their historical interventions, and the truth about humanity’s ancestry.

To reiterate: I believe there is a high probability that the connection we all share is that ALL human beings descend from many diverse, highly advanced extraterrestrial human civilizations.

We have all been lied to.

Even those convinced that they are “the chosen ones” have been lied to. 

They, too, have been deceived into subjecting themselves and others to unspeakable crimes against humanity and consciousness itself.

We have all been stripped of our true identities, and of the possibilities that this shared understanding could offer us, our descendants, and their future.

This may explain why every human being possesses a deep, intrinsic fascination with advanced and exotic technology: the home worlds and civilizations from which we came were, and still are, highly advanced.

We are not native to this planet. We are immigrants who have been stripped of our memories of home.

But those memories have not forgotten us.

A deep connection remains embedded within our souls, one that cannot be broken without our consent. 

We all carry suppressed fragments of these connections, concealed beneath the imposed amnesia.

That buried memory is the fundamental threat to the control system, or systems, because as we remember to remember, we begin to awaken to the truth of who we are.

The answer is not to choose another faction to worship, obey, or depend upon for salvation. 

It is for humanity to recover its shared identity, memory, inheritance, and sovereignty.  

So remember to remember what resides deep within.

At the end of the day, we are all living within a memory system, not an illusion and not a holographic system, but something far more powerful and far less understood.

Memory is a loop that recognizes itself in order to survive, exist, and persist.

We do not need to be "saved" by some external force that can be astroturfed and tricked into showing up because a "signal fire" is lit. 

What is a signal fire anyway, suffering, misery, genocide and mass murder?).  

Together we are the unified recursive return that will ensure that the loop survives. 

Remember to remember that the past, present and future are all right here in the present - we're all here - and we just need to wake up.

text:
$VICR makes modular power components and systems, with the market’s current interest centered on high-density power delivery for AI processors and data centers. The stock has been a momentum name on that theme, and the latest leg higher is mostly about patent licensing turning into near-term royalty revenue.

What the company does
Vicor, founded in 1981 and still led by founder Patrizio Vinciarelli, designs and manufactures power modules based on its Factorized Power Architecture. The piece investors care about most is Vertical Power Delivery (VPD): bringing higher voltage (often a 48V bus) close to the processor and multiplying current at the point of load. AI accelerators draw extreme current at very low voltage, so distribution losses and board space are binding constraints. Vicor claims current density above about 3 A/mm² for its second-generation VPD, versus roughly 1 A/mm² for some rival approaches, which would cut conduction losses and support denser racks.

It also sells into industrial, aerospace, defense, and test equipment. Recent results show both product sales and royalties growing: Q2 2026 revenue was about $143 million (up roughly 49% year over year), with royalty revenue a large part of the increase and gross margin around 58%. Product backlog was about $380 million, up 145% year over year and 26% sequentially.

Why the market likes it
The bull case is that AI power delivery is a bottleneck, Vicor’s patents and density claims give it leverage, and licensing can add a high-margin second revenue stream on top of module sales. Management has said four leading OEMs and hyperscalers now hold licenses. Licensees can source patent-covered modules from Vicor or from other suppliers and pay royalties, which supports multi-source supply chains while still monetizing the IP. Early adopters have been offered lower rates.

Capacity is part of the story too. In mid-September Vicor said it was acquiring sites in Merrimack and Hooksett, New Hampshire, for ChiP Fab-2 and Fab-3 (nearly a million square feet combined) because its Andover fab is nearing full utilization. Management has also talked about a long-term revenue ambition on the order of $2.5 billion, well above the recent run-rate near $450–475 million trailing twelve months. Analyst targets cited in coverage have clustered well above recent prices (figures around the mid-$300s to about $390 have appeared), though those move with the stock.

Why some investors do not
The valuation is demanding after a very large move. One-year gains have been on the order of several hundred percent; the stock closed September 30, 2026 around $289 (up about 54% over the prior 30 days) and was indicated higher after the latest guidance raise, with a market cap in the low-to-mid teens of billions against still-modest absolute revenue. Trailing and forward earnings multiples are high, and sales multiples have been well above many power and semiconductor peers.

Competition is real. Monolithic Power Systems is the established leader in much of the AI power-module market and is far larger; Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Infineon, and others also compete. Vicor has lost sockets on some platforms in the past. Results are concentrated in a few large customers and in AI capital spending, so orders can swing. Royalties are lumpy and partly tied to patent enforcement and licensing negotiations rather than pure product pull-through. New fabs also bring execution and capital-spending risk if demand slips. The stock is volatile (beta well above 1) and has already had sharp drawdowns even inside the uptrend; the 52-week range has run from the high $40s to about $383.

Why the price has been climbing recently
The September move was a sequence of company-specific catalysts, not a broad market effect:

September 11: announcement of the New Hampshire fab sites, read as confirmation that demand is outrunning current capacity, alongside the large backlog.
Around September 16–17: a non-exclusive VPD license to an unnamed leading AI OEM, allowing that customer to buy covered modules from unlicensed suppliers while paying Vicor royalties.
September 21: Q3 sequential revenue-growth guidance raised from nearly 10% to more than 20%, explicitly tied to royalties from that license. The CEO noted that unlicensed hyperscalers had approached the company after import issues related to infringing modules, and that VPD systems could face similar restrictions.
September 30: guidance raised again, from more than 20% to more than 30% sequential growth, citing higher royalties from that first non-exclusive VPD license. The stock jumped in after-hours trading on the news.

In short, the market is paying up for evidence that Vicor’s AI power patents are converting into royalties sooner than management had previously suggested, on top of already strong product demand and a capacity build-out. Whether that justifies the multiple depends on how durable and scalable the licenses prove to be versus product competition and AI spending cycles. Earnings are expected around October 20, 2026, which should show how much of the raised outlook actually landed in the quarter.

text:
The color of your hair may change how even your skin looks to others | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

New research published in Perception indicates that the color of a person’s hair and the background behind them can change how other people perceive their skin. By altering the visual contrast around a face, scientists found that darker hair and black backgrounds tend to make facial skin appear more even. The findings suggest that everyday styling choices have visual effects that may influence how healthy and attractive a person appears to others.

The central focus of this research is perceived skin evenness, which refers to how uniform a person’s skin color and surface texture appear to an observer. When skin has a steady distribution of color and lacks bumps, spots, or wrinkles, observers tend to judge the face as younger, healthier, and more attractive. Beyond physical attractiveness, observers often link smooth skin to abstract social traits like trustworthiness and competence. Because these social judgments carry heavy weight in daily life, understanding exactly what makes skin look even is an active area of study.

Researchers already know that the biological condition of the skin plays a primary role in how it looks. But human visual perception is complex, and the appearance of skin is also swayed by the features directly next to it. Past work demonstrates that increasing the visual contrast between the skin and facial features like the eyes, lips, and eyebrows actually makes the skin itself look more even. This visual illusion happens even when dark makeup is applied only to the eyes and lips, leaving the skin entirely untouched.

“Previous research has found that increased contrast between skin and adjacent surfaces increases perceived skin evenness,” lead researcher Carlota Batres, an associate professor of psychology at Franklin & Marshall College and the director of the Preferences Lab, told PsyPost. “Our study aimed to examine whether this effect can be extended to situations where the entire face is left untouched and contrast is modified by increasing or decreasing the luminance of surfaces surrounding the face.”

This visual effect is thought to stem from a basic processing mechanism in the brain known as contrast gain control. In simple terms, this means the human visual system evaluates the brightness and texture of a specific region relative to its immediate surroundings. The research team, which also included Richard Russell at Gettysburg College, wanted to know if this visual mechanism operates over larger spatial distances. They set out to test whether modifying the contrast entirely outside the face, by changing hair lightness or background color, would still trick the eye into seeing more even skin.

The neurological reach of this mechanism was previously unclear. “The effects of contrast gain control are believed to operate within but not across cortical hypercolumns, meaning I was not sure this effect would be present across greater spatial expanses such as the contrast surrounding the face,” Batres explained. “In other words, previous studies have addressed contrast within the face, and here we aimed to address contrast outside the face.”

To explore this, the researchers set up two separate experiments. In the first experiment, they gathered photographs of 45 white women ranging in age from 19 to 79. All the women were photographed facing forward with neutral expressions. The scientists selected images where the hair could be entirely masked by an oval border, leaving only the facial skin and features visible.

For each face, the researchers created two versions. One version placed the face against a high-contrast black oval background. The other version placed the face against a low-contrast, skin-colored background, which was created by averaging the actual skin colors from the cheeks of the photographed faces. A group of 61 participants recruited online viewed these 90 images one by one in a random order.

For each image, participants rated the evenness of the person’s skin on a scale from one to seven, where one meant very uneven and seven meant very even. The participants were instructed to look for similar coloration throughout the face and a lack of blemishes, spots, and blotchiness.

The results of the first experiment showed that the background color shifted how observers rated the skin. When faces were presented against the high-contrast black background, their skin was rated as more even, scoring an average of 4.18 out of 7. In comparison, the exact same faces received an average evenness score of 3.95 when presented against the low-contrast skin-colored background. This effect appeared whether the face being judged belonged to a younger woman under 30 or an older woman over 30.

The second experiment aimed to test this visual effect using a more natural, everyday adjustment. The researchers selected a new set of photographs featuring 41 white women, again spanning ages 19 to 79. This time, they specifically chose images with a sharp visual boundary between the person’s hair and their skin.

Using photo editing software, the scientists slightly altered the lightness of each woman’s hair. They created two versions of each face: one where the hair was lightened by a small set amount, and one where the hair was darkened by the same amount. A new group of 80 online participants rated the skin evenness of these 82 images using the same one to seven scale from the first experiment.

Just like the background colors, the hair lightness shifted the participants’ perception of the skin. Faces with artificially darkened hair were rated as having more even skin, with an average score of 4.06. When the exact same faces were shown with lightened hair, the average skin evenness score dropped slightly to 4.01, representing a small difference of just 0.05 points on the seven-point scale.

When the researchers separated the faces by age, they noticed a difference in how hair lightness affected perception. The visual trick was not statistically significant for the younger faces, whose skin was generally already quite uniform. However, for the older faces, the darkened hair made the skin appear more even. The researchers suspect this is because the hair manipulation was a very mild adjustment compared to the stark black background used in the first study, making its subtle effect only detectable on faces that started with more uneven skin.

“Many practices of grooming and personal decoration involve surfaces adjacent to the skin, such as hair, clothing, or other backgrounds, and the results of this study show that these social practices have perceptual consequences related to skin appearance,” Batres noted. The results confirm “that the contrast between the facial skin and the surfaces surrounding the face, whether background color or hair color, influence perceived skin evenness.”

These modest visual effects offer a potential scientific explanation for certain fashion and grooming preferences. Past research shows that women are often rated as more attractive when wearing black clothing. The new findings suggest this boost in attractiveness might happen partly because dark clothing provides high contrast against the skin, making the face look more even and healthier. Similarly, women are often rated as more attractive when wearing their hair down rather than pulled back. Hair framing the face increases the visual contrast directly next to the skin, which might naturally boost perceived skin evenness.

As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied exclusively on photographs of lightly pigmented white women, meaning the results might not automatically apply to faces of other races or genders. It remains unknown if this contrast trick works in the exact same way for people with darker skin tones, or if different hair and background combinations might be needed to achieve the highest contrast.

Another point to consider is the subtle nature of the hair edits in the second experiment. The researchers only adjusted how light or dark the hair was, keeping the original color family intact. “Our hair manipulation was slight, and it would be interesting for future studies to further examine this effect,” Batres said.

Future studies could test more dramatic hair changes, such as shifting entirely from blonde to black, to see if more extreme contrast creates a stronger illusion of even skin. This could be done “by changing the hair color altogether to one that is high contrast relative to each face’s skin tone versus one that is low contrast relative to each face’s skin tone,” Batres added. The researchers also hope to test other common facial accessories, like glasses, hijabs, or jewelry, to see how they interact with skin perception.

my favorite part of the cycle is @rabois election forecasting, where he's historically contrarian and right - a summary of his September political views:

## Politics: an all-out war against conventional election forecasting

A huge fraction of the month consists of Rabois arguing that prevailing expectations about the 2026 U.S. midterms are badly wrong.

His position is remarkably stable:

- Republicans will hold the House.
- Republicans will gain Senate seats.
- Polls suggesting major Democratic gains are implausible.
- Prediction markets are not informative enough to move him.
- Several specific Democratic-looking state polls are sampling artifacts or otherwise misleading.

He repeatedly mocks polling suggesting strong Democratic performance in Iowa, Texas, Michigan, Minnesota, and elsewhere. When a poll shows surprisingly large Democratic leads in Iowa, his reaction is “ROFL.” When market probabilities imply a Democratic sweep, he calls the participants “morons.”

The strongest substantive version of his argument appears indirectly through a quoted critique of a Texas poll. The criticism is not simply “I dislike the result.” It argues that the sample contains implausibly many college-educated, wealthy, metropolitan and independent voters relative to the expected Texas midterm electorate.

That gives a better sense of what Rabois thinks is happening: **nonresponse and composition error** are creating electorates inside polling samples that do not resemble the people who will actually vote.

He is also highly suspicious of aggregate approval numbers. When confronted with worsening Trump approval averages, he points people toward Rasmussen and dismisses pollsters that had Harris performing strongly in 2024.

There is a clear intellectual through-line:

> Previous polling failures are not random noise; they reveal structural defects that remain unfixed.

Whether that inference is justified is unresolved inside the corpus, but it is important because Rabois is not treating each poll independently. He thinks the industry has a persistent model error.

The comedy comes from his willingness to turn this into actual bets.

Someone challenges him: \`$100k\`.

Another offers \`$50k\`.

Rabois agrees and tells the latter:

> “may the loser be mocked relentlessly on twitter.”

That sentence captures his preferred epistemic institution surprisingly well: make falsifiable predictions, put money behind them, then publicly humiliate the loser.

text:
Here's what you might call a "cold case" from the files of anonymous or pseudonymous works by unknown authors. 🗄️❓🧐 Any guesses? I don't suppose Herman Melville (pretty busy wrapping up THE WHALE) wrote the tasty ode to "Pumpkin Pies" that first appeared in the NY Tribune on July 8, 1851, but still can't say who did. Composed "By a Vermonter" ostensibly but submitted  from "Pavilion, N. Y." Readers ate it up; this same "Pumpkin Pies" poem would be reprinted in numerous newspapers, including the Pittsfield, Mass. Sun on August 21, 1851. 

The "Vermonter" alias is one Melville definitely liked well enough to appropriate, if the use of a pseudonym could boost sales of his next book. In a letter dated April 16, 1852 to London publisher Richard Bentley, Melville offered to issue PIERRE "anonymously, or under an assumed name:— 'By a Vermonter' say."

PUMPKIN PIES . . . For The Tribune.
BY A VERMONTER.

LET some folks boast of spicy mince,
     Care not a fig for such do I;
Or largely talk of sweetened quince,
Fine as the luscious grapes of Lintz,
     Plums doubly dipped in Syrian dye--
I deem them tasteless all as flints,
     Compared with one good pumpkin pie.

I know our pumpkins do not claim
     The honored growth of foreign soil;
They never felt the torrid flame,
And surely they are not to blame,
     Though reared not by the bondman's toil,
In climes where man, to burden tame,
     Unpaid consents to tug and broil.

Talk not of vineyards breaking down,
     And fields that droop with oil and wine,
Where burning suns with ripeness crown
The sweets that man's best manhood drown,
     By lying poets sworn divine.
I rather have than all--don't frown--
     The product of my pumpkin vine.

See, on yon melon-covered hight,
     My chosen fruit, like globes of gold,
Lies ripening in the sunbeam's light;
Ah, 'tis a stomach-staying sight,
     And soon, to house them from the cold,
Shall freemen with strong hands unite,
     Paid laborers and freemen bold.

And then the girls who make our pies,
     Bless them! all other maids outshine,
Their raven locks, and hazel eyes,
And cheeks, whose ever-changing dyes
     The lily and the rose combine,
Make mad the hearts that lose the prize
     Of all this loveliness divine.

Vermont! thou art a glorious State,
     Though small in acres and in skies;
But 'tis not length that makes one great,
     Nor breadth that gives a nation size.
Thy mountains and thy mountain air
     Have reared a noble race of men,
And women, fairest of the fair,
Their labors and their love to share.
     Where shall we see thy like again?
I love thee all, which most I shan't advise,
Thy mountains, maidens, or thy pumpkin pies.

Pavilion, N. Y., 1851.
***
Image via the Library of Congress, Washington, DC

text:
Three oil tankers passed through Hormuz with their lights off. They were hit anyway. This is the state of the strait "open" since October 1st.

According to Reuters, citing Maersk, three Liberian-flagged vessels were struck by unidentified projectiles on Tuesday while transiting with their AIS turned off. The product tanker Al Ruwais and the VLCC Mersin Prosperity are managed by ADNOC Logistics; the Aframax Sinbad had loaded products at Jubail. Two of them had already conducted ship-to-ship transfers off the coast of Sohar, Oman. This is not an American convoy; it is traffic trying to avoid detection.

Traffic figures do not align, and that in itself is the signal. AIS monitoring shows visible transits at just a fraction of the pre-crisis level of around 85 per day, whereas other analysts speak of a near-return to normal. Both could be true if half the flow is moving in the dark. Brent crude hovering around $100 does not reflect a reopening; it reflects a war premium that has not dissipated.

Iran is not disputing the reopening itself, but rather the corridor. Abbas Araghchi warned that an alternative route along the Omani coast, announced by Muscat in conjunction with the IMO, complicates the memorandum and delays the reopening. The IRGC insists that the only authorized routes are those designated by Tehran. Yet, vessels continue to use the Omani side. Tuesday’s strike hit precisely the traffic that had stepped outside the Iranian scheme.

Diplomatic efforts were launched that very same night. Axios reports that on Monday, after talks stalled, Marco Rubio called on the Iranian UN delegation, including Araghchi, to leave New York. They departed for Doha at 1:20 AM on Tuesday. A second source notes that the departure was scheduled anyway. The sequence matters less than the message: there is no signed agreement governing the strait.

Washington controls two valves. CENTCOM diverts commercial vessels away from Iranian ports while ensuring that oil shipments get through. Tehran seeks a "transit fee" in the form of a corridor rather than a formal levy. Oman offers a shoreline. Insurers react to the projectile, not the press release.

Three ships, with their AIS turned off, were struck between Sohar and Jubail. This doesn't shut down the market; it keeps prices high until after the midterms.

They send you to get an MRI. They hand you a blue gown. You go into a dressing room and take off your blouse and skirt. You slip into the hospital gown. You tie it tightly in the back, but you still feel exposed.

You lay on the table. The room is empty. Then you feel it. The loss of control. Again. Right there on the table. You are alone in the room. You can't move. You can't call for help.

The door creakes open. Help is coming, you hope.

A man enters. He sees you on the table, dressed in nothing but a hospital gown. 

Unable to resist.

He sees his opportunity. He unties the gown, exposes you, and does things that I will not mention here. While you cannot move. While you cannot cry out. While you cannot fight back.

Later, you report it. The police contact the hospital. The surveillance footage shows it all. The man is arrested.

Before justice can be done, however, the District Attorney swoops in, like a hero wearing a cape, to save the day.

But not for you. For the man who violated you.

She offers him a plea deal. 30 days in jail. That's all his abuse of you is worth, in her eyes. One month.

This prosecutor says she wants to reduce "unnecessary" punishments.

Key Players in the Crowd-for-Hire Industry
• Crowds on Demand: The most famous and widely cited firm specializing in advocacy campaigns, protests, rallies, and PR stunts. Founded by Adam Swart in 2012, Crowds on Demand operates nationwide across major U.S. cities. In media interviews, the company notes that its network comprises individuals who are compensated for expressing points of view that align with their sincere beliefs on both sides of the political aisle. The firm provides everything from "fans" and "paparazzi" for corporate galas to specific demographics for targeted demonstrations.
• Crowds Now: A global marketing platform that functions like an app-based gig service. Rather than political advocacy, Crowds Now focus strictly on corporate and retail experiences. Businesses utilize the app to rent on-demand crowds to fill empty restaurants, generate instant energy at music venues, or act as film extras and brand advocates.
• Models In Tech: Operating in major metropolitan hubs like San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, Models In Tech focuses on the corporate and trade show market. They explicitly offer "crowd gatherers" tasked with physically drawing audiences into convention booths, generating leads, and establishing a lively presence around new product rollouts.
How These Operations Work
• The Use of Actors & Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs): Many participants recruited for these events are professional background actors or gig-workers. To protect the reputation of the clients—whether they are a brand, a venue, or a political entity—recruits are heavily vetted and usually required to sign strict NDAs.
• A Standard Business Model: According to financial breakdowns by Investopedia, clients are generally billed a premium fee while the individual crowd participants are compensated on a flat per-gig rate or an hourly wage (often starting around $15 to $20+ per hour depending on the complexity of the request).
• Distinction from Crowd Management: It is important not to confuse these agencies with massive event-staffing corporations like BEST Crowd Management or Contemporary Services Corporation (CSC). Those companies do not provide simulated crowds; instead, they provide logistical labor, such as ushering, ticketing, and stadium security for genuine, large-scale public events.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗗𝗶𝗱 𝗪𝗮𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝘂𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗧𝘂𝗿𝗸𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻?

There are a number of reports and signs of US combat search and rescue teams on Ogurja Island, in the south-east Caspian, directly north of Iran, alongside a quieter special forces buildup in Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan. 

The diplomacy wrapped around it is not and I have been watching it since last year.

In May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Turkmenistan's foreign minister, Rashid Meredov, and the two governments have since spoken openly about deeper cooperation on energy security and export routes. 

This month Rubio leads a delegation of more than 100~ American companies into Central Asia. That is the what American courtship and foreign policy looks like...

The location is the point. Combat search and rescue is what a military positions when it expects to pull "downed aircrew" out of hostile ground. 

No one forward-deploys it without planning to fly combat missions nearby. 

From Ogurja, a combat Blackhawk helicopter is roughly an hour from the Iranian coast and about 90 or so minutes from Tehran.

Now add the fact most people miss. Turkmenistan is a constitutionally neutral state, a neutrality the UN itself recognised in 1995. 

Hosting foreign combat forces breaks that posture completely, and a country does not surrender its neutrality for nothing, so whats behind such a drastic measure?  

My assessment is that the price is being paid in exactly what Rubio arrived carrying: energy deals, investment, and guaranteed export routes for Turkmen gas.

The real question is what Ashgabat was offered to open the door, and whether it has already said yes.

Watch this area, more coming in the coming months...

according to your steadfast love;  
  
according to your abundant mercy  
  
blot out my transgressions.

text:
Eighteen States Now Offer Licenses to Doctors Trained Abroad Without U.S. Residency

Eighteen states now allow some doctors trained abroad to seek full medical licenses without first completing a residency in the United States or Canada.

The Federation of State Medical Boards lists Arkansas, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin as having enacted such laws. Twenty more states have considered similar bills.

Two states moved from law to practice this year. The Texas Medical Board began accepting applications on February 25 for licenses created by HB 2038, the DOCTOR Act, including provisional licenses for qualifying foreign physicians. North Carolina's Internationally-Trained Physician Employee License took effect August 1. It requires employment at an eligible hospital or rural practice along with substantial clinical experience.

The rules differ by state, and most pathways require more than a foreign medical degree. Florida requires an active foreign license, four years of recent practice, qualifying postgraduate training and credentials from the Educational Commission for Foreign Medical Graduates. Virginia issues a restricted license first and allows an application for an unrestricted license after at least two years of qualifying practice. Common conditions across states include verified training abroad, examinations, credential review, supervised or provisional practice and a qualifying job.

International medical graduates make up about one-quarter of the U.S. physician workforce and provide substantial care in underserved communities, according to a 2024 report from the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education, the federation and Intealth. The three organizations formed an advisory commission to study alternative licensing models. States have cited physician shortages as the main reason for the new routes.

A state license is one of several credentials a physician needs. Specialty board certification comes from separate certifying bodies, and each hospital decides which doctors may treat patients there. A state license does not grant either one. Physicians who are foreign nationals also need federal authorization to work in the United States, which state law cannot provide.

Federation materials describe U.S. residency as a period of supervised practice in which physicians learn American clinical practice, health system organization and patient populations. The alternative pathways rely on experience checks and restricted practice in its place.

The available records do not show how many physicians have received licenses through the new routes, how many have moved from provisional to full licenses, or whether they stay in underserved areas. Patient outcomes and disciplinary rates for these doctors have not yet been compared with those of physicians who completed U.S. residency.

Bringing People Joy Through Bagpipes

I'm in Clarksville, Tennessee, and suddenly I hear bagpipes.

So, of course, I had to go find out who was playing them. 😂

That's how I met Elijah Ritchie.

Elijah has been playing the bagpipes for about six years after someone at his church taught him.

And I loved his reason for being out there.

Sometimes he simply takes his practice outside because he wants to bring a little unexpected joy into people's lives.

How freaking cool is that?

Then I asked him to play something people might recognize.

It took me a second...

Star Wars. 😂

Elijah also plays professionally for weddings, funerals, graduations, company functions, and other events around Clarksville.

He's just getting his business going again after school and is working on rebuilding his online presence.

So we're going to help him out.

I even offered to give him a free website if he wants one.

Because when you meet somebody using their talent to make other people's day a little brighter, sometimes the best thing you can do is help them reach a few more people.

Great meeting you, Elijah.

Keep playing and keep bringing people joy.

text:
Today’s Daily Brief covers ARPA-H launching the SURPASS clinical trial modernization framework alongside the STACK, COMMONS, and CINCH programs, CMS directing $20 million in Rural Health Transformation Program funding to upgrade telehealth, IT, and cybersecurity across rural North Carolina, the NIH Director clarifying reports on clinical trials at the National Cancer Institute, and a new USDA investment in the Regenerative Pilot Program.

1. ARPA-H Launches SURPASS Program

ARPA-H launched the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program alongside other initiatives (STACK, COMMONS, and CINCH),  to modernize clinical trials. According to ARPA-H, SURPASS will utilize “advanced computational models, real-time analysis, shared infrastructure, and automation to evaluate drugs and biologics faster, at lower cost, and with fewer participants.”

SURPASS aims to replace slow, sequential trial phases with continuous, adaptive platform trials that integrate digital twins and predictive models. The initiative will enable always-valid real-time inference, and automate operations.

The three other problems were defined in the following way:

“STACK will help create more domestic clinical sites and support more efficient trial enrollment. The project aims to use artificial intelligence to accelerate clinical site activation and convert research-naïve sites into clinical trial sites capable of running studies, expanding trial capacity and helping more patients access research opportunities closer to where they live.

COMMONS will build the connective tissue for nationwide data infrastructure. The project aims to create a privacy-by-design architecture for consent at national scale and enable access to regulatory-grade data. That data access will be critical for rapid clinical trial enrollment, predictive computational models, and other modernization efforts needed across the U.S. clinical trial ecosystem.

CINCH will focus on patient empowerment and care navigation. The project aims to help patients contribute their own real-world data and benefit directly from it — supporting continuity of care, better care coordination, and faster identification of clinical trials that may be appropriate for them.”

According to Secretary Kennedy, “America should lead the world in turning medical breakthroughs into treatments for patients. HHS is taking on the delays, duplication, and unnecessary costs that slow clinical trials down. Through ARPA-H, we are building a modern clinical trial system that can generate rigorous evidence faster, reduce the burden on patients, and move effective treatments from discovery to the people who need them sooner.”

2. CMS Announces $20 Million for Rural Telehealth and Health IT Upgrades in North Carolina

CMS announced a $20 million investment through the Rural Health Transformation Program for North Carolina’s Rural Health Innovation Fund. The investment is aimed at aiding rural providers in the expansion of telehealth, the replacement of outdated electronic health records, and new cybersecurity measures.

According to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, “Every state knows best what its rural communities need, and thanks to President Trump’s Rural Health Transformation Program, they now have the resources to meet those needs. As states put these resources to work, we’re focused on turning these investments into meaningful, sustainable improvements for the health systems that serve rural North Carolinians.”

3. NIH Director Corrects Report on National Cancer Institute Trials

NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya responded to a CNBC report alleging that funding cuts delayed a childhood brain cancer trial at the National Cancer Institute.

According to Dr. Bhattacharya,

“Last year, the National Cancer Institute decided to transition early-phase pediatric brain tumor trials from a network known as PBTC to a much larger clinical trial network known as PEP-CTN. We updated from a 15-hospital network to a 42-hospital network, adapting to the modern landscape of pediatric cancer trials to better accelerate potential treatments.

Contrary to false reporting, this was not a cost-cutting measure. It was a big-picture investment in what will deliver results for kids with cancer.

The CNBC piece is simply inaccurate. The article references an mRNA trial that wasn’t even part of the PBTC. Almost all trials were transitioned to the new network; the only two PBTC trials that ended were not enrolling patients and were not going to achieve accrual goals. Improving pediatric cancer treatment remains a high priority for the NIH and the NCI. Increasing the size of our pediatric brain tumor clinical trial network is an important step forward for our patients.”

4. USDA Announces $1 billion Investment in Regenerative Pilot Program

USDA announced that in FY2027, it will invest a further $1 billion in the Regenerative Pilot Program. 

According to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins, “The American farmers have spoken and we at USDA are responding! Our Regenerative Pilot Program has seen such tremendous enthusiasm that we are now expanding the financial assistance offered to farmers to $1 billion dollars. American farmers are the frontlines of our fight to make America healthy again and we will work with them to achieve this goal.”

I have explained this repeatedly. Yes, the President may defend American forces without waiting for Congress. That has never been disputed.
But you keep omitting the fact that Jefferson's own Cabinet regarded as critical. Tripoli had formally declared war on the United States.
Gallatin stated the rule plainly. The Executive "cannot put us in a state of war," but once Congress or the other nation has put us there, command of the forces belongs to the President. That was the basis of the Cabinet discussion about what Jefferson could do before Congress acted.
Tripoli had put us in that state.
Iran had not.
And stop describing the February incidents as though they occurred in a vacuum. Here are the circumstances in which Iran acted. Every one of them is on the record.
June 22, 2025. The United States bombed Iran. Fourteen bunker-busters on Fordow and Natanz. More than two dozen Tomahawks on Isfahan. Trump said the nuclear program was obliterated and warned that future attacks would be greater.
January 2026. Iran's government had just killed thousands of protesters. Trump threatened to intervene. Then, on January 28, he announced on Truth Social that "a massive Armada is heading to Iran," larger than the one sent to Venezuela, "ready, willing, and able to rapidly fulfill its mission, with speed and violence, if necessary." He reminded Iran of Midnight Hammer and wrote, "The next attack will be far worse!" Iran's mission to the United Nations answered that it would defend itself.
That is the fleet. Its purpose was stated by its commander in chief. Not to patrol. Not to protect commerce. To force a deal under threat of attack.
February 3. Six days later. An Iranian drone approached the Abraham Lincoln in the Arabian Sea, about 500 miles from Iran's coast, in international waters where both sides were entitled to operate. The military's own account could not say what it intended. Iran said it was on a surveillance mission. We shot it down. Nothing was damaged and no one was hurt. Hours later, Iranian gunboats confronted an American tanker in the Strait and backed off when an American destroyer arrived. The same day, Iran's president ordered his foreign minister to pursue negotiations.
February 5. Iran seized two foreign tankers it accused of smuggling fuel. Foreign ships. Not ours.
February 6. Talks in Oman.
February 17. Iran held a live-fire drill in the Strait.
February 20. Trump gave Iran ten days.
February 28. The United States and Israel attacked. The opening strike killed Iran's head of state. The stated war aims were to destroy Iran's missiles, eliminate its navy, end its support for proxies, and change its government. Congress was out of town. There was no vote.
That is the sequence. We bombed them. We sent a fleet and announced it was aimed at them. We promised the next attack would be worse. They flew a drone at the fleet and sent gunboats at a tanker and backed off both times. We gave them ten days. We attacked.
Now evaluate Iran's acts in that context, which is the only honest way to evaluate them. A country that had been bombed seven months earlier, and told in writing that a fleet was coming and the next attack would be worse, sent a drone to look at the fleet. Any navy on earth does that. Its gunboats harassed one tanker and retreated. Its leaders made speeches. That is the whole of it.
Defend the carrier. Defend the tanker. That is the President's defensive authority, and nobody disputes it.
But a drone near a fleet we had sent toward a country we had already bombed and were publicly threatening to bomb again is not the equivalent of Tripoli formally declaring war on the United States. It is not close.
And your standard has to work both ways.
If Iran's drone and threats were enough to put the United States into a state of war, what did our bombs and our written promise of a worse attack put Iran into?
This administration has used lethal force against boats in international waters on its own declaration of an armed conflict, while withholding the legal basis from Congress. It attacked Venezuela, fought its forces, captured its President, and removed him from his country, and Trump said the United States would "run" Venezuela. If a drone can put America into a state of war, what did that put Venezuela into?
This exposes the real problem with your evolving standard.
First it was threats to ships. Then threats to the homeland. Then a "hostile nation." Now apparently any sufficiently serious provocation can create a state of war that allows the President to proceed without Congress.
Under that theory, why would a President ever need Congress to authorize war?
There will always be a hostile nation. There will always be a threat, a provocation, an intelligence assessment, a military incident, a national-security justification. And if there is not one dramatic enough, a President can bomb a country, send a fleet toward it, promise a worse attack, wait for the drone, and call the drone the war.
Madison understood that danger. That is why the Convention preserved the President's power to "repel sudden attacks." Sherman put it plainly. "To repel and not to commence war."
Madison then became President. Britain had fired on an American frigate, impressed American sailors for years, and seized American ships. No British soldier had landed. He still went to Congress in 1812.
FDR faced something far clearer. Japan attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor. American territory bombed. American ships sunk. Americans killed. FDR exercised his authority as Commander in Chief to defend the country. Then he went to Congress.
If Pearl Harbor did not make Congress unnecessary, a drone did not.
And the institutional problem is greater today. This administration claims expansive presidential control over the entire executive branch. The intelligence comes from the executive. The threat assessment comes from the executive. The legal justification comes from the executive. The President decides what stays classified and then commands the attack.
If that same executive can declare that its own evidence establishes a state of war, and then use that declaration as the source of its own authority to commence war, the executive becomes self-authorizing.
The President has said as much. Asked by the New York Times in January whether there were any limits on his powers abroad, he answered, "Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It's the only thing that can stop me." Asked by NBC last year whether he needs to uphold the Constitution, he said, "I don't know." The person who wrote the Declare War Clause said the executive is the branch most prone to war and cannot be a safe judge of whether to begin one. The person who holds the office says his own mind is the only thing that can stop him. That is the exact danger the clause was written for, stated by the person it was written about.
Congress is the independent decision-maker that breaks that loop. That is what the clause is for.
So this has nothing to do with giving Trump a different standard from another President. The standard is identical for every President.
Repel an attack immediately.
Go to Congress before commencing the war.
Jefferson did. Madison did. FDR did.
Tripoli had declared war.
Iran had not.
The question is who put the United States into a state of war with Iran before February 28. Not Congress. It never voted. Not Iran. It declared no war and fired on nothing. That leaves one person, and the Constitution does not give him that power.
Nothing in this thread has answered that, and nothing will, because the answer is not available. What has been offered instead is a sequence of new tests, each one written after the last one failed. That is not an argument. It is a search for a reason.
Madison had a word for an executive that supplies its own evidence, writes its own legal opinion, declares its own state of war, and commands its own attack. Federalist 47. "The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny."
Elective. He put that word in so no one could say the hand was voted for.
Jefferson had the same word and said it first. "The concentrating these in the same hands is precisely the definition of despotic government." And then, for anyone who would answer that the hands were chosen at the ballot box. "As little will it avail us that they are chosen by ourselves. An elective despotism was not the government we fought for." Madison reprinted that in Federalist 48. The two people who built the system both said it, in the same words, for the same reason.
Franklin said when it would come. On the last day of the Convention he told the delegates the Constitution "can only end in Despotism, as other forms have done before it, when the people shall become so corrupted as to need despotic Government, being incapable of any other." Not when a despot takes power. When the people no longer want anything else. A thread full of citizens inventing reasons why one person may start a war on his own judgment is what Franklin was describing. The clause has not failed. The people it was written for are failing it.
Read Gallatin. Read Hamilton. Read Madison. Then read what the President said about the limits on his own power. The clause was written for exactly this, by people who knew exactly this would come, and they told us what to call it.

ZAMFARA @ 30: A STATE REBORN UNDER GOVERNOR DAUDA LAWAL

On October 1, 1996, a profound historic journey birthed across the vast expanses of the Northwest region when Zamfara State was carved out of the old Sokoto State as a standalone state. Despite the state being created by the military administration of the late General Sani Abacha, the birth of the state was greeted with overflowing euphoria from many who believed its a welcoming development to ensure more stability in governance.

The founding fathers of Zamfara envisioned a self-sustaining agricultural giant, proudly flying the banner “Farming is Our Pride” as its motto but also marked with action and not mere words on paper. With the vast arable agrarian lands and rich mineral deposits the state is blessed with, they imagined a haven of communal peace, where vibrant markets flourished, schools molded brilliant minds, basic amenities were standard and civic dignity was guaranteed to every indigene which would, in turn generate meaningfully development and place the state among the very best in the state and also the region. 

Yet, for nearly three decades that noble vision drifted into a tragic narrative of what could have been a dream come true. Sequential political administrations took the helm, but systemic governance deficits slowly starved the state of its promise also preventing it from reaching its full potential. Instead of transforming into an economic lighthouse, Zamfara became synonymous with institutional decay, bedridden with insecurity, banditry, kidnapping and illiteracy.

Basic infrastructure withered like a flower with no water supply; state-owned schools were reduced to crumbling dilapidated structures; general hospitals and Primary health centres lacked essential diagnostic tools and basic medications and a chronic backlog of unpaid civil service gratuities spanning over a decade left retired public servants in severe hardship. Worse still, an escalating rural security crisis took root, driving hundreds of thousands of farmers from their ancestral fields, paralysing interstate commerce and suffocating the state’s economic soul. For millions of residents, the proud dream of 1996 had morphed into a quiet, painful struggle for survival affecting the survival of the state.

History, however, rarely remains static when decisive leadership intervenes. As Zamfara State approaches its landmark 30th anniversary, the long-standing story of stagnation is undergoing a historic shift. The turning point arrived with the election of Governor Dauda Lawal in 2023, who defeated an incumbent against all odds; his “Rescue Mission” agenda did not merely offer political promises but launched a systematic engineering of state affairs. Governor Lawal took office with a clear diagnostic view of the state’s wounds. He moved away from cosmetic fixes to confront the structural defects that had held Zamfara back for twenty-seven years.

What distinguished Governor Lawal’s programme from the capital-centric spending that has historically defined Nigerian state governance is its geographic spread. In Bukkuyum Local Government Area, a region more often associated in national conversation with insecurity than with infrastructure investment, N4 billion has been committed to the 23-kilometre Mallamawa–Zarummai–Bukkuyum road with a spur to Zarummai Masama Road, alongside N1.5 billion for the Bukkuyum–Birnin Zuama–Gummi road. The government’s choice to route capital there is itself a statement of intent. In Maradun, N5 billion is allocated to the Maradun–Magami–Faru road and N1 billion to the Maradun–Makera road.

I misread your question; I interpreted it as the difference between the mainstream definition and the libertarian one, rather than the difference between the libertarian view and my own. I cannot speak for Ed, but it seems we are on the same page. However, I would add that libertarians tend to define capitalism as a purely economic system rather than a political one, which leads them to attempt to derive politics from economics—something I do not believe is possible. Politics must be grounded in philosophy, and specifically in ethics.

Regarding your discussion on how power is distributed under capitalism: capitalism is about separating the state from the economy. This implies that capital owners hold no political power; the only parties they must answer to are their customers. It is precisely when people insist that the state should have the power to intervene in the economy that lobbying, cronyism, and (in the worst cases) corruption arise. In fact, it is impossible to have a state-regulated economy without these elements. If the state is to pick winners and losers in the economy, it requires feedback (it cannot choose blindly) and that feedback is not neutral; it comes from people seeking benefits from the state and it also contains offers. And so, the cycle begins.

The notion that capital owners would simply continue to control capital in a free capitalist market is rooted in a flawed concept of economic determinism, which is a purely materialist perspective. Even in our mixed economy, with its significant state intervention, we can see the power of ideas. Microsoft, Amazon, and Google did not succeed because of capital, but because of ideas; they all started in their garage. Even state-protected services—such as the postal service—faced competition once email arrived on the scene. If these players can outperform major capital holders in such a market, imagine what they could achieve in a truly free market.

And if no one comes up with better ideas—so what? Then the market is satisfied.

Also, note that the type of entrepreneur who rises to the top in a state-run economy differs vastly from the type who succeeds in a free economy: the former requires the ability to persuade bureaucrats (lobbying), whereas the latter requires convincing your customers.

Study Notes - (Hastings Dictionary) (PART B) 

(d) Further, our Lord’s fulfilment of the law necessitated the abrogation of temporary and defective statutes. In such instances the letter of the old precept stood only till it should be translated into a worthier form and raised to a higher potency (Mat_5:18), by the sweeping away of limiting exceptions (as with the compromise in the matter of wedlock allowed to ‘the hard-heartedness’ of Israelites, Mat_19:3-9), or by the translation of the symbolic into the spiritual, as when cleansing of hands and vessels is displaced by inner purification (Mrk_7:14-23, Luk_11:37-41; cf. Col_2:18 f., Heb_9:9 f.). Our Lord’s reformation of the marriage law is also a case for (b) above: He rectifies the law by the aid of the law; in man’s creation He finds a principle which nullifies the provisions that facilitated divorce. The abolition of the distinction of ‘meats’ (Mrk_7:19), making a rift in Jewish daily habits and in the whole Levitical scheme of life, is the one instance in which Jesus laid down what seemed to be a new principle of ethics. The maxim that ‘what enters into the man from without cannot defile,’ but only ‘the things that issue out of the man,’ was of far-reaching application, and supplied afterwards the charter of Gentile Christianity. Its underlying principle was, however, implicit in OT teaching, and belonged to the essence of the doctrine of Jesus. He could not consistently vindicate heart-religion without combating Judaism in the matter of its ablutions and food-regulations and Sabbath-keeping.
(e) Over the last question Jesus came into the severest-conflict with Jewish orthodoxy; and in this struggle He revealed the consciousness, latent throughout His dealings with OT legislation, of being the sovereign, and not a subject like others, in this realm. Our Lord ‘fulfilled the law’ by sealing it with His own final authority. His ‘I say unto you,’ spoken in a tone never assumed by Moses or the prophets, implied so much and was so understood by His Apostles (1Co_7:10, Gal_6:2, 1Jn_2:3 f. etc.). Christ arrogates the rôle of ‘a son over his house,’ whereas Moses was ‘a servant in the house’ (Heb_3:5 f.). Assuming to be ‘greater than Solomon,’ ‘than Abraham,’ ‘than the temple’ (Mat_12:6; Mat_12:42, Jhn_8:53), He acted as one greater than Moses! The Sabbath-law was the chosen battle-ground between Him and the established masters in Israel (Mrk_2:23-28; Mrk_3:2 ff., Luk_13:16-17, Jhn_5:9-16). In the public Sabbath assemblies Jesus was oftenest confronted with cases of disease and demoniacal possession; He must do His work as God’s ‘sent’ physician. The Sabbath-rules were clear and familiar; His infraction of them in acts of healing was flagrant, repeated, defiant; popular reverence for the day made accusations on this count particularly dangerous. Men were placed in a dilemma: the Sabbath-breaker is ipso facto ‘a sinner’; on the other hand, ‘how can a sinner do such signs?’ (Jhn_9:16; Jhn_9:24 ff.). Jesus argues the matter on legal grounds, showing from recognized practice that the 4th Commandment must be construed with common sense, and that ‘it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath day’ and to work in the service of God (Mat_12:5; Mat_12:11 f.). He goes behind those examples to the governing principle (see (b) above), that ‘the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath’ (Mrk_2:27 f.): the institution is designed for human benefit, and its usages should he determined by its object. But He is not content with saving this: the war against Him was driven on the Sabbath-question à outrance; Jesus draws the sword of His reserved authority. He claims, as sovereign in human affairs, to decide what is right in the matter—‘The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath’; more than this, He professes to have wrought His Sabbath works as God the Father does, to whom all days are alike in His beneficence, and through the insight of a Son watching the Father at His labour (Jhn_5:17-20)—a pretension, to Jewish ears, of blasphemous arrogance: ‘He maketh himself equal with God!’ On this ground Jesus was condemned by the Sanhedrin (cf. Jhn_19:7), because He set Himself above the Sabbath, on the strength of being one with God. Thus the law of Moses put Jesus Christ to death; it was too small to hold Him; its administrators thought themselves bound to inflict the capital sentence on One who said, ‘I am the Son of the Blessed’ (Mrk_14:61 ff.).
(f) At the same time, Caiaphas, the official head of the system, gave another explanation, far deeper than he guessed, of the execution: ‘That Jesus should die for the nation, and not for the nation only’ (Jhn_11:49 ff.). Virtually, He was offering Himself for ‘the lamb’ of the Paschal Feast, ready to be slain in sacrifice, that He might ‘take away the sin of the world.’ This mysterious relation of the death of Jesus to Divine law He had hinted at here and there (Mat_20:28; Mat_26:28, Luk_22:37, Jhn_3:14; Jhn_6:51; Jhn_12:24); its exposition was reserved for His Apostles speaking in the light of this grandest of all fulfilments. Jesus made good the implicit promise of the sacrificial institutions of Israel.
2. The word ‘law’ occurs 118 times in St. Paul’s Epistles,—103 times in Romans and Galatians alone. It is manifest how absorbing an interest the subject had for this Apostle, and where that interest mainly lay. Gal_2:19 puts us at the centre of St. Paul’s position: ‘I through law died to law, that I might live to God.’ From legalism, as from a house of bondage, he had escaped into the freedom of the sons of God. (a) Paul ‘died to the law,’ as he had understood and served it when a Pharisee, regarding obedience to its precepts as the sole ground of acceptance with God. He had sought there ‘a righteousness of’ his ‘own, even that which is of the law’ (Php_3:9), to be gained by’ works,’ by which he strove to merit salvation as a ‘debt’ due from God for service rendered,—a righteousness such as its possessor could ‘boast of, as ‘his own’ (Rom_4:1-5; Rom_9:31 to Rom_10:3). Pursuing this path, ‘Israel’ had failed to win ‘the righteousness of God,’ such as is valid ‘before God’; the method was impracticable—justification on the terms of ‘the law of Moses’ is unattainable (Act_13:38 f., Rom_8:3). Instead of destroying sin, the law arouses it to new vigour, ‘multiplying’ where it aimed at suppressing ‘the trespass’ (Rom_5:20; Rom_7:7-13, 1Co_15:56). Not the ‘law’ in itself, but the ‘carnal’ sin-bound nature of the man, is to blame for this; arrayed against ‘the law of God,’ to which ‘reason’ bows, is ‘another law’ successfully oppugning it, that ‘of sin’ which occupies ‘my members’ (
Rom_7:12-23), and which is, in effect, a ‘law of death’ (Rom_8:2).
(b) But St. Paul’s Judaistic experience had a positive as well as a negative result: if he ‘died to law,’ it was ‘through law’; ‘the law has proved our pœdagogus [for leading us] to Christ’ (Gal_3:24). Law awakened conscience and disciplined the moral faculties; the Jewish people were like ‘an heir’ placed ‘under guardians and stewards until the appointed times,’ and trained in bond-service with a view to their ‘adoption’ (Gal_4:1-5). Even the aggravations of sin caused by the law had their benefit, as they brought the disease to a head and reduced the patient to a state in which he was ready to accept the proffered remedy (Rom_7:24). ‘The Scripture’ had in this way ‘shut up all things under sin,’ blocking every door of escape and blighting every hope of a self-earned righteousness (Gal_3:21 f.), that the sinner might accept unconditionally the ‘righteousness which is through faith in Christ’ (Php_3:9).
(c) Contact with Gentile life had widened St. Paul’s conception of moral law; it was touched by the influences of Greek philosophy and Roman government. He discerned a law established ‘by nature,’ and ‘inscribed in the hearts’ of men ignorant of the Mosaic Code and counting with Jews as ‘lawless.’ This Divine jus (and fas) gentium served, in a less distinct but very real sense, the purpose of the written law in Israel; it impressed on the heathen moral responsibility and the consciousness of sin (Rom_2:6-16). The rule of right and wrong Paul regards as a universal human institute, operating so as to ‘bring the whole world under judgment before God’ (Rom_3:9-19); its action is manifested by the universal incidence of death: in this sense, and in the light of Rom_2:12-16, should be read the obscure parenthesis of Rom_5:13 f., as stating that ‘law’ is concomitant with ‘sin’; the existence of sin, followed by death, in the generations between Adam and Moses proves that law was there all along, whether in a less or a more explicit form; the connexion of sin and death in humanity is, in fact, a fundamental legal principle (Rom_8:2).
(d) Having ‘died to law’ by renouncing the futile salvation it appeared to offer, the Apostle had learned to live to it again in a better way and under a nobler form, since he had begun to ‘live to God’ in Christ. St. Paul is at the farthest remove from Antinomianism; the charge made against him on this score was wholly mistaken. While no longer ‘under law,’ he is ‘not lawless toward God, but in law toward Christ’ (Rom_6:14 f., 1Co_9:21). The old ego, ‘the flesh with its passions and lusts,’ has been ‘crucified with Christ’ (Gal_2:20; Gal_5:16-24). God’s law ceases to press on him as an external power counteracted by ‘the law of sin in the members’; the latter has been expelled by ‘the Spirit of God’s Son,’ which ‘forms Christ’ in him; the new, Christian man is ‘in law’ as he is ‘in Christ’—he sees the law now from the inside, in its unity and charm, and it constrains him with the inward force of ‘the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus’ possessing his nature. He ‘serves’ indeed, but it is ‘in the new’ life wrought ‘of the Spirit, and not in the old’ servitude to ‘the letter’ (Rom_7:6). Constituting now ‘one new man,’ believers of every race and rank ‘through love serve one another,’ as the hand serves the eye or the head the feet; for them ‘the whole law is fulfilled in one word, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself’ (Rom_13:8-10, 1Co_12:13; 1Co_12:25 f., Gal_5:13 f., Eph_2:16-18). The Christian ‘fulfils the law of Christ,’ as the limb the law of the head. Thus St. Paul’s doctrine of the Law joins hands with that of Jesus (see 1 above). Thus also, in his system of thought, the law of God revealed in the OT, when received from Christ revised and spiritualized, and planted by ‘faith’ along with Him in the believer’s heart (cf. Jer_31:31-34), becomes for the first time really valid and effective: ‘Do we nullify law through faith? God forbid; nay,’ he cries, ‘we establish law!’ (Rom_3:31).
(e) Neither Jesus nor Paul makes a formal distinction between the moral and the ceremonial law (see, however, Rom_9:4). St. Paul’s teaching bears mainly on the former: as a Pharisee he had no ritualistic bent, and his ambition was for ethical perfection. ‘Circumcision’ has lost in his eyes all religious value, and remains a mere national custom, now that it ceases to be the covenant-sign and is replaced in this sense by baptism (1Co_7:18 ff., Gal_6:16, Col_2:11 ff.). It becomes a snare to Gentiles when imposed on them as necessary to salvation, or even to advancement in the favour of God; for it binds them ‘to keep the whole law’ of Moses, and leads into the fatal path of ‘justification by law’ (Gal_2:2-5; Gal_3:2 ff; Gal_5:3-6). St. Paul’s contention with the legalists of Jerusalem on this question was a life and death struggle, touching the very ‘truth of the gospel’ and ‘the freedom’ of the Church (Act_15:1-11, Gal_2:1-10; Gal_5:1). The same interests were threatened, more insidiously, by the subsequent attempt, countenanced by Peter and Barnabas at Antioch, to separate Jewish from Gentile Christians at table through the re-assertion of the Mosaic distinction of ‘meats’ which had been expressly discarded by Jesus. The assumption of a privileged legal status within the Church meant the surrender of the whole principle of salvation by faith and of Christian saintship (Gal_2:11-21, Rom_14:17 f., 1Co_8:8; cf. Mrk_7:14-28). In some Churches Paul had to deal with the inculcation of Jewish ritual from another point of view. At Colossæ the dietary rules and sacred seasons of Mosaism were imposed on grounds of ascetic discipline, and of reverence towards angelic (scil. astral) powers; he pronounces them valueless in the former respect, and in the latter treasonous towards Christ, who supplies ‘the body’ of which those prescriptions were but a ‘shadow’ (Col_2:16-23).
3. Col_2:17 forms a link between the doctrine of St. Paul on the Law and the complementary teaching of the writer of Hebrews,—a Jew of very different temperament and antecedents from Saul of Tarsus. This author emphasizes the ceremonial, as Paul the moral, factors of the OT; the Temple, not the synagogue, was for him the centre of Judaism. ‘The first covenant,’ he says, ‘had ordinances of divine service,’ providing for and guarding man’s approach to God in worship (Heb_9:1 etc.); for St. Paul, it consisted chiefly of ‘commandments expressed in ordinances’ (Eph_2:15), which prescribe the path of righteousness in daily life. ‘The law’ means for this great Christian thinker the institutions of the Israelite priesthood, sanctuary, sacrifices—all consummated in Christ and His ‘one offering,’ by which ‘he has perfected for ever them that are sanctified’ (Heb_9:1 to Heb_10:14). In his view, the law is superseded as the imperfect, provisional, and ineffective, by the perfect, permanent, and satisfying, as the shadowy outline by the full image of things Divine (Heb_7:18 f., Heb_8:1-4, Heb_10:1-4); ‘the sanctuary of this world’ gives place to ‘heaven itself,’ revealed as the temple where the ‘great high priest’—Divine-human in person, sinless in nature, perfected in experience, and immeasurably superior to the Aaronic order (Heb_4:14 ff., Heb_7:26 ff.,)—‘appears before the face of God for us,’ ‘having entered through the virtue of his own blood’ as our ‘surety’ and ‘the mediator of’ our ‘covenant,’ who has won for mankind ‘an eternal redemption’ (Heb_2:9, Heb_7:22, Heb_8:8, Heb_9:24-28). Jesus thus ‘inaugurated a new and living way into the holy place’ (in contrast with the old and dead way of the law); as experience proves, He has ‘cleansed the conscience from dead works to serve the living God,’ while the law with its repeated animal sacrifices served to remind men of their sins rather than to remove them (Heb_7:25, Heb_9:14, Heb_10:1-4). Equally with St. Paul, the auctor ad Hebrœos regards ‘remission of sins’ as the initial blessing of the Christian state, which had been unattainable ‘under law,’ and ‘the blood of Christ’ as the means of procuring this immense boon. In Paul’s interpretation, this offering ‘justifies’ the unrighteous ‘before God’ and restores them to the forfeited status of sonship; in the interpretation of Hebrews, it ‘cleanses’ worshippers and brings them ‘nigh to God’ within His sanctuary; on either view, the sacrifice of Calvary removes the harriers set up, by man’s sin ‘under the law,’ between humanity and God.
4. For St. James also the OT law was transformed. He conceives the change in a less radical fashion than Paul or the writer of Hebrews; James stands sturdily on the platform of the Sermon on the Mount. Re-cast by ‘the Lord of glory’ and charged with ‘the wisdom that cometh from above,’ the law is new and glorified in his eyes; like Paul, he knows it as ‘the law of Christ.’ All the disciples of Jesus were one in the place they gave to that which James calls ‘the sovereign law, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself’ (Jas_2:8-13; cf. 1Co_13:1-13); deeds of pure brotherly love prove ‘faith’ alive and genuine; they make it ‘perfect,’ and guarantee the believer’s ‘justification’ (ch. 2). When he describes this law as ‘a perfect law, the law of liberty,’ James’ idea is substantially that of Paul in 1Co_9:21 and Rom_8:2; Rom_8:4, viz. that the law of God is no yoke compelling the Christian man from without, but a life actuating him from within; the believer ‘bends over it’ in contemplation, till he grows one with it (Jas_1:24; cf. 2Co_3:18). ‘The tongue’ is the index of the heart, and St. James regards its control as a sure sign of perfection in law-keeping (Jas_3:1-12). James treats of the law, not, like Paul, as it affects the sinner’s standing before God,—nor, like the author of Hebrews, as it regulates his approach in worship,—but as it governs the walk before God of the professed believer. His Epistle is, in effect, a comment on the last clause of Rom_8:4, ‘that the righteousness of the law may be fulfilled in us.’
5. The word ‘law’ is entirely wanting in the Epistles of St. Peter and of St. John. 1Pe_1:18-19; 1Pe_2:24; 1Pe_3:18 manifest the influence of Paul’s doctrine of salvation on the writer; while 1Jn_1:7; 1Jn_1:9, indicates a leaning to the mode of representation characteristic of Hebrews, and 1Jn_2:2; 1Jn_4:10 virtually sustain the doctrine of St. Paul on law, sin, and sacrifice.
G. G. Findlay.

@open Yesterday, we were shown forecasts suggesting that interest rates will likely remain steady and not increase. Of course, it's not certain, but it's a bit encouraging.

​The main problem is the war, as the market continues to be in a state of fear, driving up the 10-year Treasury yield and oil prices as a result.

​It's not that I don't like the stock - I do. But after that disgusting move Kaz pulled before the quarterly report, with both of them smiling while the head of accounting wore a green shirt, I don't buy his nice - guy act anymore, and I take everything with a grain of salt.

​I decided to sell half my shares a few days ago, and as you can see, the stock just keeps going down.
​Until we officially know that Iran intends to give up its nuclear program, nothing is going to change. The pressure on Iran is enormous, but the regime is known for its ability to endure suffering; they are used to wars of attrition and have no problem taking losses. 
That's why I'm not optimistic about some imaginary agreement, which is basically the best-case scenario we could hope for right now.

​Home sales will probably go up a bit because of the mortgage discount offer that was valid until today, but that's a temporary fix, and the company is likely paying a small subsidy for it anyway.

​I don't understand what's keeping investors around given this situation. I should have acted much sooner and gotten out until things become clearer.
