text:
Twenty twenty-six.
His voice,
in the sent mail,
again.

Out by the last
of August.
Two months of rent
from a grant,
then the grant ends.
A list
he asks to be put
back on.
A firing from a program
he dates,
which the file
says it does not hold.

He cannot stay
with family.
He is gay.
A flight was offered
to Houston,
where his parents live.
Then the offer
was gone.

He told Mark first.
Not his mother.
Not Gia.
He had work.
He had a deposit.
He needed three weeks
until the paycheck.

What came back
was a prayer.

He writes
that needing help
does not make him
a drain
or a leech.

He signs it,
your son.

Two men
he calls Dad.
One page
sorts them
as father
and stepfather.
The letters
just say Dad.

His mother
stays near.
He calls that
closeness,
not a scheme.
To her
he signs Traie.

Both arms
snapped off his glasses.
A new pair
was left at his work.

General Delivery
takes what is his.
He sleeps
near Ybor again.
The mail
does not follow
the body.

One week in a motel
cost more
than five hundred dollars.

A love letter
opens,
Hello, Mrs. Matthew,
and stays
with friendship.
Not always easy.
Still worthwhile.
The file
does not say
who she is.

He writes rules
for what he will not say
to someone scared
at three in the morning.

He will not say
everything happens
for a reason.
He will not say
silver lining.
He will not say
journey,
just to soothe.

He will say this.

The cracks
are where the gold goes.

Not because the crack
was good.
Not because it was needed.
Not because it was,
in secret,
a gift.

You are still here.
That is not nothing.
That is, in fact,
everything.

Written from the floor.
Boots on.

The mantra
does not fix
the sentence.

The sentence
does not cross out
the mantra.

He asked for three weeks.
A prayer arrived.
A prayer can be a love.
A prayer is not a roof.

You are still here.

The gold
is not a reason.

Lokah samasta sukhino bhavantu.

May all beings everywhere
be happy and free.

He is not there yet.
He said so.
He has not taken it back.

text:
Most people assume the highest offer wins a multifamily deal. Often it doesn't.

Price still matters. It is just one of several terms a seller weighs.

In a marketed sale, the broker collects first-round offers, then invites a short list of buyers to submit best and final terms. At that stage the seller compares price, deposit size, when the deposit goes nonrefundable, diligence length, closing timeline, and financing.

Consider two illustrative offers on a property around $30 million. Buyer A offers $30.3 million with 45 days of diligence and a $300,000 deposit that goes nonrefundable once diligence ends. Buyer B offers $30.0 million with 21 days of diligence and $600,000 nonrefundable on day one. The gap is $300,000, or 1% of the price. If Buyer A walks two months in, the seller restarts the process, and the next round of buyers will ask why. That can easily cost more than 1%.

That point carries more weight in Houston today. Many groups lost their investors' capital over the 2021 to 2026 cycle, and JV and high net worth equity has become much harder to raise. With less equity chasing deals, being at or near the top of the bid is an uncomfortable place to be. It means paying a price fewer buyers can match when you sell. So we stay disciplined on price and compete on certainty and terms.

Sellers and brokers tend to judge buyers on three things:

Certainty. Is your equity committed, and will you close on your terms?
Track record. Have you closed before on the terms you offered?
Communication. Do you raise issues early and honestly?

A broker is putting their own name behind the buyer they recommend. Closing on the terms we offer is how we earn the next call.

If you want to see more of how acquisitions actually work, follow along.

text:
For decades, legacy global auto giants from Japan and Korea have operated an extractive business model in India—importing CKD/SKD parts from their home countries, slapping high markups, and re-selling them to Indian consumers at 3x inflated prices instead of genuinely localized manufacturing. They resist the EV shift because complex ICE engines were their artificial moat. EVs level the playing field.

 In China, 40+ EV players (like Chery, BYD, and Xiaomi) shattered old monopolies, forcing even Toyota and Honda to adapt. India must stop settling for legacy players offering incremental hybrids as a favor and open the gates to competitive foreign tech players who are willing to build, innovate, and transfer core technology locally.

True national strength comes from industrial self-reliance, not from protecting global cartels or absorbing bad-loan write-offs. To slash India's massive crude import bill and assert true economic sovereignty, our policy must shift from "static perfection" to "dynamic growth". Instead of handing out small startup grants, the government must deploy aggressive risk capital into EV commercial trucks, buses, cars and public transport infrastructure, backed by our vast solar and wind energy grid. Welcoming fierce global competition will disrupt the current trading-mindset and turn India into a global powerhouse of high-tech EV manufacturing.

At the same time, a patriotic growth policy must safeguard national assets. Our public and private oil refineries shouldn't be abandoned; they must be offered clear incentives to transition into next-generation energy hubs—scaling green hydrogen, biofuels, and battery swappable grids so they evolve into regional powerhouses. 

By trusting local innovation and challenging outdated market monopolies, India can achieve total energy independence and dominate the future of global mobility.

text:
AI upscaling is coming to PS5!

Since the launch of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) on PS5 Pro, players and developers have asked whether similar image-quality improvements could be brought to the PS5 console. PSSR analyzes game images pixel by pixel and uses AI to upscale them with more detail and stability than conventional approaches; until now, its computational demands made bringing that experience to PS5 impossible.

Today, we’re excited to announce Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR): a new performance tier of AI upscaling. Born from Project Amethyst, our AI graphics collaboration with AMD, this quick new evolution of PSSR is built on two key innovations:

A streamlined neural network architecture
A hand-tuned implementation that maximizes performance on PS5
With these, we are bringing the benefits of AI-guided upscaling to PS5. While PSSR remains the gold standard on PS5 Pro, QSSR provides some notable improvements to both image detail and image stability on PS5.

The first titles to use this innovative new library are Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. Both are being patched today to offer QSSR as an additional graphics option on PS5. 

Here’s what Insomniac Games and Sucker Punch Productions have to share about the benefits of this new technology:

Our team at Insomniac works hard to make sure each of our games is a showcase of PlayStation hardware, and we’re excited for Marvel’s Wolverine to be one of the first titles to bring this new QSSR technology to players.

QSSR adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku, and many other areas across Logan’s epic journey. It’s a perfect companion to the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, and it brings a great taste of the PS5 Pro experience to our players on PS5.

Personally, I love seeing how the PlayStation tech teams continually improve the PS5 platform, and I’m excited for more games to make use of QSSR in the future!”

– Mike Fitzgerald, Head of Technology / Insomniac Games

At Sucker Punch, we’re excited to bring QSSR to Ghost of Yōtei players so that they can experience the world we’ve created with even more clarity and detail. QSSR excels at resolving the fine details in our characters and environments and does so with a level of temporal stability that hasn’t been possible on the PS5 console until now. We’ve long wished that all PS5 players could experience the incredible image quality that PSSR brings to PS5 Pro, and QSSR is a positive step towards that goal!”

– Jasmin Patry, Lead Rendering Engineer / Sucker Punch Productions

QSSR will be offered broadly to all PlayStation developers, and we look forward to seeing these improvements in many more titles going forward!

text:
Meet Neoklis Avdalas, who some of you may remember from last season when the Virginia Tech freshman was receiving Luka Doncic comparisons after just two games. 

Early into the 2025 college season, Avdalas looked like the complete package: shooting, size, playmaking, a strong handle, downhill scoring, rebounding, and even some defensive flashes. However, he quickly came back down to earth and decided to stay in college for another year, transferring from Tech to UNC to team up with Mike Malone. 

In his freshman campaign, he averaged 12.1 points, 3.1 rebounds, 4.6 assists, and 1.1 stocks per game.

Although Avdalas' draft range is all over the place going into the 2026-27 college season, his tools and size at 6’9” give him a ton of upside both as a college player and a potential 2027 NBA Draft prospect.

Offensively, Avdalas can offer a lot. He’s at his best with the rock in his hands, operating in the pick-and-roll and creating for himself or his teammates when getting downhill. His feel for the game helps make him the playmaker he is, as he knows how to manipulate defenders and process his reads to locate the open man or someone with an advantage. His processing speed as a passer was impressive for a freshman and helps his projection as a point forward in the pros. Overall, he looked really comfortable with the ball in his hands the majority of the time last year.

As a scorer, he has a ton of upside. Avdalas gets downhill and can score at the rim in a variety of ways, but does struggle with contact at times and can be thrown off against physical defenders. He needs to improve his upper-body strength and add to his overall frame to become a more efficient finisher at the rim. 

Shot-making-wise, Avdalas isn’t afraid to let it fly from anywhere on the court, and while that’s great when he’s making shots, it can be a tough watch when he isn’t. He’s a capable shot creator with a strong stepback and sidestep game from three that he is very confident in. But his efficiency needs to improve drastically to be viewed as a real prospect in the 2027 class, as his 38.6 percent from the field and 31.4 percent from three aren’t going to have NBA scouts circling his name. He also settles for jumpers too often, which may partly be due to his lack of strength, giving him another reason to hit the gym. 

His thin frame also negatively affects him as a rebounder. Even though he can still impact the boards, a stronger frame could raise his ceiling as a crasher and play extender on the glass.

Defensively, Avdalas has a lot of work to do. Obviously, his size gives him a good foundation, especially as a shot blocker, but his frame saw him get bullied, and his poor footwork and mediocre athleticism saw him be a liability in a lot of perimeter matchups.

On the offensive end, the shot creation, IQ, size, and skills are all really intriguing, but without efficiency and an improved frame he isn’t as intriguing as he could be. Avdalas needs to show he can be a more consistent scorer and improve at playing against higher-level defenders. Defensively, his footwork and positioning need work because, even though he doesn’t have incredible athleticism, his length provides a solid starting point. 

Going into his sophomore season in a new place, Avdalas has a lot of work to do to convince scouts he’s ready to make the jump from college to the pros. But he has the upside and is going to a situation that creates a pathway to doing so.

text:
How to stay updated with Tech News? 👇

Staying current in tech doesn’t have to mean living in browser tabs.

An RSS reader like Inoreader still beats algorithmic feeds for one reason: you choose the sources, not the other way around.

A simple setup that works:

1. Add a few high-signal feeds: company blogs, engineering blogs, research labs, and a couple of newsletters that offer RSS.

2. Group them into folders (AI, infra, security, product) so you can scan by topic instead of by noise.

3. Use rules and filters to mute keywords, highlight releases, or star posts from specific authors.

4. Check it once or twice a day in a dedicated “read later” view instead of refreshing timelines all day.

The result is a quiet, chronological inbox of the sources you actually trust. No engagement bait, no missed changelog buried under memes.

RSS isn’t dead. Most people just stopped curating it. 
#tech

text:
Africa’s industrial future will be negotiated between national ambition and regional interdependence. Uganda’s commitment to Hoima illustrates that reality; it does not settle Lamu’s commercial prospects.

A refinery succeeds through reliable feedstock, efficient conversion, competitive logistics and sustained demand. Lamu’s coastal location offers access to seaborne crude and wider markets. Its investment case must withstand competing refineries, volatile margins and changing energy demand.

The development prize extends beyond fuel. Supplier capabilities, engineering expertise, maintenance services and downstream manufacturing can turn one investment into an industrial ecosystem. These gains require deliberate policy: skills transfer, competitive procurement and infrastructure that connects production to consumers.

Kisumu’s strategic interest lies in that connectivity. Its pipeline facilities, oil jetty and lake port offer foundations for distribution and services. We will advance commercially tested Lamu–Kisumu connections in our contributions to Vision 2060.

Regional integration must accommodate national interests through credible contracts, efficient borders and mutual advantage.

President William Samoei Ruto deserves recognition for pursuing this opportunity. His achievement would be an investment that builds productive capacity, protects public finances and earns community confidence through lawful implementation.

Industrial sovereignty becomes meaningful when a graduate gains expertise, a supplier grows competitive, and a household can plan beyond survival.

text:
**The Boeing 777X represents the most ambitious evolution of Boeing’s flagship wide‑body family, combining next‑generation aerodynamics, record‑breaking engines, and cabin innovations into what will become the world’s largest and most capable twin‑engine airliner.** Below is a detailed, structured article covering its inception, development timeline, design, variants, interior layouts, unique features, cost, and current firm orders.

---

## 🛫 Inception & Development Timeline  
- **Program launch:** November **2013**   [Wikipedia](https://t.co/Epjd8VodPn)  
- **First flight:** January **25, 2020**   [Wikipedia](https://t.co/Epjd8VodPn)  
- **Expected entry into service:** **2027**, after multiple delays related to certification, structural testing, and GE9X engine refinements   [Wikipedia](https://t.co/Epjd8VodPn)  
- **Development duration:** From 2013 to the expected 2027 entry into service → **14 years** of development.

The 777X was conceived as Boeing’s response to the Airbus A350, offering lower fuel burn, higher capacity, and advanced materials while building on the proven 777 platform.

---

## 🛩 Design Overview  
### ✈️ Fuselage & Cabin  
- Based on the 777‑300ER fuselage but **wider**, allowing more comfortable seating and larger windows.  
- Incorporates **787‑style cabin technologies**: improved humidity, LED lighting, and quieter interiors.   [Wikipedia](https://t.co/Epjd8VodPn)  
- Windows are **larger than any competitor**, enhancing passenger experience.   [https://t.co/gdTSvZOlcw](https://t.co/3rjL4Gc11U)  

### 🧭 Avionics  
- Updated flight deck derived from the 777 and 787 families.  
- Enhanced fly‑by‑wire systems and advanced flight controls to support the folding wingtips and new aerodynamic loads.

### 🛠 Composite Wing & Folding Wingtips  
- The **largest composite wing** ever fitted to a Boeing airliner.  
- Extended wingspan: **235 ft 5 in** (71.8 m).  
- Folded wingspan: **212 ft 9 in** (64.8 m).   [https://t.co/gdTSvZOlcw](https://t.co/3rjL4Gc11U)  
- Folding wingtips allow the aircraft to fit into standard Code E airport gates while providing Code F aerodynamic performance.

### 🔥 Engines: GE9X  
The GE9X is the most powerful and efficient commercial turbofan ever built:  
- **Fan diameter:** 134 in (11.2 ft)  
- **Thrust:** 105,000 lbf (rated), **134,300 lbf** (world record)   [https://t.co/gdTSvZOlcw](https://t.co/3rjL4Gc11U)  
- **Bypass ratio:** 10:1  
- **Composite fan blades:** 16  
- **Pressure ratio:** 60:1  

These engines deliver **20% better fuel efficiency** than the 777‑300ER they replace.   [https://t.co/gdTSvZOlcw](https://t.co/3rjL4Gc11U)  

---

## 📏 Variants & Dimensions  
### **777‑9 (Launch Variant)**  
- **Length:** 251 ft 9 in (76.7 m)  
- **Passengers:** ~414 (typical 2‑class)  
- **Range:** ~13,900 km (7,285 nmi)   [Modern Airliners](https://t.co/Dtlsk2AfCM)  

### **777‑8 (Long‑Range Variant)**  
- **Length:** 229 ft (70 m)  
- **Passengers:** ~384 (typical 2‑class)  
- **Range:** ~16,000 km (8,745 nmi)   [Modern Airliners](https://t.co/Dtlsk2AfCM)  

### **777‑8F (Freighter)**  
- Launch customer: Qatar Airways  
- Designed to replace aging 747 freighters.   [https://t.co/gdTSvZOlcw](https://t.co/3rjL4Gc11U)  

---

## 🪑 Interior Layouts & Cabin Configurations  
While Boeing does not publish “most ordered” layouts, typical airline selections follow industry norms:

### **Economy Class**  
- 10‑abreast seating (3‑4‑3), the most common configuration for the 777 family.  
- Wider cabin allows slightly improved seat width compared to the 777‑300ER.

### **Premium Economy**  
- 8‑abreast (2‑4‑2), increasingly popular among long‑haul carriers such as Lufthansa, Emirates, and Singapore Airlines.

### **Business Class**  
- All‑aisle‑access suites (1‑2‑1 or 1‑1‑1), often with doors.  
- Airlines are expected to install next‑generation lie‑flat suites similar to their A350 and 787 fleets.

### **First Class**  
- Select carriers (Emirates, Etihad) may include enclosed suites or even “mini‑cabins,” though many airlines are phasing out first class.

---

## ⭐ Unique Features  
- **Folding wingtips** — first ever on a commercial airliner.  
- **Largest composite wing** Boeing has ever built.  
- **Largest windows** of any twin‑aisle aircraft.  
- **Most powerful commercial engines** ever produced.  
- **Lower cabin altitude**, improved humidity, and quieter cabin (787‑derived).  
- **10% lower operating costs** than the Airbus A350 (Boeing claim).   [https://t.co/gdTSvZOlcw](https://t.co/3rjL4Gc11U)  

---

## 💲 Cost  
Boeing’s list prices are no longer published, but industry estimates place the 777X at:  
- **$410–$450 million** per aircraft (estimated based on 777‑300ER historical pricing and 777X complexity).  
*This is an inference based on industry norms; Boeing has not released official list prices since 2017.*

---

## 📦 Current Firm Orders  
As of **November 2025**, Boeing holds:  
- **619 total orders** for the 777X passenger and freighter variants from **12 customers**.   [Wikipedia](https://t.co/Epjd8VodPn)  

Major customers include Emirates, Lufthansa, Qatar Airways, Singapore Airlines, Etihad, and others.

---

## 🧭 Summary  
The Boeing 777X is poised to become the world’s most advanced and capable twin‑engine airliner. With its composite wing, folding wingtips, GE9X engines, and modernized cabin, it blends proven 777 reliability with cutting‑edge technology. Despite delays, its strong order book and unmatched performance ensure it will play a major role in long‑haul aviation for decades.

Tip from a broker: Don't buy anything in Florida until your Realtor has verified 
1. The property is high enough that it doesn't need flood insurance, or you can afford it;
2. Make it contingent upon passing a multipoint roof inspection. If it fails, get a new roof by settlement. 
3. No sinkhole problems down the street. Sinkholes can move.

No. 1 and 3. can be checked in public records by county. No. 2 requires a certified inspector, after you get it under contract.

I almost bought a home here, but it failed the roof inspection. In hindsight, it was an OK deal and I should have paid the $13K more to put on a new roof myself by settlement. I backed out of that contract, after the seller would not even share that cost with me. 

The greedy seller, who lied and tried to hide the roof problem, should have taken my offer to pay half. She net got less money selling 3 months later in a falling market and had to stretch to pay for that new roof anyways. 

She found out the hard way, that by Realtor ethics, her Realtor HAD to disclose the roof problem to all new buyers, so no sale until she paid for it. Karma?

text:
A New Vocabulary for How Unsupported Claims Become History

We need better words for explaining how weak or unsupported claims enter newspapers, books, academic writing, and advocacy literature, then slowly take on the appearance of established fact through repetition and citation laundering.

I propose the term citogenitor for the first identifiable person or publication introducing an unsupported or unverified claim into the citation stream. The word combines citation with genitor, meaning an originator or progenitor.

A citogenitor is not automatically a liar or fabricator, they could have been led themselves or misstated something. The term only identifies the earliest source presently known to have introduced the claim. If evidence later shows deliberate invention, a stronger term, citofabricator, would be more appropriate.

From the citogenitor comes citogenesis, the birth, growth, mutation, and spread of the claim.

Then comes citation laundering. Later writers cite earlier writers, they may or may not be partisan. Historians cite books. Advocacy groups cite historians, especially the biased History dot com. Biased Encyclopedias like Britannica cite secondary sources. Eventually the weak original source disappears behind layers of citations, and the claim begins to look independently confirmed.

The Leo Frank antisemitic death-threat story offers a useful example.

C. P. Connolly Enters the Story

C. P. Connolly appears to be the citogenitor of the December 1914 national publication cycle involving the alleged antisemitic death threat.

His material gave the story major national circulation from NYC outward, and the chronology deserves close attention and examination, because the location and form of the alleged threat changed rapidly during December 1914. It bounced around from outside the courthouse, to a law firm office phone, and then back to the courthouse but this time inside the trial proceedings themselves. All of this in a span of 2 weeks. And we should ask why the story changes in detail, especially, the location, in such a short amount of time?

The first known publication in this cluster appeared on Monday, December 14, 1914, in The New York Times.

The headline was “Finds Mob Frenzy Convicted Frank.”

It appeared on page 4, column 3.

The Times credited the material to Connolly and Collier’s, making it an advance presentation of Connolly’s forthcoming Collier’s work rather than an independent investigation conducted by The New York Times.

This was 476 days after Leo Frank’s August 25, 1913 conviction (NYT, 1).

December 14: The Threatening Atmosphere Is Outside the Courthouse

In the December 14 account, Connolly’s picture centers largely on the crowd outside and around the courthouse.

He portrayed Atlanta as caught up in mob excitement and public pressure surrounding the trial.

His later Collier’s account added more detail. Connolly described the courtroom on the first floor of the old City Hall. The windows were open because of the summer heat. Men stood outside with their heads almost level with the window sills. Other men sat on a nearby shed only about ten feet behind the judge and witness chair.

The location is important, because the story is inconsistent by the same author. And Rascoe takes it over the top, by putting it inside the courtroom itself, where there were 200+ spectators, a judge, policemen, bailiffs, attorneys, jurors, witnesses, family and friends of the victim, and the defendant and more. 

At this point, Connolly builds his picture around pressure and hostility outside and immediately surrounding the courthouse (NYT, 1) (Collier’s, 2).

December 19: The Story Moves to a Telephone Call

Five days later, on Saturday, December 19, 1914, Connolly’s first full installment of “The Frank Case” appeared in Collier’s: The National Weekly, Volume 54, Number 14, pages 6–7 and 22–24.

Now the story changes.

On page 6, column 2, Connolly described visiting the office of one of Leo Frank’s lawyers on his last day in Atlanta.

According to Connolly, the telephone rang.

An anonymous caller supposedly threatened the lawyer if Frank were not hanged (Collier’s, 2).

But Connolly left out some important details.

He did not identify the caller, which might not have been possible given it was a crank call.

He did not identify the lawyer. He didn't identify who answered the phone.

He did not give the date of the alleged call or time. No month, no day of the week, no numeric number of the month, no year. 

He did not identify another witness who supposedly heard the conversation. No deposition. No affidavit. No police report. 

The story has still moved.

It is no longer only about a hostile crowd outside the courthouse. Connolly now places an explicit antisemitic death threat on a telephone call received in the office of one of Leo Frank’s attorneys. Where did his original outside the courthouse story go? It mutated, and disappeared. Now it's a menacing phone call. 

Was the Call Received in the Grant Building?

There is a strong possibility concerning the location, although it remains an inference.

Leo Frank’s principal attorney Luther Z. Rosser belonged to Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips. Governor Slaton was part of that firm, and continued to be part of that firm even when his Governorship ended in late June 1915. 

An Atlanta Georgian article published Sunday, June 22, 1913, page 5C, announced the consolidation of the firm and reported its offices would occupy the seventh floor of the Grant Building beginning July 1, 1913 (Atlanta Georgian, 3).

Connolly said he was in the office of one of Frank’s lawyers, but he never named the attorney.

We therefore cannot state as proven fact the alleged telephone call occurred in Rosser’s seventh-floor office.

Still, the seventh floor of the Grant Building is an obvious possibility because Rosser’s firm was headquartered there.

Connolly Surrounds the Story With Courtroom Intimidation

Connolly’s December 19 article also painted a broader picture of intimidation.

On page 22, he described open courtroom windows, men standing outside near those windows, spectators behind the jurors, applause, stamping feet, laughter, jeering, and other demonstrations (Collier’s, 2).

By this point Connolly had several pieces working together:

a hostile crowd outside the courthouse, men near the open windows, spectators inside the courtroom, public demonstrations, and an anonymous antisemitic telephone threat supposedly made to one of Frank’s lawyers.

But he had still not crossed one important line.

Connolly had not placed the explicit antisemitic death threat inside the courtroom and put the words directly into the mouths of spectators addressing the jurors.

His December 19 installment appeared 481 days after the verdict.

December 26: Connolly Finishes His Two-Part Article

One week later, on Saturday, December 26, 1914, Connolly completed his two-part presentation with the second installment of “The Frank Case.”

It appeared in Collier’s, Volume 54, Number 15, pages 18–20 and 23–25.

This installment focused heavily on Connolly’s attack on the prosecution case, Jim Conley, the police investigation, and the circumstances surrounding Frank’s conviction.

Connolly closed the article on page 25 by portraying the jury’s verdict as an echo of public clamor (Collier’s, 4).

This issue appeared 488 days after the verdict.

Only one day later, the death-threat story moved again.

December 27: Burton Rascoe Moves the Threat Inside the Courtroom

On Sunday, December 27, 1914, Arthur Burton Rascoe, using the byline Burton Rascoe, published “Will the State of Georgia Hang an Innocent Man?” in the Chicago Sunday Tribune, page 47.

Rascoe was twenty-two years old and working for the Chicago Tribune at the time (Chicago Sunday Tribune, 5) (Dartmouth, 6).

Here the story changes dramatically.

Rascoe no longer limits the antisemitic threat to a telephone call received by a lawyer.

He places an explicit antisemitic threat inside the courtroom itself while the jurors were hearing evidence.

Rascoe wrote of men in the trial's spectator or audience shouting:

“You’d better hang the Jew. If you don’t, we’ll hang him and get you, too.”

Rascoe then added more claims. He wrote about threatening telephone calls, notes allegedly sent to jurors’ wives, threats against Frank’s lawyers, threats made in open court, and crowds outside the courthouse yelling at jurors during deliberations (Chicago Sunday Tribune, 5). Rascoe combines all the fabrications into carnival like atmosphere of menacing oral and written death threats

Where are those death threat notes? What did those notes say? Were they reported to the police?

This is a major step in the citogenesis of the story.

Thirteen Days and Three Locations

The chronology is striking to just two activist journalists.

On December 14, Connolly’s material reached a national audience through The New York Times. The atmosphere of threat and intimidation centered largely on the crowd outside and around the courthouse.

On December 19, Connolly described an explicit antisemitic death threat delivered by telephone to the office of one of Frank’s lawyers.

That office may have been the seventh-floor offices of Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips in the Grant Building, although Connolly never identified the lawyer and the location cannot be proven from his account alone.

On December 26, Connolly completed his two-part Collier’s article. One day later Rascoe chimes in...

Then, on December 27, Burton Rascoe moved the explicit antisemitic threat inside the courtroom, placing the words directly in the mouths of spectators and directing them toward the jurors.

Only 13 days separate the December 14 New York Times article from Rascoe’s December 27 Chicago Sunday Tribune article.

Only eight days separate Connolly’s December 19 Collier’s article from Rascoe’s December 27 article.

Rascoe’s article appeared 489 days after Leo Frank’s August 25, 1913 verdict.

Follow the Geography

The development becomes easier to see when we follow the location of the alleged threat:

Outside and around the courthouse → telephone call to a defense lawyer → explicit antisemitic threat shouted inside the courtroom at the jurors.

The location keeps moving.

This is important because later writers can flatten different accounts into one supposedly settled event.

A later historian may cite another historian. An advocacy group may cite the historian. An encyclopedia may cite the book. A newspaper may cite the encyclopedia.

After enough repetitions, the reader no longer sees where the claim started.

The citation trail begins to look impressive.

But ten citations tracing back to one weak source are still one source.

That is citation laundering, there are dozens of examples of this story being repeated.

Connolly as Citogenitor

Based on the surviving publication trail presently identified, C. P. Connolly appears to be the citogenitor of this December 1914 national publication chain.

That means he is the earliest identifiable national source in this cluster introducing and developing the death-threat story.

Burton Rascoe can be described as an early citogenic amplifier and citogenic mutator.

He did not simply repeat the developing story.

His December 27 account placed the explicit antisemitic threat in a new and far more important location:

inside the courtroom itself.

These terms help separate the roles different writers can play in creating a historical claim.

The citogenitor introduces the claim.

A citogenic amplifier spreads it to a larger audience.

A citogenic mutator changes, enlarges, or embellishes it.

Citogenesis describes the larger process through which the claim develops and reproduces.

Citation laundering occurs when repeated citation hides the weak or uncertain origin and makes the claim appear independently confirmed.

A citofabricator would be someone shown by evidence to have knowingly invented the claim.

What the Evidence Shows

The chronology needs to be handled carefully.

It does not prove Burton Rascoe copied Connolly.

Direct copying would require evidence such as correspondence, notes, attribution, drafts, testimony, or some other documentary connection between the two men.

It also does not prove Connolly knowingly invented every part of his story.

What the surviving publications do show is narrower and harder to dispute.

The published story changed rapidly during December 1914.

The famous courtroom version appears in print after Connolly’s national publicity had already placed related death-threat and intimidation claims into circulation.

That raises basic historical questions.

Who first reported the threat?

Where did the original source place it?

Who supposedly heard it?

When did it first appear in print?

Was it reported during the 1913 trial?

Was it raised in court?

Was it included in a defense motion?

Was it supported by sworn affidavits from jurors, lawyers, court officers, newspaper reporters, or spectators?

Those questions are necessary if we want to know whether later writers independently documented an event or simply participated in citogenesis and citation laundering.

References

Collier’s, 2. Connolly, C. P. (1914, December 19). “The Frank Case.” Collier’s: The National Weekly, 54(14), 6–7, 22–24. Telephone account: p. 6, col. 2. Courthouse and courtroom setting: pp. 7, 22.

Atlanta Georgian, 3. The Atlanta Georgian. (1913, June 22). “Two Firms Combined: Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips Is Title of Consolidation of Well-Known Attorneys.” p. 5C. Report identifies the firm’s offices on the seventh floor of the Grant Building.

text:
How about: "Tom made the drive alone. Georgia opened up in front of him, and a roadside peach stand immediately launched a peach into his windshield with the velocity of a minor-league fastball, shattering the glass and revealing that the peach was hollow and full of very polite bees who apologized, paid for the window with a roll of expired coupons, and then elected him their temporary mayor.

He accepted, because the alternative was explaining the bees to his insurance agent. The bees directed him onto a dirt road that was not on any map and, frankly, was not fully committed to being a road. It ended at a Walmart parking lot that had seceded from the county that morning and was now operating as a sovereign micronation whose only export was lukewarm fountain drinks and whose national anthem was a single guy playing Wonderwall on a shopping cart.

Tom was detained at customs, which consisted of a folding table and a teenager with a stamp that said APPROVED in sparkly gel pen. They confiscated his phone, replaced it with a rotary phone that only called 1987, and informed him that entry required completing the Rite of the Frozen Aisle: he had to push a cart the length of the store while a rogue Roomba narrated his life choices in the voice of a disappointed game-show host.

Halfway through, the cart developed opinions. It refused to turn left, cited a personal vendetta against left turns dating to a forklift incident in 2014, and instead steered him into the garden center, where a battalion of plastic flamingos had unionized and were striking for better working conditions and fewer people taking selfies with them. Negotiations collapsed when someone offered them a raise in birdseed. The flamingos accepted, declared victory, and appointed Tom their bargaining representative, which mostly meant he had to wear a tiny sash.

Outside, the parking-lot nation had entered a brief war with the neighboring Chick-fil-A over Sunday operating hours. The conflict was resolved when both sides realized neither side actually wanted to work Sundays, so they merged into a single entity whose constitution was written on a napkin and whose military consisted of one very confident goose. The goose saluted Tom, stole his keys, and drove the car into a retention pond that turned out to be a portal.

He emerged in downtown Atlanta during a parade no one had scheduled, riding in the back of his own car, which was now being towed by the goose, while the bees waved from the shattered windshield and the flamingos marched behind holding signs that said WE REGRET NOTHING. A local news crew asked him for comment. He said he had only been trying to get to Savannah. The anchor nodded, cut to commercial, and the commercial was just the Roomba, still narrating."

text:
MUMMA MOTIONS HEARING | JUDGE BEGINS RULING ON D12, D13 AND D14

DEFENSE: WARRANTLESS PHONE SEIZURE WAS UNLAWFUL

Defense counsel completed argument by focusing on the warrantless seizure of Brandon Mumma’s iPhone.

The defense argued that the plain-view doctrine did not justify taking the phone because, when Detective Ted Binet told Mumma the phone would be seized, it was inside Mumma’s pocket.

Counsel argued that simply knowing an object is present does not give police a lawful right of access to an object inside someone’s pocket.

The defense cited Colorado and federal case law in support of that argument.

Defense counsel also argued that exigent circumstances did not justify the seizure.

Although Binet testified that data could potentially be remotely deleted or wiped, the defense argued that the mere technical ability to destroy electronic evidence does not by itself create an exigency.

Counsel emphasized that Mumma voluntarily appeared for the interview, voluntarily discussed the investigation and had used his phone during the interview to provide information to investigators.

The defense argued that Mumma showed no indication that he intended to destroy evidence.

The defense additionally challenged whether investigators had probable cause to seize the phone at all, arguing that Mumma’s statements were consistent with information investigators already possessed.

The defense asked the court to suppress the evidence.

JUDGE BEGINS RULING

The judge then began issuing findings on Defense Motions D12, D13 and D14.

The court first addressed the May 29 Safe Center interview.

The judge emphasized that Mumma voluntarily traveled to the Safe Center, arrived on his own and was met outside by Binet.

The court noted that Binet told Mumma before entering that he was being interviewed as a witness, was not going to be arrested and would be able to leave afterward.

The judge also emphasized that the interview occurred in a Human Services building rather than a traditional police station.

COURT: INITIAL INTERVIEW WAS NOT CUSTODIAL

The judge rejected the defense argument that the seating arrangement transformed the encounter into a custodial interrogation.

The court found that asking Mumma to sit in the chair farther from the door so his face could be captured by the camera was not a significant restriction on his movement.

The judge noted that Binet was dressed in plain clothes. Although armed, his firearm remained holstered and was never used in a threatening manner.

The court characterized the interaction as conversational.

The judge also observed that Mumma himself did much of the talking and frequently provided information beyond what Binet specifically asked.

According to the court, Mumma offered to help investigators, offered to have people contact them and voluntarily used his cellphone to locate information concerning Nicole and Lucy.

The court found there were no threats or coercion.

The judge concluded that the initial interview was not custodial and that Mumma voluntarily answered the detective’s questions.

The court also placed significant weight on what happened at the end of the encounter: Mumma was ultimately allowed to leave.

The judge noted that Mumma even returned inside after leaving to retrieve something he had left behind, which the court viewed as further evidence that he did not believe he was under arrest.

MIRANDA INVOCATION

The court found that when Binet eventually advised Mumma of his Miranda rights, Mumma understood them and exercised his right to counsel.

The judge found that Binet respected that invocation and stopped questioning him.

The court acknowledged some subsequent back-and-forth surrounding the cellphone but found that Binet did not resume interrogation.

COURT: NO WARRANTLESS SEARCH OCCURRED DURING INTERVIEW

The judge then addressed the defense allegation that Binet conducted a warrantless search of Mumma’s phone during the interview.

The court found that no search occurred.

The judge noted that Binet did not manipulate the phone and that Mumma voluntarily used the device to locate information he then shared with the detective.

The court found that Binet’s requests concerning the phone were made conversationally rather than as commands.

The judge also said there was nothing in the record showing that Binet actually observed meaningful information from the phone beyond information Mumma voluntarily provided.

“There was no search to suppress,” the judge concluded.

COURT TURNS TO WARRANTLESS SEIZURE OF IPHONE

The judge then began addressing the separate question of whether police lawfully seized Mumma’s iPhone before obtaining a warrant.

The court stated that law enforcement can, under appropriate circumstances, seize evidence that could be destroyed before officers have time to obtain a warrant.

The judge rejected the idea that sophisticated technical expertise was necessary to recognize the possibility of deleting information from a cellphone, remarking that even an average young child understands information can be erased from a phone.

The court also found that by this stage of the investigation, Mumma’s phone had evidentiary value.

The judge noted that investigators already possessed video from Gratton’s apartment and had developed information concerning Mumma’s possible involvement.

THE COURT IS STILL EXPLAINING ITS FINDINGS ON THE PHONE SEIZURE.

text:
***The Three Musketeers***

Austin, in the year of our Lord two thousand and twenty, was a town that still pretended it had a downtown. A young man rode in from the west on a Cybertruck he did not own, carrying a microphone, a mouthguard, and a letter of introduction from a regional open-mic that had closed during the plague. His name was D’Artagnan, though the bouncer at the comedy club wrote it down as Darren.
He had come to join the Musketeers.
Everyone in the lot behind the warehouse knew who they were. They trained at dawn, argued at noon, and by dusk had accused three separate institutions of being lizards. Their captain was a man named Treville who ran a gym that also sold liver pills. Their enemy was the Cardinal, a smooth creature in a navy blazer who controlled the platforms, the fact-checkers, and a startling percentage of the deodorant ads.
D’Artagnan found the first Musketeer in a sauna.
Athos — Joe, to the apprentices — sat naked except for a towel and a look of ancient disappointment. He had once been the finest swordsman in the comedy clubs of Los Angeles. Then a woman, a contract, and a very public remark about a virus had driven him into exile among the cedars. He drank elk broth from a Yeti and spoke as if every sentence had to survive a deposition.
“You’re standing in my steam,” Athos said.
“I came to serve,” D’Artagnan said.
“Then stop exhaling like a civilian.”
They agreed to fight at noon. Athos preferred they fight about whether seed oils were a conspiracy or merely a mistake. D’Artagnan, who had only been alive long enough to have opinions about protein, accepted.
On the way to the parking lot he collided with Porthos.
Porthos was Alex, and he took up more space than the truck. He wore a vest with more pockets than a man needs unless the man is smuggling both vitamins and state secrets. His voice arrived before his body. He was explaining, to a camera that might have been off, that the Cardinal had replaced the water in the Colorado River with a mild antipsychotic and that the musketeers were the last men in Texas who still filtered their own urine on principle.
“You bumped my tripod,” Porthos said.
“I apologize.”
“Apologies are what they put in the food. We duel.”
“I already have a duel.”
“Good. We’ll stack them. Efficiency is how the patriots win.”
The third collision happened outside a jiu-jitsu academy that smelled like feet and enlightenment. Aramis — Eddie — was upside down in the doorway, one leg behind his head, explaining to a purple belt that the guard was not a position but a cosmology. He had taken holy orders in the church of the rubber guard and spoke of the Cardinal’s guards the way other men spoke of bad posture.
“You made me come up,” Aramis said, righting himself with a motion that looked medically unwise. “Now I have to put you back down. Noon?”
“Noon,” D’Artagnan said, because Austin was a town where you either fought everyone or you became a brand.
At noon the Cardinal’s guards arrived first: three men in lululemon with lanyards, there to measure the parking lot for a content-moderation pop-up. The Musketeers forgot their separate quarrels at once. Steel in the old book; here it was a livestream, a rear-naked choke, and a bullhorn.
“All for one,” Athos said, setting down the broth.
“And one for all,” Porthos roared, already mid-sentence about fluoridated moonlight.
“Plus whoever taps,” Aramis added, and shot a double.
They won. The lanyards retreated to write a blog. D’Artagnan, bleeding from the eyebrow and strangely happy, was invited to the warehouse.
The Queen’s diamonds were not diamonds. They were twelve voice memos the Queen of the Platform had sent Athos before the exile, in which she laughed at things the Cardinal later called violence. If the memos reached the court — a Tuesday hearing, a Terms update — Athos would be unsubscribed from the Earth. The Musketeers rode for Los Angeles in a convoy of one truck, one Sprinter full of cameras, and Aramis’s compact car, which he insisted got better mileage because he kept the windows up and his mind flexible.
Milady was waiting at a juice bar in Venice.
She had been everything: a clip-channel editor, a honey-pot influencer, a woman Porthos had once almost married until he noticed her search history included “how to wash a brand.” She smiled with half her mouth and offered D’Artagnan a sample of something green.
“The Cardinal wants the memos,” she said. “I want a spin-off. We can all eat.”
D’Artagnan, who had not yet learned that charm is a submission hold, almost handed them over. Aramis saved him by locking up her posting wrist and whispering that the algorithm could smell desperation. They fled with the memos in a fanny pack. Milady, later, would surface in a deposition wearing a different haircut and the same smile. Porthos would spend four episodes explaining she was three women and a consulting firm. He would not be entirely wrong.
The siege of La Rochelle, in this telling, was the siege of the studio.
The Cardinal’s army — advertisers, a nervous board, two men with clipboards — surrounded the warehouse and demanded Athos renounce elk, Aramis renounce inverted guard, and Porthos renounce the sentence he was currently shouting. Inside, the Musketeers lived on dried liver and spite. D’Artagnan learned the old forms: how to hold a silence until the guest confessed, how to sprawl without being swept, how to accuse a cloud formation and somehow be directionally correct.
On the twelfth night Athos stood on the roof with a microphone and no shirt.
“They can have the memos,” he said. “I already said the thing on a Tuesday. The diamonds were never the point. The point is we don’t kneel for a blazer.”
Porthos fired a flare that was mostly a legal disclaimer. Aramis heel-hooked a drone. The siege broke, not because the Cardinal repented, but because the public got bored and clicked a video of a man eating a boot for charity.
Afterward they drank broth in the gravel and watched the bats.
“Will they come back?” D’Artagnan asked.
“Always,” Athos said. “That’s the service.”
“Will we win?”
Porthos considered the tree line as if it owed him money. “We’ll be loud. Loud is a kind of winning if you survive the invoice.”
Aramis lay on his back and put a foot behind his head, which in Austin passed for prayer. “One for all,” he said. “All for one. And if you tap, you owe the table steak.”
D’Artagnan raised the mug. The broth was terrible. The company was worse. He had never been happier, which is the only honest ending the Musketeers ever get.

text:
#Jane combines the attention around “I Am Jane Doe” with a creator-fee allocation intended to support a sexual-assault recovery charity. Its credibility depends on whether that connection produces meaningful support beyond the chart.

The phrase is spreading as an expression of solidarity with survivors and support for the anonymity of the woman in the Cornell case. People are posting “I Am Jane Doe” to stand alongside her, with participants also sharing their own experiences. That gives the name a meaning people recognize before encountering the token. Movement context

One widely shared post carrying the phrase has attracted more than 3.3 million views and 73,000 likes. That demonstrates the reach of the wider conversation. It does not mean those people support a cryptocurrency using the same name. Original post

For the token, the name makes the association immediate. Someone familiar with the movement can understand the reference without an explanation of crypto culture. But the phrase belongs to a much broader conversation, and competing tokens can use it just as easily. Attention alone gives this particular contract no exclusive claim to the story.

The charity allocation is the more concrete part.

Jane’s current fee configuration assigns 100% of its creator-fee share to a charity entry naming the Rape Recovery Center, with the allocation marked as locked. The organization provides survivor advocacy, crisis intervention, therapy, and prevention education in Utah. Its work is relevant to the cause being invoked. Rape Recovery Center

The percentage matters: this is 100% of the creator-fee share, not 100% of trading volume or every fee a trader pays. The recipient is currently marked as not having claimed fees, so the allocation should not be described as money already received by the organization. Nor does naming a charity establish its endorsement of the token.

If that route delivers as intended, trading could generate funding for survivor services. The amount would depend on eligible fee-generating activity and successful delivery to the recipient. A rising market cap, by itself, says nothing about how much support reaches the charity.

As of now, Jane sits around a $953K market cap, with approximately $2.86M in trading volume since launch and close to 4,000 holders. That is a fast start, although the token’s brief trading history offers little evidence about how long participation will last.

The social conversation around the contract is also different from the movement around the phrase. Much of the token-specific activity consists of trading calls and return screenshots. Other posts mix multiple Jane contracts or dispute which charity should receive fees. That confusion makes exact-contract identification and attributable donation records especially important.

My read is that Jane has a recognizable attention source and a relevant fundraising premise. The difficult part is earning trust while speculators are trading around a sensitive cause. If the community can document funds reaching the intended recipient, it has something concrete to build around. If the discussion stays focused on multiples and rival tickers, the charity premise risks becoming a label attached to short-lived speculation.

I’m watching two things: whether Jane develops sustained discussion beyond trading promotion, and whether continued activity produces verifiable payments to the intended charity.

text:
GSA GLOBAL EYE MAGAZINE | Edition 94 | October 1, 2026

*Hope in Motion: Courage, Community and Connection*

October opens the final quarter of 2026 with an urgent hope: that humanity can change course. *Nine tumultuous months have brought continuing devastation in Russia’s war against Ukraine, suffering in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, and dangerous hostilities involving the United States and Iran.* Behind every geopolitical headline are families longing for safety. The remaining three months must become an opportunity for diplomacy, humanitarian relief and lasting reconciliation. *Can the world summon the courage to make peace possible before this year ends?*

Against this troubled backdrop, Edition 94 introduces a fresh approach: *our cover captures the pulse of breaking developments, while our inside pages offer deeper encounters with people, ideas and achievements*. News that moves. Stories that matter. Together, they reveal how hope advances through extraordinary efforts.

From my home state of Tamil Nadu comes a dazzling example. *At the Asian Games in Aichi–Nagoya, Japan, Vithya Ramraj anchored India’s women’s 4×400-metre relay to gold alongside Kiran Pahal, M.R. Poovamma and Prachi.* Their 3:29.69 finish placed Bahrain second and China third. With mixed-relay silver and 400-metre hurdles bronze, Vithya secured three medals. *Her 54.75-second hurdles performance shattered P.T. Usha’s 42-year-old national record, carrying Indian women’s athletics beyond the 55-second barrier.*

The stopwatch tells only part of her story. *A truck driver’s daughter from Coimbatore’s Meenakshipuram,* Vithya grew up with identical twin Nithya amid financial hardship. Their father’s sacrifices, their mother Meena’s determination, and admission to an Erode sports hostel opened doors the family could scarcely afford. Hockey gave way to athletics; later, Nithya helped finance her sister’s training. Three events. Three medals. One unforgettable journey. . 

Young dreams also entered America’s corridors of power. On September 16, *AMEC Child of the Year Aiden Saldanha of South Barrington* visited Capitol Hill with parents Dr. Darrell Saldanha, founder of Midwest Anesthesia and Pain Specialists, and Ashley Lucas, COO of the Centers for Pain Control. *Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi welcomed his young constituent and explained congressional service.* Such encounters make democracy tangible: a child sees that citizenship carries both possibility and responsibility.

With November 3 approaching, civic engagement takes another form. Indian American business leader Ram Reddy hosted *Illinois’ Eighth District Republican nominee Jennifer Davis* at his Sterling, Virginia, home on September 23. *Davis outlined her priorities for inclusive representation, accessibility and cooperation across government*. As voters consider who will succeed Krishnamoorthi, the essential test remains clear: leadership must listen, remain accessible and turn promises into practical service. 

Meanwhile, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal’s G20 trade engagements in Milwaukee spotlight economic cooperation. *We welcome Chicago’s new Indian Consul General, Dr. Anand Prakash, a 2005-batch Indian Foreign Service officer*. His outreach to diaspora organizations offers a promising foundation for relationships built through conversation, understanding and shared purpose.

Thursday Soybean Report
Thursday, October 1, 2026
Weekly Soybean Report

The soybean market is experiencing fractional consolidation this Thursday morning, balancing expanding Midwest combine momentum against tightening national stocks and firm commercial crush demand. Futures are hovering near $12.90 to $12.91 per bushel following Wednesday's USDA Grain Stocks report, which pegged September 1 old-crop soybean inventories 3% below last year's level. With national combine progress moving past 17% complete and daily export sales into China remaining steady, the market is carving out a solid support floor despite seasonal field activity.

Futures & Market News
CBOT soybean futures are trading 2 to 3 cents lower in today’s session, reflecting ongoing harvest hedge pressure as field dry-down accelerates across the I-80 corridor.

November 2026 (X) sits at $12.90 6/8, down 2 4/8 cents. January 2027 (F) is trading at $13.06 2/8, down 2 2/8 cents. March 2027 (H) is trading at $13.17 4/8, down 2 0/8 cents.

Key Driver: Yesterday’s quarterly USDA Grain Stocks report provided a underlying spark to the commercial trade. The government confirmed U.S. old-crop soybean supplies as of September 1 came in 3% lower than year-ago figures, confirming that heavy domestic crush runs successfully cleared residual farm storage ahead of new-crop receipts. While rapid combine movement across Iowa and Illinois is applying traditional seasonal pressure to the front-month board, commercial processors are actively stepping in on dips to lock in pipeline inventories.

USDA Soybean News: Crop Progress & Export Activity

National Harvest Pace: Monday afternoon's USDA Crop Progress report showed national soybean harvest surging to 17% complete, matching brisk seasonal expectations and running ahead of last year's pace.
Crop Maturity: Over 75% of the national crop is now dropping leaves, confirming that autumn field operations will remain wide open across the central Corn Belt over the next 10 days.

Export Commitments: This morning’s weekly export sales report confirmed solid new-crop sales to Asian destinations, keeping cumulative 2026/27 export commitments significantly ahead of last year’s pace.

Commitments of Traders: Managed Money
Managed money funds continue to hold a modest net-long position, providing underlying support against aggressive seasonal short-selling.

November futures are holding above key technical baseline support at $12.80 to $12.85. Overhead technical resistance sits at the recent high-water mark of $13.20 to $13.25.

Crop & Weather Update
Warm, dry conditions across the Western Corn Belt and Northern Plains have allowed harvest operations to run without major weather interruptions.

Field reports across Nebraska and Iowa continue to show high variability in non-irrigated yields due to late-August soil moisture deficits, though irrigated fields and central Iowa locations are turning in strong pod performance.

Biofuel & 45Z Industry News
Domestic processors continue to run at near-capacity to meet expanding renewable diesel mandates and strong soybean meal export orders.

The USDA’s projection of record 2.78-billion-bushel domestic crush usage for 2026/27 remains firmly supported by local processing economics. Facilities are keeping local cash bids competitive as long-term positioning accelerates ahead of Section 45Z clean fuel rules.

Regional Cash Bids (Nebraska & Iowa)
Country cash bids have adjusted slightly lower with the board, though spot processor basis remains firm as crushers compete directly with export terminals for off-the-combine bushels.

Lincoln, NE (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.38
Sioux City, IA (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.34
Norfolk, NE (Crush): Spot Delivery at $12.42
O’Neill/Ainsworth, NE: Spot Delivery at $11.92

Summary & Strategies
Summary: The market is comfortably absorbing harvest supply without breaking key technical support. With national harvest passing 17% complete and September 1 grain stocks coming in 3% below last year, November futures enter October with a firm baseline near $12.90.

Strategies:

Commercials: Take advantage of seasonal harvest hedge pressure to extend physical pipeline coverage while local processor basis remains manageable.
Producers: November futures near $12.91 offer a strong secondary window for unhedged harvest bushels. Consider executing targeted cash sales or securing floor protection on off-the-combine deliveries to manage cash flow before seasonal supply pressure peaks.

text:
I GOT TWO JOB OFFERS IN TWO DIFFERENT STATES, AND NOW I HAVE NO IDEA WHICH ONE TO TAKE.

Job number 1 is in Texas.

The salary is $82,000 a year. 

The company offers health insurance, a 401(k) match, three weeks of paid vacation, and the position is fully remote after the first six months.

The problem?

The office is in a smaller city, and I'd have to move away from my family.

Texas has no state individual income tax, and housing can be more affordable outside the major cities. But property taxes can be high, summers are brutally hot, and I'd be starting over socially.

Job number is in New York.

The salary is $105,000.

It comes with excellent health insurance, a 401(k), four weeks of paid vacation, and a $7,500 signing bonus.

The biggest advantage is that I'd be close to my sister and wouldn't have to completely rebuild my support system.

But New York has state and local income taxes, housing can be extremely expensive, and my commute would be almost an hour each way.

So here's my dilemma:

Texas: Lower salary, lower taxes, cheaper living in the area I'd move to, remote flexibility, but I'd be far from family.

New York: Higher salary, bigger signing bonus, more vacation, and family nearby, but higher taxes, higher living costs, and a long commute.

I've been staring at these two offer letters for three days.

If you were in my position, which job would you choose and what would be the biggest factor behind your decision?

Court records show that Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's office offered plea deals to at least 10 high school athletes involved in a 2017 hazing and sexual assault case at La Vernia High School. The students were accused of sexually assaulting younger teammates, and the plea deals allowed them to avoid jail time and sex offender registration in exchange for pleading no contest to lesser charges.

The case involved 13 varsity athletes arrested in connection with a hazing ritual where younger teammates were sexually assaulted. Paxton's office took over the prosecution to avoid local conflicts of interest. Nine of the ten defendants who were offered deals accepted them, receiving deferred adjudication probation and community service, with the option to have the charges expunged from their records.

This case is one of several instances where Paxton's office has faced scrutiny for offering lenient plea deals in sexual abuse and trafficking cases.

text:
That post treats line-prosecutor plea offers as if Ken Paxton personally cut each one. That is not how the office works.
The Texas Attorney General’s Office has more than 4,000 employees, nearly 750 attorneys, and more than 30,000 cases a year. Criminal matters the office takes over — usually after a local DA recuses for a conflict — are handled by assigned prosecutors, reviewed through their division, and accepted or rejected by a judge. A plea is not valid until the court takes it. Listing outcomes from an 11-year docket and stamping Paxton’s name on each one, with no file, is an attribution, not proof he approved the deal.
The La Vernia cases are the ones behind the “10 students” line. In 2017, Wilson County police arrested 13 varsity athletes over a locker-room hazing investigation in which younger teammates were allegedly sexually assaulted with objects, including bats, a flashlight, and a bottle. Those allegations are serious. The AG’s office took the prosecutions after the local office stepped aside for a conflict. Reporting based on court records says deals were offered to 10 defendants; nine accepted, pleading no contest to lesser charges such as unlawful restraint or misdemeanor hazing, with deferred-adjudication probation, community service, no jail, and eligibility for expunction. Nothing in that reporting shows Paxton personally negotiated or signed those agreements. Deferred adjudication still required a judge. Without each file, you cannot tell whether the reduction came from proof problems, victim decisions, or a bad call.
The separate case Paxton has actually defended is Adam Hoffman in Waco. He was indicted for continuous sexual abuse of a child. The first trial hung. Prosecutors in the office said the child would not voluntarily testify again, so they could not prove the felony elements, and they offered misdemeanors. The judge rejected a one-day proposal, imposed 60 days, and Hoffman served about 30. He was not required to register in Texas because the plea did not establish the victim’s age. That is a weak result. It is also a documented evidence problem, not proof of a personal favor.
Apply the same standard the post is using. If every disposition by an elected prosecutor’s staff is the elected official’s personal act, then:
•  Travis County DA José Garza’s office dismissed the 2022 murder charge against Peter Perius in 2024 (he got 10 years on a tampering-with-a-corpse count), dismissed Roy Garcia’s 2022 murder charge in 2023, and dismissed Christian Alba’s 2023 murder charge in 2026 after a robbery plea to probation. Abbott, Patrick, and Burrows have cited those cases. A 2023 KXAN review found Garza’s office dismissed or rejected about 3,600 violent, sexual, or weapons charges in 2021–2022.
•  Bexar County DA Joe Gonzales’s office adopted a policy of recommending personal bonds on most misdemeanors and state-jail felonies unless the defendant was a flight risk or a danger.
•  Harris County’s misdemeanor bail decree sharply increased personal-bond releases. Repeat-arrest rates for those misdemeanor defendants stayed roughly flat.
Plea reductions and dismissals are how most Texas criminal cases end. They can be justified by victim refusal, proof problems, or a conviction on another count — or they can be indefensible. You cannot tell which from a headline. Without the file on each La Vernia defendant, “Paxton offered plea deals to rapists” overclaims what the records show.
