text:
I’ve put the complaint, the exhibits and the older company records together because I want people to be able to follow this case without having to piece it together from screenshots and replies.

That includes both sides. Korra says he received court documents, denies the allegations and says none of this happened. His denial needs to be included.

X filed its lawsuit against Immortal Snail LLC on September 28, 2026, in the Northern District of Texas. The case number is 4:26-cv-01254. Immortal Snail is the only named defendant in the federal case. Being mentioned in the complaint doesn’t automatically make someone else a defendant.

This is a civil lawsuit about contracts, suspended accounts and arbitration. X wants to stop the arbitration brought by Snail and is suing for breach of contract. There’s no judgment in the material I’ve reviewed establishing the bribery, unauthorized-access or impersonation allegations as proven. The complaint doesn’t bring a standalone RICO claim either, although RICO comes up in an earlier letter.

The complaint itself is 31 pages. The ECF 1 package I reviewed runs to 288 pages, including the cover sheet, index and 25 exhibits. Those exhibits matter because they also include Snail’s account, letters from its lawyers, contracts and commercial records. This package isn’t the entire, up-to-date court file.

One document deserves particular attention: the January 12, 2026 letter from their own lawyers.

Kevin C. Kaplan and Christopher E. Cheek, of Coffey Burlington, say they represent Immortal Snail, Moonrail Limited B.V. and Ossi Ketola. They describe Ketola as the “principal and owner” of both companies. The letter is part of Snail’s arbitration claim, included in Exhibit 25, pages 17–18.

If you have a claim or ongoing proceedings against Ketola involving Duel or CSGOEmpire, that’s a document worth putting in front of your lawyer. It gives them a specific statement from his stated representatives to consider when looking at ownership, corporate relationships and who belongs in your case. The separate companies, directors and representatives have to be considered alongside that statement.

The letter doesn’t settle personal liability, give ownership percentages or establish that one company is a subsidiary of the other. It also doesn’t prove that the companies are fictitious or their directors are acting as fronts. What it does record is how those lawyers described their clients and Ketola’s ownership.

The platforms’ own terms identify the companies:

Duel: Immortal Snail LLC, Nevis, registration L22982.
CSGOEmpire: Moonrail Limited B.V., Curaçao, registration 148182.
Payments for Moonrail may be handled by JHOLT LTD, Cyprus, registration HE393291, under an agreement between the two companies.

Moonrail also appears in DUEL’s trademark records. The official Israeli register lists it as the owner of trademark 374583, registered on May 5, 2025. In Canada, Moonrail filed DUEL application 2342187 on August 6, 2024. The Canadian record names David S. Lipkus of Lipkus Law LLP as the trademark agent and records the application as abandoned under section 36 on July 17, 2026.

That abandonment concerns the Canadian application. It doesn’t mean every DUEL trademark was cancelled or the platform stopped operating. And these records describe different jobs: owning a trademark, operating a platform, processing payments and representing a trademark applicant aren’t interchangeable roles.

The account history in X’s complaint starts in 2024, before the purchases people are discussing.

X alleges that on March 25, 2024, Ketola and Snail took control of an account using @duel, changed its email to a Moonrail mailbox and used it to promote a casino. X says it suspended the account on March 27, after which attempts to recover it involved intermediaries and access to employees. [Paragraphs 36–39.]

X also alleges that Ketola and CSGOEmpire were involved in an intrusion into @CSGORoll reported in April 2024. It cites a livestream in which, according to the complaint, Ketola celebrated what happened, mentioned “Sticky Hand” and said he worked for him. I haven’t authenticated the original video. X says it suspended @JNSAST the following day after reports of targeted harassment, disclosure of personal information and threats. [Paragraphs 28–29.]

The complaint goes on to describe what X calls bribery and unauthorized account reinstatements. It alleges that internal information about @duel was obtained in June 2024 and usernames were changed to move @monarch to another account. It also says an employee photographed internal information in July after a $1,500 offer and was fired. Further reinstatements through contractors and further suspensions followed, according to X. [Paragraphs 39, 40 and 44–49.]

There’s a company letter in this part of the file too. Exhibit 3 contains Moonrail’s July 9, 2024 authorization for Dušan Pećić to represent it. The names beneath the signatures are Lorenza Godett and Christopher van Rosberg, acting for Xecutive Corporate Management B.V., which is identified as a director of Moonrail. HLTV also named Pećić as CSGOEmpire’s marketing manager in March 2024.

The letter authorizes representation. It doesn’t authorize hacking, bribery or threats, or show that its signatories knew about the conduct X alleges.

The dates also need to stay as written. X dates Pećić’s appeal to June 28, 2024, but the authorization letter is dated July 9. Paragraph 47 then dates the rejection to July 13, 2025. I’m not going to quietly change those dates to make them line up.

Haci Isik appears as an intermediary. X says he was engaged in December 2024 to recover @duel and looked for insiders willing to reactivate or suspend accounts for money. It says he later tried to buy the handle directly, presenting an esports and FPS gaming project in February 2025. That’s X’s description of the discussions and their purpose. [Paragraphs 41–43.]

Paragraph 43 names two different payers: according to X, Moonrail paid for @duel_temp’s Premium subscription, while Immortal Snail paid for @duel itself. The person negotiating, the subscription payer and the handle buyer have different roles in that account. We don’t have the full negotiation or complete banking records in this package.

The acquisition documents total $480,000:

A $300,000 invoice for @Duel, dated March 24, 2025.
An $80,000 invoice for @Monarch, dated April 16.
A $100,000 receipt for @Castle, paid on June 3.

Snail says it paid all three. But two documents are invoices and one is a receipt, so I’m not calling them three bank payment confirmations. The @Castle receipt says “Crypto.” It gives no wallet, network, asset or transaction hash to trace. [Exhibit 25, pp. 13–15.]

A handle can move between accounts. The 2024 events and the 2025 purchases don’t establish that one person continuously owned one underlying account.

Then there’s the Grizzly section shown in the screenshot.

X describes Grizzly as a former CSGOEmpire Product Manager who fell out with Ketola. It alleges that Ketola and Snail accessed one of his accounts without authorization in February 2025, after he published internal conversations. [Paragraph 30.]

According to X, the Discord and Telegram conversations discussed accessing Israeli government email accounts and using them to ask platforms to remove competitors’ accounts, including CSGORoll. The complaint also describes discussions about wording those requests to make them look like legitimate official requests.

The original emails and their headers aren’t in the package I reviewed, and I haven’t independently verified who controlled those mailboxes. None of this establishes involvement by the Israeli government.

Paragraph 31 quotes Grizzly claiming to have more than 6.5 GB of chat exports and other evidence. In that quoted post, he said the material included plans to disclose relatives’ personal information and references to physical attacks against Stake. He also said he feared for his life and was looking for a journalist to receive the files.

The full archive isn’t here. His statement that he had it doesn’t tell us whether he delivered it to X, a journalist or an authority.

Paragraph 32 describes a video conversation between “Gr1zzly” and “Monarch,” whom X identifies as Ketola. X attributes to Monarch references to Bosnian mafia contacts, plans for kidnappings and possible murders, obtaining personal information, services involving violence and statements about mutilations.

Those are exceptionally serious allegations. I haven’t authenticated the original video, and I don’t have independent evidence establishing that the acts described were carried out. I’m reporting what X attributes to that conversation.

Paragraph 33 describes another conversation, on Telegram, about using government emails to get accounts removed, with language involving escalation and violence. Here the complaint calls the participant “Ossi” and says he is presumably Ossi Ketola. “Presumably” is in the document. It stays in this account too.

X says one of Grizzly’s accounts was taken over, had its biography changed from “Ex-CSGOEmpire” to a message saying it had been seized by @theJNSAST, then was used to promote Duel. It also cites @monarchlawyer announcing an account takeover. A username containing “lawyer” doesn’t establish that the person using it is one. [Paragraph 34.]

Korra expressly denies these events in the post being quoted. That denial belongs alongside the allegations. I also couldn’t retrieve the original links in footnotes 15–18 in readable form, so the complaint and screenshots aren’t a substitute for authenticating the underlying material.

X makes a technical claim as well. Footnote 15 says @fastschitzobear, @CSGOEmpire, @CSGOEmpireV2, @duel and @monarch used the same Known Device Token. X treats that as evidence of previous access through the same device or browser and an indication of collaboration. Paragraph 50 also refers to matches involving devices, software, identifiers, cookies and financial accounts.

The complete logs and dates needed to check that conclusion aren’t in the package. A shared device doesn’t tell us who wrote a particular message, or whether the overlap happened before or after an account takeover.

There are further allegations about accounts critical of the business.

Paragraph 35 describes a trademark complaint with allegedly manipulated documents against a former CSGOEmpire social media manager. That role shouldn’t automatically be treated as the Product Manager role attributed to Grizzly. In paragraph 52, X alleges that Isik offered in June 2025 to find insiders who would suspend accounts critical of Ketola and his companies. These remain allegations in the material reviewed.

X says it suspended @duel, @monarch and @castle, along with related accounts, around October 21, 2025. It alleges that requests impersonating a US law firm followed, as did a $300,000 offer to an employee to reactivate accounts. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain the November letters X disputes. Paragraph 56 doesn’t give the exact date of the alleged offer.

There are two different $300,000 figures here. The first is the invoiced purchase price for @Duel. The second is an alleged bribe in a later incident. They shouldn’t be merged.

Paragraph 58 describes a May 2026 request that X says impersonated the Malaysian police, followed by complaints in India. The exhibits show the request fields, but they don’t authenticate the senders. I’m leaving out the names of people who may themselves have been impersonated.

X mentions Arya A. when linking an email identifier used in requests with one in billing documents. That is X’s attribution. It doesn’t establish a company position or authorship of every communication.

Snail’s side is in the file too, and it deserves to be read.

Its arbitration claim says it paid for the handles and then lost access without an adequate explanation, harming its business, reputation and commercial expectations. It wants the accounts restored and compensation. It also raises possible interference by competitors or an X shareholder connected to competitors. The material I reviewed neither names that shareholder nor establishes that theory. [Exhibit 25, pp. 4–8.]

Snail started arbitration in April 2026. X says the relevant contracts require disputes to go to Texas courts. Mohamed F. Sweify was appointed arbitrator in July. Kaplan and Cheek attended an August preliminary hearing; X had said it wouldn’t participate and maintained that position. The arbitration order put jurisdiction first.

Part of the dispute is which terms apply. The 2024 handle-transfer terms select a Texas forum, reserve suspension rights and include a $100 limit on liability. Snail relies on the October 2025 Marketplace terms, which include arbitration subject to US residency. How those terms apply here is a question in the case, not something this post resolves.

X’s September letter mentioned possible legal actions, including RICO. That doesn’t turn this into a filed RICO claim, a criminal prosecution or an established FBI investigation.

The federal complaint names Caitlin A. Halpern and Lauryn E. Bennett of Gibbs & Bruns, and Charles W. Fillmore of Brown Pruitt, as X’s lawyers. The public docket records the case’s reassignment to Reed O’Connor on September 30. A lawyer’s representation of a party doesn’t make them responsible for the conduct being disputed.

The older company records help explain the business relationships. They need to be read with their own limits: these are supplied historical copies, and I haven’t independently certified every file’s authenticity or confirmed its official receipt. The X lawsuit doesn’t authenticate the rest of the archive.

An August 2023 organizational chart shows Ossi owning 100% of Moonrail and Moonrail owning 100% of JHOLT. That tells us what the chart records at that time; it isn’t a current ownership certificate. [D026.]

Moonrail’s shareholders’ register goes further back. The copy marked D027 reproduces a certification dated July 29, 2024. It records Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. subscribing for all 10,000 shares on October 1, 2018, then transferring them the next day. That initial shareholding is a separate role from its later corporate administration work.

The register lists these corporate holdings from October 2, 2018, and their later transfers:

JPellikka Oy, Finland, 2881789-9: 13.65%, later recorded under Day Star Enterprises OÜ, Estonia, 14630609.
Hiirijoki & Partners Oy, Finland, 2887371-9: 12.50%, later recorded under Rotten Apples OÜ, Estonia, 14631261.
create.repeat Oy, Finland, 2662670-6: 13.65%, later recorded under Simple Holdings OÜ, Estonia, 14635334.

It dates those three transfers to December 17, 2018. It then records Ketola, who already held 44.80%, acquiring the remaining 55.20% on November 13, 2019. That remaining stake consists of the three company holdings totaling 39.80%, plus an individual holding of 15.40%.

Those entries don’t tell us the purchase price or show the payments. They also don’t make those companies current owners of Duel. [D027, pp. 3–4.]

The Estonian public register confirms the companies’ identities and gives these dates:

Day Star: registered December 21, 2018; deleted from the register August 13, 2021.
Rotten Apples: registered December 27, 2018; deleted September 8, 2021.
Simple Holdings: registered January 4, 2019; deleted November 26, 2021.

All three registration dates are later than the December 17 transfer date in Moonrail’s book. That needs an explanation from the underlying documents. I can’t resolve the legally effective transfer dates from these records or call the discrepancy proof of forgery. The public company records establish those companies’ existence; the link to Moonrail’s shares comes from the supplied shareholders’ register.

Finland’s register also shows that JPellikka Oy became Veivi Ventures Oy on January 18, 2023. A later name change doesn’t establish a present-day stake in Moonrail.

There’s more on the earlier funding in a November 14, 2025 letter addressed to the Curaçao Gaming Authority. Moonrail says its initial funding came from Ketola’s earlier business activities through Global Vault oy and the distribution of that company’s assets after liquidation.

Global Vault’s Finnish registration number is 2793380-4. It was registered on November 9, 2016, and dissolved on April 1, 2019. The register confirms those facts. The explanation connecting its funds to Moonrail comes from Moonrail’s letter; it isn’t bank verification and doesn’t establish that Global Vault operated CSGOEmpire. [D050, pp. 1–3.]

The historical PRH/Virre extract issued on August 14, 2026 lists Ossi Eemeli Ketola as Global Vault’s board member and managing director from November 9, 2016 to July 5, 2018. It lists Satu Maarit Ketola as a deputy board member over the same period, and Lari Hiirijoki as a procurist, meaning a holder of a commercial power of attorney, from November 2017. His later appointment as liquidator was registered on July 5, 2018.

Those are documented business roles. They don’t establish family relationships or positions for those other individuals at today’s operators. [Global Vault PRH/Virre extract, pp. 1–3.]

The January 18, 2019 liquidator’s report in D050 identifies Ketola as holding all 100 shares and the rights to Global Vault’s asset distribution. Lari Hiirijoki signs as liquidator. This adds to the ownership and funding history, but it still doesn’t supply the records of transfers between the people and companies involved. [D050, pp. 10–11.]

There’s a one-year difference between two documents that I’m keeping visible. Moonrail’s November 2025 letter says Ketola owned 100% of Moonrail from November 13, 2018. The shareholders’ register puts his purchase of the final 55.20% on November 13, 2019. I don’t have enough to settle which date is correct.

The same letter gives Moonrail’s licensing account: Cyberluck N.V. in 2018, Antillephone N.V. in 2021, then the Gaming Control Board/Curaçao Gaming Authority framework. That is Moonrail’s account of its sublicensing and licensing history. It doesn’t establish permission to operate everywhere, and it can’t simply be applied to Immortal Snail. [D050, p. 1.]

The February 2025 assessment in the archive identifies missing documentation and recommends conditions covering management identification, anti-money-laundering measures, responsible gambling, territorial access and media policy. These are recommendations, not a sanction or proof that every proposed condition was imposed. [D029.]

A later business plan, identified in the archive as October 30, 2025, names Irene Rosenblatt as CEO, Matt Tanner as CFO and Sampsa Saarela as CTO. It names Rokas Daugirdas as compliance manager and Pearl Reiph as MLRO, the money-laundering reporting role. Xecutive is described as the board, with the CEO responsible for daily operations and reporting to it. Those are the roles this historical plan gives them. I haven’t verified that they still hold them, and the titles don’t prove involvement in X’s allegations. [D041, pp. 1–2 and 4–5.]

Moonrail’s advertising policy is worth reading in full as well. Version 1.0, dated May 29, 2025, requires prior advertising review, influencer agreements, sponsorship disclosure and territorial controls. It prohibits presenting gambling as a solution to financial difficulties, associating it with violence or dangerous behavior, and using content or influencers that appeal to minors. Advertising materials require compliance approval. Moonrail and its agents are also prohibited from offering players credit or loans to gamble. [D037, pp. 4–6.]

Those are written rules for Moonrail at that date. To assess a particular campaign against them, we’d still need to check the campaign itself, when it ran and which policy applied. Having a policy doesn’t tell us how it was followed in every case.

The archive also contains an August 1, 2025 response attributed to Xecutive on Moonrail’s behalf about Coffeezilla. It denies bribery. It says former managers proposed investigating a competitor without senior authorization, denies asking anyone to suppress or change coverage of Moonrail, and says the people who acted without authorization were removed. They aren’t named. The letter describes the owner as providing strategic guidance, separate from operational campaigns. That response needs to accompany the allegation. [D038.]

The August and November 2025 letters both present Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. as a director of Moonrail. Their signature blocks name Analissa Heiland and Lorenza Godett as its representatives. That establishes how they are presented in those letters, not participation in the alleged conduct. These letters and the other historical copies remain subject to the authenticity and date limitations explained above. [D038, p. 2; D050, p. 2.]

The regulatory decisions have their own official sources.

Spain’s decision ES/2025/011 imposes a €5 million fine and a four-year disqualification from conducting gambling activities on Moonrail for operating without the required Spanish authorization. It identifies CSGOEmpire and orders the activity to stop. The DGOJ announced the sanction in November 2025. I haven’t verified whether it was paid or the outcome of any appeals.

Sweden prohibited Moonrail from providing gambling without the required license in a decision dated November 2, 2023. Denmark’s official list includes https://t.co/wm4kIZPtIu among the domains blocked by court order in July 2023.

Those decisions apply to the countries and dates they cover. They don’t prove X’s allegations of bribery or unauthorized access. A declared Curaçao or Anjouan license doesn’t establish permission to operate in every other market either.

For people with disputes over balances or affiliate earnings, the terms themselves also matter. CSGOEmpire’s terms, marked as updated on July 7, 2026, promise withdrawals even when an account is closed and, where necessary, compensation for unclaimed referral earnings or rewards. They also contain exceptions and restrictions for abuse, self-referrals, dormant accounts and reversed trades. Any particular withholding needs to be checked against the terms that applied, the clause relied on and the account records. The page alone doesn’t prove a breach in someone’s case.

I also need to be open about my own position. I’ve filed a police complaint over a separate dispute. It records my allegations; it isn’t a judgment proving them. X’s case doesn’t settle my claims either. I’m leaving out amounts that still need reconciliation and keeping the two proceedings separate.

What we have here is a civil complaint, Snail’s arbitration claim, commercial records, a letter from lawyers describing Ketola’s ownership of both operators, historical company documents and official regulatory decisions. The most serious allegations in the complaint haven’t been established as proven in the material I’ve reviewed.

If I’ve got a document, page or date wrong, point me to it. I’ll correct it. I’ll also include responses supported by documents.

text:
The biggest problem in the 🇳🇬 stock market

A GOOD POST

The hidden risk of the Nigerian stock market: Buying a stock is easy, but getting your cash out isn't always guaranteed.

If you have invested in the Nigerian stock market before, you might have experienced it. It takes you just 3 seconds to buy a stock and then sometimes weeks or months to sell those same stocks. You might have wondered why? Everything boils down to LIQUIDITY.

Liquidity is how easy it is to buy or sell an asset. Let’s say, you have 10 bags of garri to sell today and in front of you are 30 buyers willing to buy your 10 bags of garri, so you will definitely sell the 10 bags immediately and immediately close your shop. Because you had a lot of buyers, there’s a lot of liquidity and remember that’s the same reason why you can immediately close your shop and call it a day. Now also imagine you have 10 bags of rice to sell but you only have 2 customers, each buys one bag of rice from you and then leaves your store with eight remaining, and so you will need to WAIT for more buyers to come and buy the remaining eight before you call it a day and close your shop. Now the reason why you’re waiting is because there’s low liquidity and this is exactly how the stock market works and why some stocks, when you try to sell, you need to wait for weeks or months for a new buyer to buy it.

A highly liquid stock has lots of buyers and sellers, so you can usually buy or sell quickly without moving the price much. A low liquidity stock has fewer buyers and sellers, so a large order can move the price significantly because if you eventually wait for a month before a third buyer comes to buy a bag of garri from you and instead of paying #20,000 the usual price, he offers to pay #18,000. You’re most likely to sell to him at #18,000, so in a low liquidity stock, an order can move the market price significantly (slippage).

Unlike a high liquidity market where you’re selling a bag of rice for #20,000 and you have 30 customers immediately wanting your 10 bags of rice, if one bids for #18,000. You’re not going to sell to him because there are 19 other buyers willing to buy at #20,000.

There are a lot of hidden gems in the Nigerian stock market that could potentially do 10X and perhaps 100X in years to come but then investing where there’s low liquidity becomes super risky.

There are still other problems I would like to talk about, but I want to make this post short, so they will be reserved for later. In the meantime, Don’t be the exit liquidity, my frens. Move smarter and stay humble.

“Follow your passion” sounds inspiring—but building a fulfilling career in medicine takes more than passion alone.

Choosing a specialty or career path can shape decades of your life, and Dr. Zwade Marshall explains why that decision deserves a much broader perspective.

What does the day-to-day work actually look like? Does the specialty fit your personality and strengths? Do you genuinely enjoy the work? What kind of schedule and work-life balance will it offer? And will those priorities still make sense as your life changes?

The things that matter to you during medical school or residency may look very different once you’re building a family, pursuing leadership opportunities, starting a business, or simply deciding how you want your life outside of medicine to feel.

Passion can absolutely be part of the equation—but it shouldn’t be the entire equation.

A sustainable career is often found at the intersection of what you enjoy, what you’re good at, how you want to live, and what you want your future to look like.

At Doc2Doc, we believe healthcare professionals deserve the freedom and resources to think beyond the next milestone and build careers—and lives—that continue to work for them as their priorities evolve.

text:
Can the labels “genocide” and “apartheid” accurately describe Israel? a new academic study by Philippe Karpe and Günther Jikeli, examines the accusations of genocide, apartheid and colonialism against Israel through their respective legal and historical definitions and the available evidence.  written by Alex Carson in The Jerusalem Post reports.

Regarding Genocide alienations: the researchers argue that the evidence examined does not establish the specific intent required under the Genocide Convention to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinian population as such.

Among the issues they examine are the supply of food and humanitarian assistance to Gaza, restrictions on aid, and the destruction of the Al Basma IVF clinic. They argue that these events, even when involving serious humanitarian consequences, do not by themselves establish genocidal intent, which is a central legal requirement for the crime of genocide.

Regarding Apartheid: the researchers distinguish between discrimination and inequality, which they acknowledge exist, and the specific legal definition of apartheid.

They note that Arab citizens of Israel participate in elections, serve in the Knesset, and have access to the Israeli legal system. Regarding the West Bank, they acknowledge that the prolonged occupation, settlements and separate legal and administrative arrangements present a much more complex case. Nevertheless, they argue that the evidence does not establish all the elements required for the legal classification of apartheid.

The study also examines “settler colonialism,” arguing that while the concept may illuminate certain aspects of the Zionist experience and the Israeli Palestinian conflict, it does not, in their view, adequately explain the full historical context of Zionism, including the Jewish historical connection to the land, its national and refugee character, and the absence of a conventional colonial metropole.

The buttmum line: the researchers are not arguing that Israel should be beyond criticism, or that there are no serious questions concerning the conflict. Their central argument is that serious allegations require serious evidence, and powerful legal and historical terms should be applied according to their precise definitions rather than as broad political labels.

Whether one agrees with their conclusions or not, the study offers an important contribution to a debate that too often moves directly from disturbing facts to sweeping legal and historical conclusions, without sufficiently examining the evidence and the definitions behind them.

Professor Jikeli is a historian and sociologist specializing in antisemitism, Jewish studies, modern European history and contemporary hate. He's a professor at Indiana University Bloomington.
Dr. Karpe is a senior researcher at CIRAD, the French research organization, specializing in law, society, development and land-related issues.

text:
"Boys in ‘Make America Great Again’ Hats Mob Native Elder at Indigenous Peoples March" was how the NYTimes initially framed the Nick Sandmann incident. 

I was speaking of the legacy media more generally, but if you'd like to limit it to the NYTimes, consider the October 17, 2023 explosion at Al-Ahli Arab Hospital. 

Within hours, the NY Times led with a headline along the lines of “Israeli Strike Kills Hundreds in Hospital, Palestinians Say,” and a news alert that treated the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry’s account as the story: an Israeli airstrike, at least 500 dead. That framing went out before the claim could be checked. It landed in the middle of the war that began with the October 7 attacks, and it fed protests, campus actions, and the cancellation of a planned Biden meeting with Arab leaders.

On October 23 the Times published an editors’ note saying the early coverage “relied too heavily on claims by Hamas, and did not make clear that those claims could not immediately be verified,” and that it “left readers with an incorrect impression about what was known and how credible the account was.” Editors later said they should have hedged more; internal Slack messages reported by Vanity Fair showed some staff had urged that and were overruled.

Some additional ones:

1) Russian bounties on U.S. troops (June 2020). A front-page Times story reported that U.S. intelligence had concluded Russia secretly offered bounties to Afghan militants to kill American troops, and that President Trump had been briefed and had not acted. The story dominated coverage and was used to argue the administration was soft on Russia or indifferent to soldiers’ deaths. In April 2021 the Biden White House said the intelligence community had only “low to moderate confidence” in the bounty claim

2) Sarah Palin and the Giffords shooting (June 2017). After a left-wing gunman shot Republican congressmen at a baseball practice, a Times editorial said the link between political incitement and the 2011 shooting of Gabby Giffords was “clear,” and tied it to a Sarah Palin PAC map with crosshairs over Democratic districts. No such link was ever established. 

3) Rudy Giuliani and a supposed FBI warning (April 2021). text:
Before Lena Horne became an enduring icon of American entertainment, she was already breaking barriers that Hollywood had spent decades enforcing.

In 1942, Horne signed with MGM, becoming the first Black performer to secure a long-term contract with a major Hollywood studio. She refused to accept the demeaning roles routinely offered to Black actresses and went on to build a career spanning film, music, Broadway and television. 

Her life also became part of a Black and Jewish story. In 1947, Horne married Jewish composer, arranger and MGM musical director Lennie Hayton. Their interracial marriage was kept private for nearly three years amid the intense racial prejudice of the era. Hayton would also serve as Horne’s musical director during their life together. 

Horne later became an outspoken civil rights advocate, participating in the 1963 March on Washington and using her platform to support organizations including the NAACP and National Council of Negro Women. 

A trailblazer on the screen, on the stage and far beyond both.

text:
Christopher Wood’s interview with Kushal Lodha

The AI boom is the bubble

Wood has watched three big blow-ups: Japan in the early 1990s, Asia in 1997, and the US housing crisis in 2008. He thinks today’s real bubble is AI spending in America.

His simple point: new technology is usually overhyped at the start and underestimated later. The internet was a real thing, but in 2000 people built far too much fiber-optic cable. Companies went bust. Amazon’s stock fell about 95%. Then the cheap leftover cable helped online shopping explode.

He compares AI to US railroads in the late 1800s. The tracks got built and helped the economy. Most of the railroad companies still went bankrupt, and there was a depression. Useful technology, bad investments.

Right now four giant US tech companies — Meta, Alphabet (Google), Microsoft, and Amazon — may spend up to about $1 trillion next year on AI data centers and chips. Wood’s base case is that they will not earn enough from this to justify the spending. They are doing it partly because they fear being left behind, not only because they see a clear profit.

Example: imagine four shop owners each borrowing huge sums to build the biggest warehouse in town, all selling the same thing. The warehouse builders and the cement suppliers get rich immediately. The shop owners may never earn the rent back.

So far, the money has gone to the “picks and shovels” companies — the ones selling the tools, not using them. First that was Nvidia (the chip designer). More recently it has been memory-chip makers: Samsung and SK Hynix in Korea, and Micron in the US. Wood says Samsung and Hynix alone are forecast to earn almost three times what all 50 Nifty companies earn combined. That is why their stocks soared.

He also flags three accounting tricks that make the spenders look healthier than they are:

They stretch out how fast they write down the cost of the equipment, so profits look better for longer.
Some data-center deals sit off the balance sheet, often with private credit.

“Circular financing”: Nvidia helps fund customers such as OpenAI so those customers can buy Nvidia’s chips. Similar to a shop lending you money so you can buy its products.

Early on, these giants paid with their own cash. Now they are borrowing. Wood’s warning: the longer this goes on with debt, the more likely it ends in a credit bust. He does not say that happens tomorrow. He says the test is each quarter: if they raise spending plans again, does the market still cheer, or does it finally say no?

Why this is mainly an American problem

AI building is driving about half of US growth, he says. The other driver is rich households spending because their stocks are up. About 10% of US households do half of discretionary spending. So the stock market can look great while ordinary people feel poor. That is the “K-shaped” economy: one arm up, one arm down.

China’s AI spending is roughly one-tenth of America’s. Wood thinks China is in a better spot: the US is ahead on chips, China is far ahead on electricity. Data centers need huge power. He also thinks the US is chasing “AGI” (a machine that truly thinks), which he doubts will arrive just by making chatbots bigger. China, in his telling, just wants cheap tools that are “8 out of 10” and good enough to sell.

If the AI trade cracks, foreigners who left India to buy Korean memory stocks would have a reason to come back. India has almost none of this AI capex, so it is a kind of opposite bet.

Why foreigners sold India

Not because India suddenly broke. Dedicated emerging-market funds have to follow a benchmark. Three stocks — TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix — became about 30% of that benchmark. For 20 years those funds were underweight Korea and overweight India. In the last 18–24 months they had to chase Korea. India looked dull by comparison, even if it did not crash.
He is not underweight India. He still says: if he could own only one stock market for 10 years and not sell, it would be India. The excitement, in his view, is mid and small companies, not just the Nifty. The Nifty Midcap 100 nearly doubled since 2023; the Nifty rose less than a third. Valuations are high, so a shock (oil, war) can hit them hard. He still likes a lively small-company market more than a market where everyone only buys the index.

Indian IT services have been “derated” — investors pay less for each rupee of earnings — because AI may replace some outsourced coding. He is less worried about GCCs (the tech centers global companies run inside India). Software in general is at risk unless a company has a real lock-in. Microsoft’s edge is that everyone is already on it; switching is a hassle.

Bonds, the dollar, and why he hates US Treasuries

He cares more about the 10-year US government bond yield than the Fed’s short-term rate. The 10-year is what sets mortgages, corporate borrowing, and the cost of funding America’s deficit.

His traffic-light rule from the interview: above 4.5% is a yellow warning; a clear break of 5% is red. Yields had just touched 5%. Two reasons they rose: growth and inflation picked up, and investors want extra pay for lending to governments with huge debts.

His fiscal point: US entitlements plus interest are almost equal to all federal tax receipts. Any slowdown makes the budget look untenable. He says a sane investor is not paid enough at 5% for 10-year US debt. He would rather own Brazilian local bonds at about 14.5%, or Indian, Chinese, and Singapore government bonds in local currency. Since he sold G7 bonds in March 2020, that portfolio has beaten G7 bonds by more than 60 percentage points in dollar terms, on his numbers.

He expects the dollar to stay weak unless the next Fed chair really raises rates and Washington cuts spending. He does not expect that. Elon Musk’s DOGE cost-cutting, he notes, lasted about two months.

Gold

If bond yields keep rising toward 6%, he thinks Washington will eventually cap them, as Japan did in 2016 (“yield curve control”: the central bank buys whatever it takes to hold the yield down). That stops bond prices falling, but the currency weakens and gold rises. On that path he has talked about gold at $10,000 an ounce. He does not know when.

Near term he sees a range: top around $5,500, bottom around $3,800–$4,000, with a floor nearer $4,300 more recently. After a big run he had suggested trimming; now he is fine with about 20% in gold if you can tolerate it. If you own none, start. He also likes gold-mining stocks (especially North American ones, or the GDX ETF) because their profits jump when gold rises and costs stay tame — though higher oil hurts miners.

Indian households hold nearly $4 trillion of gold, he says. Gold loans let people use that as collateral. He likes that market, but the stocks have already run.

India: rates, banks, property, power

He hopes the rupee has bottomed. Supports he cites: a bigger-than-expected NRI foreign-currency deposit inflow, possible RBI rate hikes, a cheaper real exchange rate, and a weaker dollar. Oil is still the short-term risk, but less deadly than 20 years ago.

He is tactically more positive on banks than NBFCs if the RBI hikes, because NBFCs’ borrowing costs rise faster. Long term he prefers NBFCs: they are more entrepreneurial, and bank CEO pay is capped by the RBI, so talent prefers NBFCs. His model portfolio had sold HDFC Bank and bought Bajaj Finance earlier; that was not a “right now” call.

Property: easy money is made. He still owns DLF and Lodha at 5% each as long-term holds, out of favor because people fear rate hikes. He sees last year’s slower sales as a mid-cycle pause. Broader private capex, not just property, is finally picking up — companies at his conference sounded more confident.

The sector he is most excited about is power: electrification plus solar and batteries. Chinese battery storage has made solar cheaper than coal in his telling. India’s question is whether it can use that technology.

He raised Eternal (Zomato) to 5%, betting it stays the long-term e-commerce winner, while accepting competition in quick commerce.

Index level: domestic mutual-fund inflows are strong, but new share supply (IPOs, placements) soaks them up almost one for one, so the index stays flat even if earnings grow. He thinks 15% a year is possible from earnings if supply eases. A worse war would cut supply; a sudden stop in SIPs would crash prices and then attract foreigners. SIPs are not stopping.

Oil, wars, and hedges

He assumes the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed and Red Sea access is also impaired, so oil “should” be higher. Diesel has risen more than the headline oil price. The only practical hedge he offers is owning energy stocks (few in India; majors in the US). Renewables are the long game; you still need jet fuel now.

He also says do not forget Ukraine. He thinks Western talk of Russia collapsing is hype, and that Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukrainian energy. In Germany and the UK, gas prices were about 10 times US levels. He links that to Europe dropping Russian gas plus lost Qatari LNG. Germany’s AfD is rising on immigration and a wish to restore Russian energy; the chancellor’s approval was about 12% when he last checked.

His 3-year buy/sell jars

From the chit game:

Sell: US Treasuries, US dollar
Buy: gold lenders, Indian real estate, gold, Indian banks

Where he could be wrong: if the US really cuts spending and lives with higher rates, or if the hyperscalers actually earn a good return on AI capex.

These are one strategist’s views, not forecasts you should treat as fact. The useful core is the distinction he keeps making: profits booked today by chip sellers are not the same as profits the spenders will earn tomorrow, and India’s quiet period has more to do with that global scramble than with India itself.

These are Christopher Wood’s views (Jefferies), not advice.

Source: Conversation with Kushal (Kushal Lodha)

text:
But again - your arguments operate from the framing that the current budgets are the baseline, while they are not. They have grown more than twice the rate of cumulative inflation since the covid overspending of 2020. And, as usual, budget/tax reform of any kind is always framed as cutting from the status quo, as opposed to re-examining budgets annually from a zero basis & working up based on audited necessity. As you ought to know all too well from your political experience, it's why we get the charade of a bureaucracy demanding 10% increases via Democrats in a 2-3% inflationary environment and when Republicans counter with only a 6% increase, the headlines scream "budget cuts threaten <fill in the blank with whatever is scariest>". You're doing the same thing here.
Now - if you're positioning your think tank to be the go-to for smaller counties who will need to identify & fix true non-waste related spending priorities after Amendment 3 passes by offering analysis and trade offs, fine - that's honestly what I think you ought to be doing with whatever expertise you can offer them. But it should come attached to the kind of audits Igoglia has been running on counties identifying waste, and hopefully one of the ways Amendment 3 will be implemented will be with a DOGE-like group created by the state as a resource for counties looking to trim fat and not bone. That's governing too, at least it ought to be.

But here's something that will look like a tell to a lot of us out here: where are your projections, possibilities and analyses of the positive economic effects Amendment 3 will have? You've been on a jihad against property tax reform since momentum began for it over a year ago. Where are the analyses of the likely positive results of it? 
I can think of a couple of categories offhand:
A. Immediate/Short Term: with sizable amounts of money returned to homeowners who have already budgeted in higher property taxes, how would that stimulate the Florida economy? Especially if the mindset of those people was that the money was already dedicated to their homes? Upgrades, repairs, HVAC, energy systems, roofing, landscaping, appliances.... what items on their improvement lists suddenly get a boost and how would that spending stimulate local businesses or the economy in general? And where else would that money be spent or invested? Private school tuition? In-state vacations? Bigger purchases such as cars? Where's the study on that? (Oh, and show your work. If my position is philosophical that property taxes & government budgets drunk on rising assessment values & government caused inflation is basically theft via taxing unrealized capital gains at the threat of eviction, I think my work is done). Also, how would all the Democrats opposing Amendment 3 feel about all that new consumer spending, especially with the Keynsian multiplier effects they love to talk about? You'd think they'd be in favor of it, but I guess not. As usual, the only "Keynsian" stimmy the Democrats like is when their own politicians print money & cut checks to their supporters. But that's another debate entirely. Back to this one...
B. Intermediate/Long Term: Whether or not this idea spreads to other states (and it will if it works, which is why the establishment fears it even more than they feared Prop 13 in California 50 years ago), and for the sake of argument let's assume the 5 year residency requirement survives the courts - how many young families move to Florida and how does the local employment/recruitment/corporations-move-to-Florida picture get affected by this? It would certainly be a big draw, especially as rates and mortgages rise nationally. And as far as retirees, negating the fear that rising assessments & property taxes would cause seniors on fixed income to possibly lose their homes or have their finances slammed is removed - so now Florida gains a big advantage over other retiree destination states like Arizona, Nevada, Texas, Tennessee, etc. Would this mean more planned retirement communities developed in Florida, attracting generational wealth and spending as well? More construction in general, driving all sorts of related industries and jobs? 

If I (and others on here I'm figuring by the way you routinely get dogpiled in the comments) saw material addressing stuff like this (or whatever other positive economic effects would/could result from Amendment 3) coming from your posts, like I said before, we might be more open to your claim to be the lighthouse keeper, as opposed to the establishment shining the lighthouse beam in our eyes to blind us.

text:
Not just crypto. How much is enough, lady, for your Dear Leader to benefit from his office? 

From Grok:
The pattern
Unlike recent predecessors, Trump did not put his assets in a blind trust or divest. His revocable trust still benefits him; his children run the operating companies. In the first term the Trump Organization said it would pursue no new foreign deals. In the second term that constraint was dropped. The company’s stated policy bars new material transactions with foreign governments but allows deals with private foreign companies. Ethics lawyers have long said that line is thin, because private developers in the Gulf and elsewhere often sit next to sovereign funds and officials.
The 2025 financial disclosure put his total reported income above $2B. Crypto was the largest slice. The rest still matters.
Clubs as an access toll
Mar-a-Lago, Doral, and nearby golf clubs are the domestic version. The Miami Herald found those four S Florida properties produced about $265M in 2025. Mar-a-Lago alone brought more than $75M, roughly triple the annual range in the first term, after the initiation fee was raised to $1M before the election. Doral brought about $121M.
Campaign committees must disclose spending, and they did: more than $1M at South Florida Trump properties in 2025, and Guardian/CREW tallies put political spending at Trump properties above $1.3M since January 2025. Foreign governments and corporations do not have to itemize the same way. CREW counted more than 50 special-interest events at Trump properties and repeated visits by foreign officials, including Israeli diplomats and Argentine officials around the time Argentina secured a large U.S.-backed financing package. Membership and event fees are not campaign donations. They still route money to the president’s business from people who want time near him.
The Qatari jet
Qatar offered a luxury 747, valued around $400M if new, for use as a temporary Air Force One. The administration’s legal theory is that the plane is a gift to the U.S. government, blessed by White House counsel and the attorney general. Trump said publicly that only a fool would refuse it “on behalf of our Country,” and reporting described a plan to transfer it later to his presidential library foundation, which would leave him personal use after office.
The foreign emoluments clause bars an officeholder from accepting a present from a foreign state without congressional consent. Critics, including some Republicans, called the arrangement a flying emolument, especially given Trump’s later claim of broad, hard-to-review power in foreign affairs. Fact-checkers noted that a true government gift used only as AF One is legally different from a plane that ends up as a personal library perk. The Reagan Library’s retired Air Force One did not start as a foreign gift. Whether the transfer happens as described is still the hinge; the conflict exists either way while the donor has live interests in U.S. policy.
Markets and the rest of the ledger
The same disclosure showed more than 21k securities trades in 2025, with a notional range in the hundreds of millions to nearly $2B. Later monthly filings continued the pace. Some trades landed near government contracts or presidential comments, including Dell purchases before public praise and a large contract. The White House says the accounts are discretionary, model-driven, and closed to direction from Trump or his family. The New York Times reported it found no evidence he ordered the trades. The ethics point is narrower: recent presidents generally used blind trusts or broad funds so that even well-timed trades would not look like bets on their own decisions.
Family-adjacent deals sit in the same file. Jared Kushner’s private-equity firm has taken large Gulf sovereign commitments. Steve Witkoff’s family sold a Manhattan hotel interest to Qatari buyers for a reported $623M. Those are not Trump’s personal P&L, but they are the circle that travels with the office

Yes, the Connecticut Department of Social Services (CDSS) experienced a significant data breach. An unauthorized third party gained access to approximately 22,500 Medicaid-related accounts.

Details of the Breach
How the Breach Occurred
The breach was linked to compromised credentials of an employee at Hartford HealthCare.
Hackers accessed the HUSKY provider portal, which is part of the Connecticut Medicaid program.
Information Compromised
The breach involved sensitive patient information, including:
Full names
Medicaid ID numbers
Dates of healthcare services
Details of care received
Billing information
Security Measures Taken
The unauthorized access was discovered on March 25, 2026.
CDSS and Gainwell Technologies, the service provider, secured the affected portion of the portal immediately after the breach was identified.
Investigators confirmed that the unauthorized party no longer has access to the system.
Impact and Response
Social Security numbers and financial account information were not compromised.
Affected individuals are being notified and offered complimentary credit monitoring and fraud support services.

text:
This could be the end of the Cinderella run in March Madness. Calipari says nine of his players make more than his assistants and the other three make more than his entire staff. In every pro league the roster out-earns the assistant coaches, and usually head coaches too. Because the players are the product.  In college sports the head coach for years was the main attraction. College sports just became a league with a pro payroll, and it never became a league.

Pro leagues run on a cap, a draft and contracts, and those rules keep the small markets alive. ESPN counted seven different NBA champions in the seven seasons from 2019 through 2025, the longest stretch of parity in league history. Boston won the 2024 title and then traded Jrue Holiday and Kristaps Porzingis to stay under the second apron. College has none of it. The House settlement set a $20.5 million cap, and NC State's Dave Doeren said "loopholes have won the day." The Protect College Sports Act that Calipari backs stays neutral on whether athletes are employees.

So the money goes wherever the money already is. The Ringer reported that SEC schools average about $9.7 million per basketball roster, mid-majors about $2.3 million and low-majors under $1 million. A mid-major's best player gets noticed in March and gets an offer from a bigger school, and no rule stops it.

March Madness sells one thing, and it's the underdog. In 2023, 9-seed FAU made the Final Four and San Diego State played for the title. Miami's Jim Larrañaga said "anybody can beat anybody." In 2025, for the first time, all 16 of the top-four seeds won their opening game. In 2026, only four double-digit seeds advanced past the first round, the fewest since 2007, and no team seeded 13 through 16 won a game for the second straight year. That's a small sample, and the money is pointing in one direction.

Fans love the spending because it's their school doing it, and each dollar makes the next upset harder to find. The NBA shows a league can pay its players and still hand a title to a small market. College gets the payroll and skips the rules, and the bracket pays for it. A 9 seed reached the Final Four in 2023, and in 2026 no team seeded 13 through 16 won a game.

Ten miles down I-10 he walked on at McNeese at about 150 pounds with no offers, earned a scholarship his first semester, and left as a two-time first-team All-Southland safety.

Roberts Defensive Player of the Year award. Undrafted to the Eagles, he became the first Yellow Jacket on an NFL roster. Iowa retired No. 16. Super Bowl LIX made him the first Jacket with a ring.

The claim is supported by a September 30, 2026, San Antonio Current review of court records and by contemporaneous local reporting from 2017–2019. Under Ken Paxton, the Texas Attorney General’s Office took over prosecutions in a La Vernia High School hazing case (to avoid local conflicts of interest) and offered plea deals to at least 10 students facing sexual-assault charges, including allegations involving minors. Nine accepted deals that avoided jail time, reduced the charges, and left open the possibility of later expungement. Arrests of 13 varsity athletes occurred in March–April 2017 after reports that younger teammates (at least 10) had been sexually assaulted with objects during hazing rituals involving football, basketball, and other teams.

Publicly named defendants (mostly adults at the time of disposition; several others were juveniles and not named in news accounts) and outcomes drawn from Wilson County News, KENS 5, KSAT, and BuzzFeed News reporting include:

- Parker Beck, Blake Borgfeld, Derek Miller, Zane Snell, and Robert Olivarez Jr.: pleaded no contest to unlawful restraint (a state-jail felony) around October 2019 and received deferred-adjudication probation.
- Christian Brock Roberts (then 20) and Colton Patrick Weidner (then 20): pleaded no contest to unlawful restraint on November 26, 2019; each received five years of deferred adjudication.
- Dustin Norman (then 21): pleaded no contest to unlawful restraint on December 16, 2019; received three years of deferred adjudication.
- John Rutkowski (then 20): pleaded to hazing (a Class B misdemeanor) on December 16, 2019; received one year of deferred adjudication.
- Alejandro Ibarra (then 20): rejected offered deals (including one that included a short jail term), maintained innocence, and was set for trial.
- Four unnamed juveniles: pleaded no contest to unlawful restraint in early October 2019; each received five years of deferred-adjudication probation plus 100–200 hours of community service (AG’s office confirmed it was the prosecuting agency).

Deferred adjudication means the cases can be dismissed and records potentially expunged if probation terms are completed; failure can result in full sentencing on the reduced charges. The original allegations, per indictments and news summaries citing court documents, involved restraint and sexual assault with objects (examples reported included a flashlight and a bottle) in locker-room settings. Not every individual charge or exact plea term for all 10 is itemized in publicly available summaries, particularly for juveniles.
