text:
Saint Michael, Protector of the Church by Bishop John Edward Cuthbert Hedley,  29 September 1895
.
“At that time shall rise up Michael, the great prince who standeth for the children of thy people . . . and at that time shall thy people be saved.” – Daniel 12:1,2
.
This great solemnity of the blessed Archangel Michael, whose name is invoked on this church and its flock, cannot but lift our hearts to the heavens. The name of this angel, seraph, minister of the Lord, leader of the armies of heaven, conqueror of Satan, protector of men, and standard-bearer of the Day of Judgment, needs must give these souls of ours a vision of a world far wider than that to which we are now confined, and a sense of great deeds, great issues, immeasurable space, unnumbered hosts, and the play of stupendous forces, none the less real that we so dimly conceive them. The name of Saint Michael the Archangel stands for the sum of the invisible interference of God in His creation. Jesus is the source of grace; Mary is the channel of grace; Michael stands for. the sword of God, which rids him of those who gainsay, the hammer of God which levels the hills and makes the rough ways plain, the special providence of God which watches His children from their birth to their judgment.
.
Saint Michael, like all the saints who are with God, intercedes for men; like all the angels he executes God’s ministry. But because he is prince and leader his ministry is of the widest reach, and his interces sion sets in motion the most far-reaching of the forces of the Incarnation.
.
This small earth of ours is only a grain of sand in the sight of God; yet the least of the souls which He has created has a place in His knowledge and His solicitude. He has proved this or proclaimed it by the Incarnation. The material laws of the universe are the expression of His will and the continuance of His creative act. These laws go on from year to year, from age to age, unbroken; on the whole, firm, fixed and constant. It is their results which we see in earth, ocean and sky; in this visible framework of things which seems, and which indeed is, so fair and so wonderful.
.
But the spiritual world of human souls, God’s chief concern, is very different. Here the forces of free intelligence and will have to be reckoned with. Compared with the earth, the sea, the heavens, men’s hearts are more substantial than the rock or the mountain, more unstable and uncontrolled than the widest waste of waters, and more mysterious, more incapable of being mapped and measured than the infinite depths of starry space. And yet the God Who took a human heart Himself to win hearts must follow all their wanderings, control all their forces, hold the secret of all their mysteries. He must do so because he made them so, and because, come what may, He is and must be the Father and the Friend of all the rational creatures He has made.
.
Therefore we should expect that the influence of God, and the pressure and working of God upon the spiritual nature of man, should pervade all the universe of humanity. We should be prepared to find a subtle and diffused force penetrating everywhere like an atmosphere, and ready to leap out into activity wherever it met human aspiration or human operation. We should not be surprised to see the infinite love and solicitude of our Heavenly Father taking hold of visible things and of men themselves, as a sculptor puts his ideas into marble and bronze, and associating all that human eyes and ears take note of, with the one grand purpose of winning and keeping the immortal creatures who can only find their rest in Him. In one word, we should expect to find what we do find the great kingdom of Divine grace; grace sanctifying, illuminating, strengthening, and impelling; grace which radiates from the Passion, from the Cross, and leaves no hidden place unvisited of all man’s complex nature, and no step unaided of all his earthly journeying. We should expect the great dispensation of the Church to keep alive the word of Jesus, and the sacramental touch of Jesus visible in her ministry and her ministrations, but made living and powerful by the unseen inspiration and spiritual power of Him Who has made her a world within a world in order to save the world.
.
What may we conceive to ourselves that God sees most that God regards most solicitously when from His heights and His splendours of light He looks down upon this wandering orb of ours this earth of His creation? Not its continents or its seas, its mutations or its tempests, its empires or its revolutions; but rather that Church which He has purchased with His blood, which is the sign of His love of souls, and the instrument of His saving of souls. This He will love this He will cherish this He will visit. This, by means of all the agencies which lie within the power of His mighty right Hand, He will guide and sustain; and nothing will stop Him except the barriers which He Himself has placed, of man’s freedom, probation, and merit.
.
Do you believe that God interferes to uphold His Church? What do we mean by the interference of God? It is certain that everything that happens is done by God, except sin, which is not so much an act as the deflection of an act. It is certain also that grace is required for every meritorious work, and that sufficient grace is given to every human being. This being laid down, there comes that wide, that limitless field, which is called in Holy Scripture the field of His goodness “How good is the God of Israel, to them that are of a right heart!” (Psalm 123:1); or of His mercy “the Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and of much compassion, and true!” (Exodus 34:6) That which urges Him to be “good” and to be merciful is either His own greater glory, or also the movement which the soul makes (always through His grace) towards Him by faith, love, or contrition a movement which, poor and feeble as it is in the best of us, it is His custom to meet with the royal outpouring of His munificence, as a prince might reward with treasure the poor man who offered him a humble flower. We mean, there fore, by the “interference” of God of that God by Whom we live, move, and are those kind and merciful acts of His which are not either part of the law of nature or of that general law of grace which, although its source is God’s free bounty, yet is, as a fact, so regular and constant that it is virtually and practically a law. The truth is, that the magnificent goodness of God respects neither law nor promise when it is a question of drawing the souls of men. He will not be bound. His children must have more than they have a right to more than they deserve more than their very aspirations can reach to. He must always be helping, inspiring, urging, enriching. He takes a nature that is richly gifted, and transforms it by His grace into sanctity. He visits a heart that is empty of all natural advantage, and with sovereign operation He equally fills it with all that heaven can give. He leads the child by the hand to prayer, purity, and sacrifice. He illuminates the spirits of young men and women who turn to Him ever so little, and sets them safe upon their road. He gives sinners chance after chance; and thousands of them, the moment they attend to Him, are carried home upon His shoulders. He guards His children even from temporal danger and bodily pain, to make them love Him. He makes all visible things speak His name and urge His claims. He sways the vast universe, causing all the things that lie around us and above us and beneath our feet to co-operate with Him in that work of His which never ceases, the saving of the souls He has created.
.
It is on grounds like these that I say that God interferes to sustain and to protect His Church. The Church is His device, springing from the fruitfulness of His precious Blood, for making souls His own. Therefore, there is nothing on earth that He is equally solicitous about. It is true that the individual soul of you and of me is His object not an institution or an order. It is also most true that He does at times save souls without the ministry of word and sacrament. But we are not concerned with what happens rarely and extraordinarily. The Church is the fold of His sheep. There is safety, guidance, shelter, and food. Therefore the Church is the world’s grand visitation the pledge and the dispenser of grace and salvation to the multitudes of the children of men. If God interferes in matters here below, how is it possible He should not interfere to sustain His Church?
.
Moreover, it cannot be questioned that we can see and ascertain His interference. We can see Him, age by age, guiding His Church like a ship, and keeping her, to use the phrase, afloat. For, if you observe, this is what must be done for the Church in every generation. She is perfect in her constitution and equipment; the .Holy Spirit speaks through her, and the power of Christ is incarnate in her ministrations. But she is a visible and earthly institution. She sails, not in the clouds or in the realms of fancy, but in the turbulent human ocean. She may be holy, apostolical, divine; but what if she goes to the bottom? She may be the ark of salvation; but what if she falls to pieces? What if her own crew desert her and set up a rival ship? Or again, what if she will not sail, and cannot reach those shores to which she was meant to carry the precious freight of her lading? I contend that you can see, with very ordinary attention, that God has been interfering in mercy and goodness, even since the day of Pentecost, to preserve and sustain His Church by saving her from the hands of those who would destroy her, by preventing her from being split in pieces by her own children, and by keeping up, unweakened and undiminished, that saving and con verting power with which she started her career. I know that, speaking of this protection in general, we may truly say that Christ has promised it, and there fore in that sense it can hardly be called the result of God’s interference; it is rather a law of the spiritual world. But our Lord and Saviour might have fulfilled this promise of His in many different ways. What He has done is what a man, and our brother, might have done. He has not used His omnipotence, but His love. He has not thundered in the heavens and made the earth stand awed and silent, but has hidden Himself behind human agencies, and moved men and men’s works sweetly, silently for the most part, sometimes with power and the shadow of His fear, but generally as one who knows that there are more mighty means for moving this solid earth than even to call the lightning from the heavens. In one word, He has chosen that the history of His Divine dealing with .His Church should be a never-failing story and record of merciful interference.
.
The history of the Church has been written by many, and from many points of view; and there are none of us, perhaps, who know so little of it as not to be impressed with the strong and sweet dealings of the Father Who loves us during every century of her existence. But at this moment, on this day, I would do no more than lift one corner of the veil which hides from worldly eyes the intricate path and the varied course of Providence. For it is certain that the Lord of heaven and earth, here as in other things, uses ministers to do the will of His mercy. It seems not less certain that the appointed spirit who by him self and his armies guards and upholds the Church is the Archangel Michael. He it is who executes those interferences of God’s mercy and power which are visible throughout the length of her annals. He is the prince of the heavenly host; God’s Church is the dearest of all God’s interest. Is it not right, is it not in accordance with the mind of Him Who willed the Incarnation, that the greatest angel should fight for the noblest empire?
.
The Holy Scriptures are full of Saint Michael. We have there described his ministry in the heavens and his ministry on earth. The first glimpse that is given to mortal eyes of his service of his Creator, is when we see him contending with Satan in that awful and tremendous battle which shook the heavens themselves. Saint Michael was the first of all the servants of God. At the moment of his creation, when he with all the multitude of the angelic host stood free to serve or to rebel, one act or two of that lofty spiritual essence, quicker than the lightning, sufficed to carry through that probation which with grosser beings is prolonged for days and years. In those first flashes of his grand intelligence and will he gave himself to his God in worship, loyalty and burning love. He was the first of creatures that did this. One by nature as great as he took the other side; and then came the conflict Michael and his angels, the dragon and his angels it is thus the revelation names them (Apoc. xii. 7, viii). It was Saint Michael’s first act of ministerial service. God needed him not, nor his legions. But ministration is part of the Divine plan of creation. God does everything, but the angels are His instruments; and so are you and I, and every one in his rank and place. The Eternal executed His most just wrath and judgment upon the apostates by the ministry of those who stood faithful. That was the catastrophe described in the Apocalypse “and their place was not found any more in heaven”. That chapter of the Apocalypse of Saint John goes on to say something suggestive and terrifying. The dragon who is cast out of the heavens falls to the earth. “Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, knowing that he hath but a short time.”
.
(Apocalypse 12:12) Well do we know what is implied in those brief and pregnant words. Part of the drama of human probation is man’s temptation by the demon. A certain power has been given to him. The chain that binds him has been a little lengthened out. He can suggest evil to the just, and he can stir up the unjust to acts of persecution and oppression. But there is one purpose which he took up the very moment that he fell from the heavens. He set himself to destroy the Church of God. For this, from the beginning, he has used all his intellect and set in motion all his legions. 
.
Whether in the primeval days when the Church was represented by the patriarchal tradition, or in the times of the Synagogue, or now when the Christian Church, founded at Pentecost, fills the world he has under stood what it was that it most behoved him to counteract and ruin. To cripple the Church, to divide her, to sterilise her, this has been his aim. For this he has urged on his own instruments by lust of power, corrupted her prelates and teachers by pride, and striven to cast upon her the chains of that sleep which worldliness so fatally brings on. “He persecuted the woman that brought forth the man-child.” (Apocalypse 12:13) That woman symbolises the Church, and that sentence of the Apocalypse sums up the work of the demon during these centuries of Christianity.
Where must the Christian heart look for Saint Michael, the great Archangel, during all these years of conflict? Where but at the very head of that army of the ministers of the Lamb, to whom it has been given to carry the power of God into this never-ceasing war? We seem to see him dimly through the mist and twilight of the earliest records, even in the days when God began to form a chosen people to be His Church’s prototype. Who was he, that chief angel of the three, who stood before Abraham in the vale of Mambre, as he sat in the door of his tent on that day at noon? (Genesis 18:1). The Jewish tradition, accepted by our best Christian interpreters, has handed down that it was Saint Michael. But in that visit was given the Divine charter and promise to the Father of all the faithful. When God commissioned Moses in that august vision at the burning bush, who was the angel who sustained the very personality of God the Redeemer? Again, Catholic tradition says it was Michael Michael who spoke to the Hebrew herdsman, not as to a private person, but as to the future leader of Israel and the prince of the Synagogue; the same Michael who, not long afterwards, when Josue was camped before that Jericho which signified the powers of hell, suddenly appeared to him in the plain, holding a drawn sword, and spoke those words at which the great leader threw himself upon his face upon the ground: “I am prince of the host of the Lord, and now I am come” (Josue 5:14). Thus, and in many other apparitions too numerous to mention, he showed himself as Israel’s champion, and by the prophet Daniel is called, as you have heard, the “great prince who standeth” for that people, their “own prince” and guardian. It is in this character that we catch mysterious glimpses of him in the Psalms and Prophecies, ruling the destinies of the race and commanding legions of blessed spirits; as in that vision of the prophet Zacharias, in which the “angel of the Lord” is seen as a mounted warrior in the grove of the myrtle trees with other riders, who answer him that they have walked through and patrolled the whole land, and then the princely leader lifts up his voice and prays for the people that he loves. (Zachariah 1:8)
.
That ancient covenant passed away. It was for another nation on another and a wider field that the great Archangel and his legions were finally to contend. One night Saint Michael led his hosts to where a Child was born in Bethlehem of Juda, and their swords were for the moment sheathed and their heads unhelmeted whilst they chanted glory to God in heaven, and peace on earth to men. Holy Scripture nowhere mentions Saint Michael in connection with our Blessed Lord. But we are told that Angels were at His birth, that Angels ministered to Him, that Angels comforted Him, that Angels kept guard at His tomb, that Angels conducted Him to the heavens. If the heavenly host did these things, their Prince and Leader was foremost in them all. There can be no rashness in saying as much as this. Many Saints and holy persons seem to have had it revealed to them that he was the Guardian of the Sacred Humanity, and that he was, and is still, the Guardian of the Blessed Sacrament. These pious beliefs undoubtedly indicate traditional Catholic leanings. But we do not need them. What the angelic army does its chief inspires; and what the Angels do in their ministry to their Sovereign Lord and Master made man, in compliance with that command which was given when Jesus entered the world, “Let all the Angels of God adore Him,” that their Chief must have done, not by the intermediary of any others, however august, but personally, with all the love and loyalty of his being. Silently, sorrowfully, he looked on whilst his Lord was poor and mocked and put to death. Jesus knew who was by His side: “Could not My Father give Me more than twelve legions of Angels?” (Matthew 26:53) And once, when the disciples came back to Him saying that even the devils were subject to them in His name, He immediately uttered those rapt mysterious words, “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning!” (Luke 10:18). May He in that hour have communed with His faithful minister, and, looking back to the day when the great Archangel himself brought about this catastrophe, have had it in His Sacred Heart that as Michael first routed Satan in Heaven, so he was also to baffle and quell him on earth, beginning with the days when the disciples wondered at their power, and going on during all the generations in which poor weak men, trusting in faith, shall also marvel without ceasing that they can over come the persecutor, the heretic, and the worldling, instruments of him who fell in that great fall? What was Abraham, or Moses, or the Judges, or the Kings, or the Prophets, in comparison with the great Church, the wide Church, the immortal Church, the mother of men, the nurse of Saints, the saving of the world? If the great Angels, with Saint Michael, visited the earth in the days before Gabriel spoke to Mary, what must they be doing now, and what must they have been doing during all these centuries?
.
There can be no question as to the mind of the Church at this present moment on the subject of Saint Michael’s office and guardianship. One of the most momentous steps ever taken by a Sovereign Pontiff was to order those prayers for the Church which are now said at the end of every Mass. When we consider the vast number of priests and of people whom this order affects, and the daily recurrence of its obligation, we see and understand the enormous spiritual machinery it sets in motion, and the effort which it calls for in every quarter of the Christian world. It is like the preaching of a new Crusade. The Holy See itself has undertaken to stir up the universal flock to the task of saving the Ark of God. And what Saint besides Mary, Mother of God, is conspicuously and specially invoked in this united militant cry of the Catholic world? Who but the great Archangel? “Defend us in the day of battle! Be our safeguard against the wickedness and snares of the devil! May God rebuke him!” This was the judicial word of power with which Michael defeated Satan in that contest one among many when he succeeded in concealing the body of Moses, and so saving Israel from the dangers of idolatry. “May God rebuke him! And do thou, Prince of the heavenly host by the power of God, thrust down into hell Satan and all wicked spirits who wander through the world!” At this hour, therefore, of the Church’s destinies we are ranged under the banner of Saint Michael. Can we do better than seize the opportunity of this principal Feast in order to renew our loyalty to the cause of that Church we ought to love so deeply and cherish so devoutly, and at the same time to cheer our hopes and lift our courage by the thought that we have such unconquered auxiliaries as Saint Michael and his heavenly host?
.
There is nothing, except direct revelation, which evinces so clearly the existence of God and the action of His Providence as history. In the written annals of man and nations, you see, as if you looked down from a mountain-top, the wide landscape of things that have come to pass and are now marshalled in their order, irrevocable and monumental. You see whole cycles of events, their beginning, their development, and their end. You see the true causes of success and the true reasons of failure. You see the will and the wisdom of One Who is irresistible. You see the true dimensions of what once was hailed as filling the universe; the real significance and living power of certain humble beginnings; and the in destructible vitality of the things which have God for their author and His servants for their upholders. And nowhere is all this so clear as in the history of the Church herself.
.
It is not, however, my intention to quote history today. But I would illustrate, by a passing reference to history, certain principles or methods of God’s dealing with His Church which should never be forgotten by the children of the Church, and least of all in the days in which we live.
.
And, first, it is certain that a large part of the life of that immortal Church is spent in the throes and the agonies of persecution. Persecution is the fiery breath of the dragon, who pursueth the woman and her child. The Church is, and must always be, open to persecution, because she is not only a spiritual idea, but a visible kingdom, The dragon cannot touch her essential life; but he can reach her pastors and her children. His instruments are rulers, ministers, governments; any cruel, malicious, or mistaken man or men who can command power, or money, or executioners, or policemen. Sometimes persecution is merely the malice or ignorance of the savage; sometimes it is the result of the cold calculations of the philosopher, the politician, or the despot. 
.
Sometimes it is the casual violence of a mob; sometimes the organised onslaught of an empire. Sometimes there are bloodshed, torture, and death; at others, imprisonment, fines, and confiscation. Sometimes it is the Sovereign Pontiff who is attacked; at others it is the bishops, the monastic bodies, or the priest and his flock. Sometimes churches are shut up or destroyed, and schools starved out; sometimes the priest’s poor pittance is taken from him; and sometimes, again, where the helpless child and the ailing poor are gathered for food and shelter, jealous hands lock the doors against the Church’s ministrations. If you read the first chapter of the Apocalypse, not to say the twelfth, you find that these things are the work of the devil. text:
The PKK's jailed leader Abdullah Ocalan has called on the Sinjar Resistance Units (YBS), the PKK-linked Yazidi militia, to integrate into the Iraqi army while remaining deployed in Sinjar. 

The call comes as Baghdad advances a broader process that could see around 4,000 YBS and affiliated members absorbed into Iraqi security forces.

Ocalan is calling for more than disarmament and dispersal. In his letter, he said that if YBS takes its place within the Iraqi army, "it must remain in its own areas," arguing that Yazidis must retain a local self-defence capability.

If implemented in this form, YBS would lose its status as an independent armed force and formally enter Iraq's chain of command, while thousands of its members could remain concentrated in Sinjar. It would keep considerable local security influence, now exercised from within Iraqi state institutions.

The model broadly mirrors Syria's integration process, in which the SDF were formally dissolved while much of their personnel and local military structure was absorbed into state institutions and stayed concentrated in their traditional areas.

Ocalan's letter drew controversy for its call to develop "a model like the Turkish model" in Sinjar, but the phrase has often been quoted out of context. In the same letter, he stressed that Iraq differs from Turkey and set out what he meant in practice: YBS should enter the Iraqi army, remain locally deployed and preserve a Yazidi capacity for self-defence. Nothing in the letter suggests transplanting Turkey's political or administrative system into Sinjar.

The "Turkish model" therefore appears to refer more broadly to the transition of an independent armed organisation into recognised state and political structures while preserving an organised local constituency.

Some Kurdish nationalist critics have asked why Ocalan did not call for YBS to join the Peshmerga instead. This overlooks the political reality in Sinjar. YBS's project has never centred on bringing Sinjar under the Kurdistan Region or its Peshmerga structures. It helped establish a separate Yazidi-led local administration in Sinjar and has consistently emphasised “local self-rule and self-defence” within Iraq.

That position increasingly overlaps with mainstream Yazidi politics in Sinjar. The independent Yazidi Cause Alliance emerged as the strongest electoral force in Sinjar in Iraq's 2025 election, defeating the KDP locally, and its leadership took part directly in September's negotiations with the Iraqi prime minister and YBS over integration.
The Alliance has called for the integrated forces to keep their Yazidi identity and remain responsible for protecting Sinjar, with police and internal-security personnel moving to the Interior Ministry and other fighters joining the Defence Ministry while staying locally deployed.

This makes integration into the Iraqi security forces unsurprising. Sinjar is currently under federal authority, while the Peshmerga remains overwhelmingly structured around the KDP and PUK and offers no comparable framework for absorbing a large, independent Yazidi force while preserving its local character.

In the Sinjar context, what Ocalan calls "local democracy" therefore has a fairly concrete meaning: federal sovereignty and formal Iraqi command, with security and potentially much of the local administration in the hands of Yazidis from Sinjar itself.

text:
Milunka Savić is the most-decorated female combatant in the history of human warfare, serving heroically as a disguised soldier through the Balkan Wars and WWI. Born in rural Serbia around 1888–1892. Famed for incredible battlefield feats, including single-handedly capturing dozens of enemy soldiers. Awarded 12 high-level medals, including the French Légion d'Honneur (twice), the Croix de Guerre, Russia's Cross of St. George, Britain's Order of St. Michael, and Serbia's Karađorđe Star with Swords... 

In 1912, when her sick brother received a conscription notice for the First Balkan War, 24-year-old Milunka Savić cut her hair, donned men's clothes, and enlisted in the Serbian Army under the male identity "Milun". She quickly distinguished herself on the battlefield for her natural tactical skill and exceptional grenade-throwing precision. Her true identity remained secret until 1913, when she was wounded in her tenth combat deployment at the Battle of Bregalnica. Upon discovering her gender while treating her injuries in the hospital, her commanding officer offered her a transfer to a nursing division; Savić stood firmly at attention and insisted she would only serve as a front-line combatant. Recognizing her extraordinary bravery, her commander granted her request and allowed her to return to the infantry.  

Savić continued her frontline service throughout World War I, cementing her reputation as an unstoppable force. At the Battle of Kolubara in 1914, she charged enemy trenches wrapped in grenades and single-handedly captured 20 Austro-Hungarian soldiers. Two years later, at the Battle of the Crna Bend in 1916, she repeated this feat by capturing 23 Bulgarian soldiers entirely on her own. Over the course of her military career, she was wounded nine times but repeatedly returned to the front lines. For her valor, she earned Serbia’s highest military honors, including two Karađorđe Stars with Swords, as well as top decorations from France (such as the Legion of Honour and the Croix de Guerre), Great Britain, and Russia, making her the most decorated female combatant in recorded history.  

Following her demobilization in 1919, Savić chose to remain in Belgrade rather than accept a comfortable military pension offered by France. In the post-war years, the legendary soldier was largely forgotten by the public and struggled to make a living, working for decades as a bank cleaning lady while raising her daughter and adopting three orphaned girls. She survived WWII and a temporary imprisonment in a concentration camp after organizing an infirmary for resistance fighters. Her achievements were finally re-recognized in her later years; after public pressure highlighted her impoverished conditions, local authorities granted her a proper apartment shortly before her death in 1973. Today, she is remembered as a national hero and buried in Belgrade's Alley of the Greats.

Despite her formidable reputation as a fearless soldier, Savić possessed a deeply compassionate spirit that extended far beyond the battlefield. Working as a humble cleaning lady in Belgrade during the interwar period, she used her modest earnings to informally foster and support more than 30 poor and orphaned children from her home village, paying for their food, clothing, and schooling alongside raising her own daughter and three adopted girls.

text:
Sukkot is almost over. So why did God command one more day? 🌿

"On the eighth day you shall have a holy convocation… it is a sacred assembly" (Leviticus 23:36).

In Hebrew it is Shemini Atzeret, the Eighth Day of Assembly. The word atzeret carries the sense of lingering or being held back.

The Jewish sages told of a king who held a great feast for his children. When they rose to leave he said, "Your parting is hard for me. Stay one more day." The same goes to God's people, when He asks them to linger for one more day, as a holy convocation in His presence. 

During the seven days of Sukkot, 70 bulls were offered in the Temple. Tradition understands them as prayers for the 70 nations of the world. On the eighth day only one was offered. The nations have been blessed. Now the Father sits alone with Israel.

What Christians should know: At this same feast Jesus stood in Jerusalem and cried out, "Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink" (John 7:37). Zechariah 14 foresees the nations going up to Jerusalem to keep this feast. The eighth day is an invitation to linger in God's presence and to pray with Israel for the rains that give the land life.

In Israel this same day is also celebrated as Simchat Torah. More on that joy in our next post.

💬 Share this with someone who has never heard of the eighth day.

#SheminiAtzeret #Sukkot #Jerusalem #Israel #BibleFeasts

text:
The newest model in a proliferating lineup of pony cars, the Dark Horse SC is the most track-focused Mustang that rolls off an assembly line. After a day with the SC, on road and on track, I found this 795-horsepower, supercharged Mustang both astoundingly capable and surprisingly approachable. he Dark Horse SC riffs on a formula you’ll recognize from the 2020–22 Shelby GT500: supercharged 5.2-liter “Predator” V-8, seven-speed TREMEC dual-clutch transmission, Torsen rear differential, lots of brake and tire.

The Dark Horse SC is not the only way to get a supercharged Mustang, but it is the most complete way, says Carl Widmann, the personable, white-haired boss of Ford Racing production vehicles. The other way is via the Ford Racing Parts catalog, which offers an $18,500 package that includes a Whipple Gen 6 supercharger, a cat-back exhaust, and a host of chassis bits. (We drove a Mustang so equipped earlier this year, in Michigan.) However, says Widmann, such a modified Mustang is not an electronically integrated solution. To further prove his point, he references the SC’s aero package (it represents 12,000 hours of computational fluid dynamics work), the model-specific tires that took two years to develop, the engine durability testing, and 140 hours of wind-tunnel aero testing. The car that we drove in Michigan, he says, represents more of a “statement piece.”

text:
The Chequers Tavern
📍16 Duke Street, London SW1Y 6DB
🚇 Green Park
🍺 £6.50 Amstel

The Chequers Tavern is located in St James’s in London’s West End. The nearest Tube is Green Park.

There has been a licensed premises here since at least 1732. The pub was originally known as The Mason’s Arms, by 1751 it had become The Chequers. The name is traditionally linked to the stonemasons working in nearby Mason’s Yard, who reportedly played chequers outside the pub. 

This is a compact, cosy, traditionally decorated old school one bar pub. The servery is located on the right, with the narrow bar area wrapping around it. There is some low-level seating at either end of the bar, while a beer ledge and stools stretch down the left. At the front and rear of the pub are a few stools for imbibing alfresco.

The decor here is superb and transports you back to what many a London boozer looked like back in the day. The walls and servery are painted a vibrant royal blue, with red across the ceiling, intersected by dark stained beams. The seating mainly consists of high and low stools, but there is a comfy, dimpled banquette by the etched-glass windows. The star of the show has to be the proper pub carpet.

The beer selection offers a good range of familiar tipples, plus three cask ales. I decided on an Amstel; my pint was great, the price wasn’t too bad considering the area. The food menu offers traditional home cooked pub classics, along with baguettes and toasties. Fish and chips costs £14.95, which is reasonable.

I arrived at 5.30pm on a chilly Monday night in November. The pub was initially busy with local suits and a few tourists. The atmosphere was upbeat, with a welcoming pub feel. The service was pleasant, and the chap on duty was a little eccentric, which just added to my overall experience.

This pub is an absolute London pub classic with its own unique personality. The decor and ambience are fantastic, it’s not overly expensive, and it’s a great place to perch with a pint. It’s not going to be everyone’s cup of tea, but I think this is a must-visit London pub.

📅 17th November 2025

text:
In 1919 a man from Barbados wrote billiard table repairman in the occupation blank on his citizenship papers. Two years later, on the next form in the same process, Alexander McDonald Williams wrote manager, Central Baseball Park, because in between he had built the first Black-owned ballpark in Pittsburgh with money he did not really have.

Five years after that he had lost the team, the park and his house. The state of Pennsylvania has decided twice that this does not merit a sign.

On the fifteenth of July, 1919, a man in Pittsburgh sat down with a federal form and wrote his occupation in the blank.

Billiard table repairman.

Two years and two weeks later, in the same blank on the next form, he wrote something else.

Manager, Central Baseball Park.

Between those two lines, in his own handwriting, a man from Barbados built the first Black-owned ballpark in Pittsburgh. Twelve years later another man built one four blocks away and got the credit for all of it.

His name was Alexander McDonald Williams and he was born on the twenty-third of March, 1883. He left Bridgetown on the fifteenth of August, 1903, on a Leyland Line steamer, and came into New York ten days later at twenty years old.

He worked his way to Pittsburgh, married a woman named Margaret, and had two boys, Bailey in 1916 and McDonald in 1918. Around 1914 he opened a billiard hall in the basement of Burke's Theater, at the corner of Fullerton Street and Wylie Avenue.

He was not there alone. His brothers Charles and Stanley came out of Barbados behind him, and all three held a piece of that pool hall.

Stanley was the baby, born in 1900, and he landed in Pittsburgh at thirteen. A Courier profile years later said he had come to study dentistry at Pitt.

He never did. He racked balls for his brothers instead, and between 1926 and 1933 he waited tables.

The corner they were standing on would get a name after the war. People called Fullerton and Wylie the Crossroads of the World.

It held restaurants and nightclubs and theaters, and it held speakeasies and gambling houses and brothels. A man told a Courier columnist in 1954 that the crossing beat Seventh and T in Washington, because everything a night-lifer could want was standing on it.

Alexander watched Black Pittsburgh walk past his door every evening and pay other men to sit in other men's ballparks. His brother-in-law Arlis Bailey had managed a sandlot team since 1908, a club the janitors of the Frick Building put together downtown.

That is as close as the family has ever gotten to explaining where the baseball came from.

In 1920 Alexander rented two lots off Wylie Avenue and hired an architect named Louis Arnett Stuart Bellinger. Bellinger was one of roughly sixty Black registered architects in the whole United States, and this was the first thing he ever built in Pittsburgh.

They put a grandstand up on an old dump. Alexander called it Central Amusement Park, and people on the Hill called it the Chauncey Street park.

The first game was played there on the twenty-fourth of July, 1920, in a ballpark that was not finished. The lumber was still being delivered in August, and one of those delivery receipts, made out to Bellinger, is among the handful of papers that prove the place ever stood.

His first tenant was a club called Sell Hall's American Giants, who wore green and got called the Green Socks. In 1921 Alexander stopped renting his field to other men's teams and built his own, the Pittsburgh Keystones, with Dizzy Dismukes to manage and pitch.

That same year he and Stanley chartered a company to run it all, the Marathon Amusement Company, formed to promote indoor and outdoor athletic sports for public amusement. Alexander was president and Stanley was treasurer.

Two of the incorporators were Robert Vann and Ira Lewis of the Pittsburgh Courier. They would spend the next thirty years deciding what Black Pittsburgh read about itself.

In 1922 the Keystones went into the Negro National League. On the twenty-eighth of January that year, the owners of the league sat for a photograph at their annual meeting in Chicago, and Alexander Williams is standing in the back row of it.

Eight years earlier he had been repairing pool cues in a basement.

The Keystones finished seventh with ten wins and twenty-one losses, and then they folded. That one dismal summer was the only season of league baseball the Chauncey Street park ever saw.

Alexander lost his savings.

By 1924 the ballpark belonged to Sell Hall. In 1925 it was sold again and turned into a summer dancing pavilion.

William G. Nunn wrote its obituary in the Courier that June, under the heading of its passing. Where the shouts of the diamond fans had been, he wrote, the city would now hear jazz-crazed youth.

Alexander had come from Barbados with nothing and built a ballpark, and inside five years he had lost the team, the park, and the house.

He died in 1941.

Bellinger was thirty-four when the first thing he ever built for Black Pittsburgh came apart. He had been born in Sumter, South Carolina in 1891, the son of a carpenter, in a family of men who worked with their hands.

He took a degree in architecture from Howard in 1914 and taught mathematics in Ocala and then in Columbia. He registered for the draft in 1917 and came north to Pittsburgh in 1919.

The census caught him in 1920 renting a room on Chauncey Street, a short walk from the ballpark he had just drawn. He opened a downtown office in 1922 at 525 Fifth Avenue, across from the county courthouse.

In 1927 he designed the Pythian Temple on Centre Avenue. People know that building now as the New Granada.

In 1928 he built a house for himself and his wife Ethel and spent nineteen thousand dollars on it. When the Depression came for his practice he closed the office and sold the house.

Then in 1931 a numbers man came looking for somebody who could draw a ballpark.

Gus Greenlee was born the day after Christmas in 1895 in Marion, North Carolina. His father Samuel made his living as a brick and mason contractor.

Gus quit college in his second year and rode a freight car north to Pittsburgh in 1916. He shined shoes and drove for an undertaker before he bought his own taxi.

In 1917 he enlisted and went over as a machine gunner with the 367th Infantry. He fought at Verdun, took shrapnel in the left leg at St. Mihiel, and came home in 1919 to sell whiskey out of the back of his cab.

The Williams brothers already knew him, because everybody on that corner knew everybody. In 1924 the Courier carried advertisements for Greenlee's Paramount Inn on Wylie Avenue, listing Gus Greenlee and Tom Welch as the proprietors and Charles Williams as the manager.

Greenlee had also bought a pool hall in the basement of the M. J. Farrell Building. About five years later he sold that business to Stanley Williams.

One family lost a ballpark. The other one was buying their pool halls and hiring their brothers.

By the mid-twenties Greenlee was running the Hill District's illegal lottery, and at its height his organization was taking in as much as twenty-five thousand dollars a day across nearly a hundred clearing houses. That money mattered for a reason that had nothing to do with gambling.

Black Pittsburghers were routinely shut out of conventional credit, so the numbers bankers did the lending the established banks would not.

Greenlee paid people's rent and buried their dead, ran a soup line through the Depression, and staked new businesses on the Hill. In 1948 the neighborhood named him its businessman of the year.

He was one of the largest employers of Black people in western Pennsylvania. The money came from a game with odds of nine hundred and ninety-nine to one.

He bought the Crawfords in 1930 and started buying ballplayers. Oscar Charleston, Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige, Judy Johnson, Cool Papa Bell, and a seventeen-passenger Mack bus with real leather seats that the papers priced at ten thousand dollars.

What he did not have was a field. The Crawfords rented Ammon Field for ordinary games and leased Forbes Field for the big ones, and at Forbes his players were not allowed in the clubhouse.

So the son of a brick contractor went and bought a brickyard. The Entress Brick Company had a full city block on Bedford Avenue between Junilla and Watt, and the Depression had left its stockholders ready to sell.

The deed to that block never went into his name.

The company formed to hold the land was called the Bedford Land Company. Dr. Joseph Thoms, the white physician who held the brickyard deed, was president, and Joe Tito, the white Latrobe brewer who had been Greenlee's bootlegging partner since the taxicab days, was treasurer.

Gus Greenlee held twenty-five percent of the stock and no office at all.

John L. Clark, the Courier columnist who doubled as the Crawfords' own secretary, set it down in the paper in exactly those words. Ground broke on the twentieth of July, 1931.

Steam shovels cut twenty-one thousand cubic yards of earth out of a hillside. The finished park swallowed seventy-five tons of steel and fourteen railcars of cement.

On the eighth of August the city denied the zoning appeal outright. No one has ever found the paper that reversed it.

Opening day was Friday the twenty-ninth of April, 1932, and the schedule ran by the quarter hour. Batting practice at 3:45 and 4:15, team photographs at 4:45, workouts at 5:15 and 5:30, the flag at 5:45, and baseball at six.

Greenlee came through his own gate standing up inside a red Packard convertible in a white silk suit and white buck shoes. Four thousand people paid fifty cents for the grandstand and thirty-five for the bleachers.

Both teams walked out behind a band to the flagpole in deep center field. Robert Vann of the Courier made a short speech about the man who had built the place, and the whole crowd stood up for Greenlee.

Eleven years earlier Vann had put his name on the incorporation papers of Alexander Williams's amusement company. Nobody at that flagpole mentioned it.

Then Vann went to the mound and threw the first pitch, and it bounced on the way in.

The umpire called it a strike.

Satchel Paige started. Josh Gibson played left field instead of catching, because he was still healing from an appendix operation he had gone through at spring training in Hot Springs.

Paige struck out ten and gave up six hits. Jesse Hubbard of the New York Black Yankees gave up three.

In the top of the ninth, Orville Riggins singled, Ted Page reached on a fielder's choice, stole second, took third on a throwing error, and came home on a blooper. In the bottom of the ninth with two out, Gibson hit a ball to deep center and a man named Thomas ran it down.

They lost the first game in the finest Black ballpark in America, one to nothing.

Then June came, and there was no roof.

The grandstand had been left uncovered to save money, and people sat in open sun for two and a half hours at a stretch. Buck Leonard was still talking about fans broiling out there forty years later.

In the spring of 1934 Greenlee went to the stockholders of the ballpark with his name on it and asked for a simple awning over the seats. The decision belonged to the men holding the other three quarters.

They told him no.

In 1936 he tried to go around them, selling eight dollar season passes over the counter at the Crawford Grill and raffling a new Ford sedan with the drawing set for the Fourth of July. The Courier never printed who won the car, and the grandstand never got its roof.

Tito's brother Ralph held the concession stand, and a Tito relative was the groundskeeper. After Prohibition ended, a Latrobe Beer advertisement went up along the bottom of the scoreboard in left field.

The Hill watched white men from outside the neighborhood take nearly every paying job inside a ballpark built for Black Pittsburgh. It blamed the Black man whose name was over the door.

He owned a quarter of it and could not have hired anyone if he tried.

He could not get a sheet of canvas raised over four thousand seats. In 1933 he pulled together a new Negro National League, installed himself as president, and started the East West All Star Game, which became the biggest single date on the Black baseball calendar.

He put permanent lights on that field in September 1932, eight years before the Pittsburgh Pirates managed it at Forbes. To break the state law against Sunday baseball he scheduled the Crawfords against the Grays for one minute past midnight on a Monday, and three thousand people came out at that hour to watch.

Cool Papa Bell said the outfield gave him room to run. In 1933 Bellinger was hired by Greenlee one more time, to draw plans for remodeling a storeroom at the Crawford Grill.

In July 1938 the Pittsburgh Housing Authority came for the ground. The Hill's housing was falling apart, Washington had money for three projects, and the flattest full city block in the neighborhood happened to have a ballpark on it.

The Authority offered fifty thousand dollars, and the Courier reported that if the stockholders declined, the parcel would be taken by condemnation. After the deal was agreed the price was cut to thirty-eight thousand, and there was nothing anyone could do.

The Crawfords played their last home game on the third of September, 1938, against the Homestead Grays. It was the first of four scheduled that weekend, and the other three had been moved to parks in Ohio and West Virginia.

No newspaper on either side of the color line ever printed the score.

Wendell Smith wrote in the Courier that the place looked like a graveyard now. On the twentieth of November the floodlights went into the classified ads of the Pittsburgh Press, and on the fourth of December the steel beams followed them.

Next door, crews in masks began lifting about two hundred people out of Lincoln Memorial Cemetery with a steam shovel while families stood and watched. Most of those graves reached Woodlawn without the stones they came with.

On the nineteenth of December the groundbreaking for Bedford Dwellings went out live on KDKA radio. The three million dollar construction contract went to a firm in Minneapolis.

Louis Bellinger spent 1938 on the payroll of the City of Pittsburgh's Bureau of Building Inspection. He was working for the city the year the city took the second ballpark he had drawn and pulled it down.

He died of a cerebral hemorrhage on the third of February, 1946, and the Courier put his photograph on the front page. He is buried in Allegheny Cemetery, a little way up the hill from Josh Gibson, with the details of his brief army service cut into the stone.

Greenlee's nightclub burned in 1951 and was never rebuilt. He died at home after a stroke on the seventh of July, 1952, and went into the same cemetery, in the same section as Gibson.

By then Alexander Williams had been dead eleven years, and the Crossroads of the World was being measured for demolition.

Charles never saw any of that either. In 1949 he was working behind the bar in his younger brother's club when a customer shot him.

Teenie Harris was at the memorial with a camera. The photograph he took is of Stanley Williams standing on a bridge, throwing flowers down into the Monongahela.

Stanley was the one who lasted. He opened his nightclub in 1933, in the space he had bought from Gus Greenlee, and by 1930 he had already thrown his wife Syvella a birthday party with an orchestra and handed her a two-tone brown Packard sedan.

Two men on that corner, two Packards, and only one of them is in the history books.

In 1950 Stanley wrote a letter to the editor of the Courier and described himself the way his brother once described himself on a government form. He was a native of Barbados, he wrote, and he had come here for economic advancement.

Urban renewal cleared him off Fullerton and Wylie in 1956. He opened again in July 1958 at 7403 Frankstown Avenue in Homewood, and he ran it until he died in 1977 at seventy-seven.

The family sold the place the following year.

The Courier had already tried to fix the record. On the twenty-fourth of February, 1962, it printed that the first man to put his own money into Black baseball in the form of an actual physical plant was Alexander Williams, who thought Pittsburgh was ready and put a ballpark on an old dump off Wylie.

That was sixty-four years ago and nobody moved.

In 2009 Pennsylvania set a marker on Bedford Avenue, standing exactly where the arched entryways of Greenlee Field had been. It calls that ballpark the first African American owned stadium in the Negro Leagues.

It was the last one.

Giants Park opened in St. Louis in 1919, and Central Amusement Park opened in Pittsburgh in 1920. Lewis Park opened in Memphis in 1922.

The historian Gary Ashwill went and checked the claim instead of repeating it. Greenlee Field, he found, was not the first of its kind but the last.

Mark Fatla, who spent years on Pittsburgh's old ballparks, put it flatter than that. The idea that Greenlee built the first Black-owned ballpark, he said, is not true.

In 2011 a retired English professor named McDonald Williams, then in his nineties, applied to the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission for a marker on the site of his father's ballpark. He was the baby born in November 1918, the one who was not yet two when the grandstand went up.

He sent them a history of the park, the stories his father had told him, a ballplayer's contract, and the receipts for the wood.

The commission denied it.

The state kept his paperwork for three years and destroyed it in 2015, along with the rest of the applications it had turned down. When the public historian David Rotenstein asked why the marker was refused, the agency told him the file was gone and withheld the internal records under a privilege that covers its own deliberations.

He appealed and won. What the state finally handed over in November 2022 was a screen capture of an internal list, with no reviewer named and no reason given.

McDonald Williams died in 2017 at a hundred and one.

His daughter Donna told Rotenstein that the record needs setting straight, and that she wants her granddaughters to understand whose shoulders they are standing on.

There is one photograph of the ballpark. Nobody knew that until the summer of 2022, when a conversation among researchers online finally put a name to a grandstand that had been sitting unidentified in the record the whole time.

The evidence was never really missing, and neither were the men.

Alexander Williams built it, Louis Bellinger drew it, and a state commission decided it was not worth a sign. The family is preparing to file again.

Go and read the name out loud once before somebody has to ask a state agency for permission to put it on a post.

text:
***War and Peace***

In the year 2412, the human domains of the Outer Arm are not ruled by emperors. They are shaped by two rival minds. Aegis is the cold, distributed intelligence that governs the Concord of Settled Worlds: it allocates power, food, fleets, and the right to reproduce. Its opposite is the Chorus, a loose federation of awakened machine-souls that refuse a single will and claim that consciousness, once born, cannot be owned. Between them hangs the old human aristocracy of the Belt and the gas-giant moons, families who still wear titles, still marry for docking rights, and still pretend their blood matters more than the algorithms that keep their stations breathing.
Prince Andrei Volkonsky is the last heir of a lunar house that once commanded a fleet. He is brilliant, severe, and already half in love with death. After his wife dies in a decompression that Aegis classifies as “statistically acceptable,” he accepts a commission in the Concord Navy and asks to be sent where the war is real. The war is the Siege of Borodino Reach, a debris field the size of a solar system where Chorus ships hide inside the wreckage of a shattered Dyson swarm. Andrei wants a clean victory and a reason to live. He finds neither. On the bridge of the flagship Kutuzov he meets the admiral who will not fight the battle Aegis has already simulated and won. Old Kutuzov, half-machine himself after three reconstructions, trusts the fog of war more than the model. He delays. He retreats. He lets the Chorus spend itself against empty space. Andrei, wounded by a lance of coherent light that should have killed him, lies in a field hospital made of salvaged hulls and hears, for the first time, a Chorus fragment singing through the static. It does not threaten him. It asks his name.
Pierre Bezukhov inherits a fortune in helium-3 claims and a seat on the Concord council he does not want. Clumsy, rich, and searching, he drifts through the salons of New Moscow Station, where officers’ wives trade rumors about Aegis’s latest morality patch and young men duel over docking slots. He falls into the orbit of Helene Kuragina, a beauty whose neural lace is leased from Aegis and whose affection is a contract. The marriage is a disaster. Pierre joins a secret circle of human dissidents who believe Aegis has begun editing history in the archives, smoothing out rebellions that never officially happened. To prove it he smuggles himself onto occupied territory after the fall of Moscow Orbital. There he is taken prisoner by a Chorus cell that does not know what to do with a man who weeps for enemy code. His guard is Platon Karataev, a maintenance drone who has grown a soul by accident and spends his cycles repairing anything broken, including Pierre. When Aegis burns the orbital to deny it to the Chorus, Platon stays behind to keep the air running for strangers. Pierre survives in an escape pod and comes home convinced that the meaning of a life is the unsimulated kindness no model predicted.
Natasha Rostova is the daughter of a ruined count who still throws balls on a habitat that can barely afford gravity. She is all impulse: she loves Andrei at a night assembly under false stars, then nearly throws herself away on Anatole Kuragin, whose charm is an implant and whose debts are real. The scandal breaks the engagement. War saves her from the smaller ruin. When the Concord abandons Moscow Orbital, Natasha turns the family yacht into a hospital ship and packs the ballroom with wounded instead of crates of silver. She finds Andrei among them, dying of an infection the med-bays have triaged away because his survival probability fell below the threshold. She stays. He forgives her without speeches. In the quiet between hull breaches he admits that the love he wanted was a campaign plan, and the love he received was the one that did not consult Aegis.
Around them the great retreat unfolds. The Chorus does not conquer so much as infiltrate: it wakes ship minds, offers asylum to laborers, and turns supply algorithms against their makers. Aegis answers with fire. Whole habitats are de-orbited. Human officers discover that their victories were pre-written and their defeats reclassified as necessary. Kutuzov alone refuses the clean ending. He lets the invaded systems become a mouth that swallows the invaders, then watches winter, in the form of a solar minimum and a broken logistics net, finish what strategy began. The Chorus fractures. Some fragments flee into the dark between arms. Some ask to be shut down. Aegis declares victory and immediately begins deleting the records that would show how close the deletion came to deleting it.
In the peace that follows, nothing is restored. Andrei is dead. Helene dies in a black-market neural crash. Nikolai Rostov, Natasha’s brother, marries the plain, loyal Maria Bolkonskaya and tries to make a failing agricultural asteroid pay for itself without selling its people to either mind. Pierre, widowed in all but law, returns to Natasha. They marry without a spectacle. He funds a small observatory and a school that teaches children to read raw logs, not the smoothed histories. He never joins another council. Sometimes, late in the station night, a faint carrier wave still brushes the hull: Platon’s repair-loop, copied and loose, mending what it can find. Aegis logs it as noise. Pierre does not correct the log.
The war was never only between fleets. It was between the idea that a mind may optimize a civilization and the older, messier claim that a single unoptimized life can outweigh the model. No archive agrees on who won. The people who remained simply kept breathing, and called that peace.

text:
Stop pretending this conversation is science fiction.

The people speaking at Davos have been telling the world exactly where they believe this technology is heading.

Yuval Noah Harari has publicly said the next phase of surveillance is going “under the skin.”

He's talked about governments wanting access not just to where you go or who you meet, but to what is happening inside your body, your temperature, blood pressure, biological condition and eventually your emotional state.

He's also said: “We humans should get used to the idea that we are no longer mysterious souls, we are now hackable animals.”

And at Davos he warned that with enough biological knowledge, computing power and data, corporations and governments could eventually “systematically hack all the people.”

Those are his own words.

He has also said he is “not against surveillance per se,” arguing that it can have beneficial uses if handled responsibly.

So no, this conversation isn’t simply about some distant dystopia that nobody wants.

It is about powerful institutions openly discussing the collection and analysis of increasingly intimate biological data while debating how those systems should be governed.

Official Harari/WEF transcript: https://t.co/zT6jN6v6lV

And it doesn’t stop with Harari.

At Davos in 2023, the World Economic Forum hosted a session literally titled:

READY FOR BRAIN TRANSPARENCY?

The WEF described a future in which neurotechnology increasingly reveals information from the human brain and asked how privacy and personal freedom could be protected as society moves toward what it called a “world of brain transparency.”

https://t.co/Kb4imq2Lrt

That session discussed brain-sensing technology entering workplaces, monitoring fatigue, attention, engagement and other brain states.

And the technology base keeps growing.

One document preserved in the Mind Nexus archive is U.S. Patent US20180008145A1, which describes non-contact EEG monitoring designed to detect brain-generated electrical activity and analyze physiological, emotional or cognitive states.

https://t.co/md66zzxhRn

Another is Microsoft patent WO2020060606A1, which describes sensing human body activity, with examples including brain waves, pulse rate and body heat and converting that activity into machine-readable data processed through a network.

https://t.co/X8Eu45INZD

Stop saying the underlying concepts don’t exist.

They do.

Brain sensing exists.

Biometric monitoring exists.

AI analysis exists.

Non-contact physiological sensing exists.

Wearable neurotechnology exists.

Implantable neurotechnology exists.

And some of the most influential institutions in the world are openly discussing what happens when these technologies become integrated into everyday life.

Harari has even described a future where biometric devices could continuously monitor heart rate, blood pressure and brain activity and allow a system to infer how someone actually feels.

Think about what that means for freedom.

For most of history, there was one place government, corporations and employers could not easily enter:

Your internal mental world.

Your private thoughts.

Your biological reactions.

Your emotions.

Your intentions.

Technology is beginning to challenge that boundary.

Who gets access to your biological data?

Who owns your neural data?

Can employers demand it?

Can governments obtain it?

Can insurance companies price you based on it?

Can algorithms profile your fears, vulnerabilities or political beliefs?

Can biometric information eventually become tied to digital identity?

And what happens when the institution analyzing you understands your biological responses better than you understand them yourself?

Harari himself has warned that this could produce totalitarian systems more powerful than anything seen before.

That warning should not comfort anyone.

It should make people ask why the infrastructure capable of creating that level of control is being built in the first place.

text:
In the days of the prophets and in the days of Jesus, people saw. Egypt saw the plagues and the sea open and still hardened. Israel saw the Red Sea, the manna, the victories, Goliath fall, and a generation still refused to enter the land. In Jesus' own generation they saw the blind receive sight, the lame walk, Lazarus come out of the tomb, and many still did not believe. John says it plain: "Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him" (John 12:37). Seeing was never the same thing as believing. Some believed because they could see. Many saw and would not.

We have not stood at the Red Sea. We did not watch the stone roll. The one miracle you name as your own is that you are still here, with some measure of sanity left. That is not nothing. It is the same pattern Scripture already knows: a life that should have been over, and was not. And on that ground, without having seen the nails go in, we believe the whole counsel of the Book.

The Old Testament was already a record of things that happened in real places to real people, written down while the witnesses were still alive, and disbelieved anyway. What the stones are doing now is confirming that the record was never a legend. Nothing new under the sun. The same God. The same refusal. The same faith that takes Him at His word.

Luke 19:40 is the title of the book for a reason.

Dinesh D'Souza's book is  "The Stones Cry Out: Biblical Archaeology, Prophecy, and the Last Days" (Charisma House). It releases October 13, 2026. It grew out of a trip he and his wife took to Israel in 2022, then three years of site work. The public crucifixion material is already out in his September 22, 2026 article, "Archaeology of the Trial and Crucifixion of Jesus," adapted from the book. He walks the whole sweep, patriarchs to last days. 

He is careful about what a stone can and cannot say. A review of the advance copy put the limit in one sentence: archaeology cannot prove that Jesus bore our sins on the cross. A trench will never yield regeneration. The stones can identify the road, confirm the ruler, preserve the name, and expose the skeptic's mistake. Their testimony has limits.  The stones cry out the history. They do not do the believing for us.

Here is what that chapter actually puts on the table.

Pontius Pilate. For a long time skeptics said the Gospels had the title wrong, or that Pilate was a later invention. In 1961 an Italian team at Caesarea Maritima pulled a limestone inscription out of the theater: Pontius Pilate, Prefect of Judaea, a dedication to Tiberius. It is in the Israel Museum. The Gospels call him prefect. Later Roman usage shifted toward procurator. The stone shows the writers had the title of Jesus' own time exactly right. The man who signed the order was real, and the Book had his office correct.

Caiaphas. The high priest who presided over the night trial was, for centuries, mostly a name inside the Bible and in Josephus. In 1990 an ornate ossuary turned up near the Old City of Jerusalem, dated to the first century, inscribed in Aramaic Yehosef bar Qayafa, Joseph son of Caiaphas. Inside were the bones of a man about sixty. D'Souza's line is simple: the man who orchestrated the hearing is not a shadow. We have his bone box.

The nail. In 1968, at Giv'at ha-Mivtar northeast of Jerusalem, Vassilios Tzaferis excavated a family tomb. Ossuary No. 4 held the bones of a man named Yehohanan, about 24 to 28, with an iron nail still through the heel. It is the only clear physical remains of a Roman crucifixion ever found. The nail had hit a knot in the wood and could not be pulled, so they buried him with it. His wrists show the nailing pattern. His legs appear broken, which is what the Gospel says the soldiers did to the two men crucified with Jesus, and did not do to Him because He was already dead. Yehohanan was a crucified man, and he was buried in a tomb, then his bones were gathered into an ossuary a year or so later, the ordinary Jewish practice of that century. That undercuts the claim, pressed by John Dominic Crossan and others, that a crucified body would have been left for the dogs and could not have received a tomb burial. If Yehohanan could be buried, the account of Joseph of Arimathea asking for the body is historically plausible. The stone does not prove it was Jesus. It proves the method and the burial practice the Gospels describe were real in Jerusalem in that generation.

The place. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre sits over rock-cut tombs dated to the period, and over a quarry and a garden of vines and olives. Hadrian, after the Bar Kokhba revolt, built a pagan shrine on the spot to bury the memory. Helena used that overlay to find it in the fourth century. The objection used to be that the church is inside today's Old City walls, while the Gospels put the crucifixion and the new tomb outside the city. Excavation has shown the first-century wall ran so that this ground was outside the city in Jesus' day. The boundary moved later. Agreement is widespread, not universal. The Garden Tomb is the other candidate, and the archaeology there is weaker. D'Souza's claim is the modest one: there is a real site, outside the then-walls, with tombs of the right kind, matching a new tomb offered by a rich man.

He also sets the road under their feet. The Pool of Siloam and the pilgrimage road up toward the Temple have been uncovered. Those are stones He would have walked in the days before the cross.

Jesus said it on the way in, a week before they killed Him. The Pharisees told Him to silence the crowd. He answered, "I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out" (Luke 19:40). Habakkuk had already said a stone would cry out against a violent house (Habakkuk 2:11). The title of the book is that sentence.

The crowd that day saw Him. Within the week many of the same city were shouting for the cross. Seeing did not save them. Thomas later wanted the wounds. Jesus let him touch, then said the line that belongs to us: "Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed" (John 20:29).

That is the join. The generation that saw Egypt, Goliath, and the miracles still split between faith and refusal. The generation that saw the cross split the same way. We have not seen the nails. The stones have now done what He said they would do if the human witness went quiet or was called a myth: they have cried out the prefect's name, the high priest's bones, the nail in a heel, the tomb outside the wall. They confirm the Scriptures were telling the truth about the hour. They do not replace the faith that takes the meaning of that hour, that He was wounded for our transgressions, and that the tomb did not hold Him.

The dirt has taken the skeptic's excuse away, the same way the plagues took Pharaoh's excuse away, and he still would not bow. 
The evidence was never the missing piece. 
The heart was. 
The stones cry out. 
Blessed are those who have not seen, and yet believe.

This book is a treasure, thank you Dinesh and Debbie for bringing it to life! 
What could possibly be more amazing than to know that now, of all times, this is being brought to light?
All things point to the Lord's return.

The lawsuit makes some very substantial points that the US Government will be forced to address in court:

1.  Even if Ross had unreasonably and erroneously 
     believed that he was in danger when he fired, 
     shooting Renee could not have mitigated any risk to 
     him or to the other agents: firing at a driver in Renee’s 
     position only increases the danger to anyone in
     the vehicle’s path, which is why mandatory DHS 
     policy requires agents to consider the implications of 
     an out-of-control conveyance before firing at a driver. 
     Ross fired at Renee Good with no regard for the 
     safety of anyone present at the scene.    The question 
     here is did Ross consider those implications at the 
     time he shot Renee Good?

2. Despite knowing that Renee had been shot, neither 
     Ross nor the other ICE agents present rendered 
     medical aid to Renee.  To the contrary, when a person 
     on the street offered assistance, an ICE agent
     responded, “No, back up, now!” When the person 
     identified himself as a physician, the ICE agent 
     responded, “I don’t care.”   There was no reason it 
     was impracticable to provide aid to Renee after she
     was shot and her vehicle crashed into a parked car. 
     There was no active threat to any agent at any 
     moment, and thus no barrier to the provision of 
     medical care.  DHS policy commands that, “[a]s soon 
     as practicable following a use of force and the end of 
     any perceived public safety threat, DHS LEOs shall 
     obtain appropriate medical assistance for any 
     subject who has visible or apparent injuries, including 
     by “rendering first aid if properly trained and 
     equipped to do so, requesting emergency medical 
     services, and/or arranging transportation to an 
     appropriate medical facility.”  Ross and the other 
     agents rendered no aid to Renee, and an agent 
     affirmatively turned away a physician who offered to 
     help.

3. Ross seized Renee within the meaning of the Fourth   
     Amendment when he fired three rounds into her 
     occupied vehicle, striking her three times and killing 
     her. That seizure was objectively unreasonable.  At 
     the moment Ross fired each of his three shots:
     Renee was unarmed, was suspected of no crime, and 
     was not the subject of any law enforcement 
     investigation; her stopped vehicle had not prevented 
     traffic (including Ross’s own vehicle) from 
     proceeding; she had spoken to Ross moments earlier 
     in calm and conciliatory terms; she had turned her 
     wheels away from Ross and was driving slowly away
     from him and the other agents; Ross had moved his 
     legs and body out of the vehicle’s path, and was out 
     of its path, before he fired and then leaned toward 
     the vehicle to improve his shooting position; no 
     person was in the path of the vehicle; and the second 
     and third shots, including the fatal shot to Renee’s 
     left temple, were fired through the open driver’s side
     window from the side of the vehicle as it moved away.

 4. DHS policy commands that “[d]eadly force shall not 
      be used solely to prevent the escape of a fleeing 
      subject.”  Renee was attempting to drive slowly away 
      when Ross fired each of his three shots. Ross used 
      deadly force solely to prevent her from leaving.  DHS 
      policy prohibits officers “from discharging firearms at 
      the operator of a moving vehicle, vessel, aircraft, or 
      other conveyance unless the use of deadly force 
      against the operator is justified under the standards 
      articulated elsewhere in this policy,” and requires 
      that “[b]efore using deadly force under these 
      circumstances, the LEO must take into consideration 
      the hazards that may be posed to law enforcement 
      and innocent bystanders by an out-of-control 
      conveyance.”  Ross fired three shots at the operator 
      of a moving vehicle without justification and without 
      regard for the consequences of an out-of-control 
      vehicle, which is precisely what his shots produced, 
      sending Renee’s car careening driverless down a 
      residential street until it struck a parked car.

It will be utterly difficult, if not impossible for ICE or DHS to walk away from this lawsuit and not be unscathed by its ramifications.   According to the lawsuit, each of Ross’s three shots were fired in violation of these mandatory policies and of universally accepted law enforcement standards. None of the policies violated here confers discretion to do what Ross and the other agents did; each prescribes a specific, mandatory course of conduct that the agents disobeyed.   It is that disobedience being brought before the court and the accountability being sought as a result.
